B. Plain-English Orientation

Jude now begins to show why the intruders’ judgment was “written beforehand” (v. 4). He reminds his readers of three well-known examples of God’s judgment:

  1. The wilderness generation. The people whom the Lord saved from Egypt were later destroyed when they refused to trust him (v. 5).
  2. The rebellious angels. Heavenly beings who abandoned their assigned place are now held in darkness until the final judgment (v. 6).
  3. Sodom and Gomorrah. The cities that pursued sexual immorality and “other flesh” now stand as a warning example of fiery judgment (v. 7).

Each example concerns people or beings who had a privileged position. Israel had been redeemed, the angels had a heavenly station, and Sodom and its neighbors lived in a fertile, well-watered land (Gen 13:10). Each abandoned that position through unbelief, rebellion, or immorality, and each came under judgment. The implication for the intruders, and for anyone tempted to follow them, is plain. Belonging to God’s people does not guarantee safety for those who turn grace into license.

Jude’s opening, “I intend to remind you,” matters too. He is not telling his readers anything new. He is calling to mind what they already know, in a way that makes its present relevance unmistakable.

C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

Ὑπομνῆσαι δὲ ὑμᾶς βούλομαι, εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ πάντα (Hypomnēsai de hymas boulomai, eidotas hymas hapax panta) — ‘I want to remind you, though you once knew all things’

The verb ὑπομνῆσαι (hypomnēsai), “to remind,” places Jude in the role of a teacher who refreshes memory rather than introducing novelty. That role fits his claim that the faith was delivered “once” (v. 3). The readers already “know all this,” literally “having known all things once” (εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ πάντα, eidotas hymas hapax panta). The participle εἰδότας (eidotas), “knowing,” is concessive: although you know. Second Peter uses the same courtesy, “I will always be ready to remind you about these things, although you have known [them]” (2 Pet 1:12, LSV).

The word ἅπαξ (hapax), “once” or “once for all,” has wandered in the manuscripts. In some it stands with “knowing” (“you who once for all knew all things”). In others it moves into the next clause (“the Lord, having once saved a people”). The SBLGNT and NA28 place it with “knowing,” and the LSV follows them: “you once having known all this.” The echo of v. 3 is deliberate: the faith was delivered once for all, and the readers once for all came to know it. What remains is to remember.

ὅτι Ἰησοῦς λαὸν ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου σώσας (hoti Iēsous laon ek gēs Aigyptou sōsas) — ‘that Jesus, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt’

This is one of the most remarkable phrases in the New Testament, and one of the most debated. The LSV reads “Jesus.” Many other translations read “the Lord” (WEB, ASV, WBS), while the BSB, like the LSV, reads “Jesus.” The difference is not a translation choice. It reflects a difference in the Greek manuscripts, explored in the deep dive below.

If “Jesus” is original, Jude says that Jesus himself, before his human birth, was the one who delivered Israel from Egypt. That is a striking claim, but not an isolated one. Paul says that the Israelites in the wilderness “were drinking of a spiritual rock following them, and the rock was the Christ” (1 Cor 10:4, LSV), and he warns, “neither may we tempt the Christ, as also certain of them tempted” (1 Cor 10:9, LSV). John says that Isaiah “saw His glory, and spoke of Him” (John 12:41, LSV), referring to Jesus and to Isaiah’s vision of the LORD in the temple. Jude’s reading belongs to the same early Christian conviction that the one revealed in Jesus was already active in Israel’s history.

The verb σώσας (sōsas), “having saved,” is the ordinary New Testament word for salvation. Its use here recalls the language of the exodus itself: “YHWH saves Israel out of the hand of the Egyptians in that day” (Exod 14:30, LSV). The exodus was Israel’s defining experience of salvation. Jude’s point depends on this. The people who were later destroyed were not outsiders; they had been saved.

τὸ δεύτερον τοὺς μὴ πιστεύσαντας ἀπώλεσεν (to deuteron tous mē pisteusantas apōlesen) — ‘afterward destroyed those who did not believe’

The phrase τὸ δεύτερον (to deuteron) literally means “the second time” or “secondly.” It can simply mean “afterward” (WEB: “afterward destroyed”), but its natural sense sets two acts side by side: first salvation, then destruction. The LSV keeps the literal “secondly.”

The reference is to the wilderness generation, which refused to enter the promised land after the report of the spies. God says to Moses, “Until when do they not believe in Me, for all the signs which I have done in its midst?” (Num 14:11, LSV). The sentence follows: “Your carcasses fall in this wilderness … who have murmured against Me” (Num 14:29, LSV). The aorist participle “those not having believed” (τοὺς μὴ πιστεύσαντας, tous mē pisteusantas) sums up the whole episode.

The warning in Jude’s first example is the most pointed of the three, because it concerns God’s own redeemed people. The intruders are inside the church. They share its meals and claim its grace. Jude’s readers might suppose that being among the saved is protection enough. The wilderness generation shows otherwise. The early church used this example often: Paul in 1 Corinthians 10 and the author of Hebrews (“we see that they were not able to enter in because of unbelief,” Heb 3:19, LSV). Jude uses it first in his series, perhaps for that reason.

ἀγγέλους τε τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν (angelous te tous mē tērēsantas tēn heautōn archēn) — ‘and the angels who did not keep their own position’

The LSV’s “messengers” translates ἀγγέλους (angelous), the ordinary word for “messengers” that, in a heavenly context, means “angels.” The LSV renders it consistently as “messengers,” but the context makes clear that heavenly beings are meant.

These angels “did not keep” (μὴ τηρήσαντας, mē tērēsantas) “their own principality” (τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχήν, tēn heautōn archēn). The word ἀρχή (archē) means “beginning,” “rule,” or “domain.” Here it most likely means the position of authority and the sphere of responsibility God had assigned them. The New Testament can call angelic powers “principalities” (ἀρχαί, archai; e.g., Rom 8:38; Eph 6:12). The LSV’s “principality” preserves that link. The WEB has “their first domain,” the ASV “their own principality,” and the BSB “their positions of authority.”

Note the first play on “keep.” The readers have been “kept” (v. 1). These angels did not “keep” what God had given them.

ἀλλὰ ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον (alla apolipontas to idion oikētērion) — ‘but abandoned their own dwelling’

The angels also “left” or “abandoned” (ἀπολιπόντας, apolipontas) “their proper dwelling” (τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον, to idion oikētērion). An οἰκητήριον is a habitation, a dwelling place.42 Paul uses the same rare word for the resurrection body: “our dwelling that is from Heaven” (2 Cor 5:2, LSV). The angels’ proper home was heaven. They left it.

Which angels, and what did they do? Jude assumes his readers know the story. As the deep dive below shows, they almost certainly did: it is the story of the “sons of God” who took human wives in Genesis 6:1–4, as expanded in the Jewish tradition preserved in 1 Enoch.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. οἰκητήριον: “a habitation: Ju 6; trop., II Co 5:2.”↩︎

εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν (eis krisin megalēs hēmeras desmois aidiois hypo zophon tetērēken) — ‘he has kept in everlasting chains under gloom for the judgment of the great day’

Now comes the second, ironic “keep.” The angels who did not keep their position, God “has kept” (τετήρηκεν, tetērēken, perfect tense: has kept and still keeps) under guard. Jude’s wordplay states a principle: those who refuse to keep their God-given place are themselves kept, for judgment.

  • “Eternal bonds” (δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις, desmois aidiois). The adjective ἀΐδιος (aidios), “everlasting,” appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in Rom 1:20, of God’s “eternal power.” The “bonds” are chains of imprisonment.
  • “Under darkness” (ὑπὸ ζόφον, hypo zophon). The word ζόφος (zophos) means deep gloom. In Homer it was used of the gloom of the underworld.43 It appears again in v. 13 (“the gloom of the darkness”) and in the parallel passages of 2 Peter (2:4, 17).
  • “Until [the] judgment of [the] great day” (εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας, eis krisin megalēs hēmeras). The imprisonment is not the final penalty. It is custody awaiting trial. The “great day” is the final judgment, the “day of the LORD” of the prophets.

These phrases match the language of 1 Enoch closely, as the deep dive shows.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ζόφος: “in Hom. the gloom of the under-world; hence, darkness, deep gloom … He 12:18, II Pe 2:4, 17, Ju 6, 13.”↩︎

ὡς Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα καὶ αἱ περὶ αὐτὰς πόλεις (hōs Sodoma kai Gomorra kai hai peri autas poleis) — ‘just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them’

The third example, Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα (Sodoma kai Gomorra), is the most famous. Genesis 19 tells how God “rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah brimstone and fire from YHWH, from the heavens; and He overthrows these cities, and all the circuit” (Gen 19:24–25, LSV). The “cities around them” (αἱ περὶ αὐτὰς πόλεις, hai peri autas poleis) are Admah and Zeboim, named in Deut 29:23 and Hos 11:8 as destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah. (Zoar, the fifth city of the plain, was spared at Lot’s request.)

τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις (ton homoion tropon toutois) — ‘in the same way as these’

The Greek τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις (ton homoion tropon toutois) means “in the same way as these.” Grammatically, “these” (τούτοις, toutois) is masculine, so it cannot refer to the cities (πόλεις, poleis), which is feminine. It most naturally refers to the nearest masculine plural, the angels of v. 6. The LSV makes this explicit by supplying “[messengers]” in brackets. (Some interpreters have suggested that “these” looks ahead to the intruders of v. 8, but the immediate sense is a comparison between Sodom and the angels.)

So the comparison is this: the cities sinned in the same way as the angels. In what way? The next phrases answer.

ἐκπορνεύσασαι (ekporneusasai) — ‘having given themselves over to sexual immorality’

The participle ἐκπορνεύσασαι (ekporneusasai) is a strengthened form of the common verb for sexual immorality, πορνεύω (porneuō). Its prefix ἐκ- (ek-) suggests going to excess, “giving oneself up to fornication.”44 The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it often describes Israel’s spiritual unfaithfulness, pictured as prostitution, but here, as the following phrase shows, the sense is literal.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ἐκπορνεύω: “strengthened form of πορνεύω, implying excessive indulgence; mid., to give oneself up to fornication: Ju 7.”↩︎

καὶ ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας (kai apelthousai opisō sarkos heteras) — ‘and having gone after other flesh’

The phrase ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας (apelthousai opisō sarkos heteras) means literally “having gone away after other (or different) flesh.” The traditional English rendering goes back to Tyndale’s “straunge flesshe” (TNT) and survives in Webster’s “strange flesh” (WBS) and the WEB’s “strange flesh” (WEB). The BSB has “perversion.” The LSV keeps the literal “other flesh.”

What is “other flesh”? This phrase has become a flashpoint in modern debates about sexuality, and it needs careful handling. The deep dive below sets out the evidence. In brief, the parallel Jude has just drawn with the angels (“in like manner to these”) strongly suggests the following: as the angels crossed the boundary between heaven and earth to unite with human women, so the men of Sodom sought sexual relations with beings of a different order, namely the angels who visited Lot (Gen 19:1–5). On this reading, “other flesh” refers above all to the attempted violation of the angelic visitors. Jude’s emphasis falls on the transgression of the created order.

πρόκεινται δεῖγμα (prokeintai deigma) — ‘are set out as an example’

The verb πρόκεινται (prokeintai), “they are set forth, displayed,” is in the present tense: the cities are still set forth. The noun δεῖγμα (deigma), another New Testament hapax, means “a thing shown,” a specimen or example, and here a warning example.45 Second Peter uses the related ὑπόδειγμα (hypodeigma): “having set [them as] an example to those about to be impious” (2 Pet 2:6, LSV).

Ancient readers believed they could still see the evidence. The region around the southern end of the Dead Sea, desolate, salty, and sulfurous, was identified with the ruined cities. The Wisdom of Solomon says of them: “even to this day the waste land that smoketh is a testimony, and plants bearing fruit that never come to ripeness: and a standing pillar of salt is a monument of an unbelieving soul” (Wis 10:7, Brenton).46 Third Maccabees says that God made the Sodomites “an example to after generations” (3 Macc 2:5, Brenton).

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. δεῖγμα: “(cl.) a thing shown, a specimen. = cl. παράδ- (cf. ὑπόδ-, II Pe 2:6), an example (a warning): Ju 7.”↩︎

  2. Wisdom 10:7 and 3 Maccabees 2:5, in Brenton’s English Septuagint (eBible.org). The Greek of 3 Macc 2:5 reads παράδειγμα τοῖς ἐπιγινομένοις καταστήσας (“having established [them as] an example to those coming after”).↩︎

πυρὸς αἰωνίου δίκην ὑπέχουσαι (pyros aiōniou dikēn hypechousai) — ‘undergoing the penalty of eternal fire’

The present participle ὑπέχουσαι (hypechousai), “undergoing,” also unique in the New Testament, means “to undergo, suffer” a penalty.47 The noun δίκη (dikē), “justice,” here means the execution of a sentence, punishment. The phrase πυρὸς αἰωνίου (pyros aiōniou) is “eternal fire,” which the LSV renders “continuous fire,” in keeping with its consistent treatment of αἰώνιος (aiōnios).

Two senses may be combined. The visible, smoking desolation of the region was understood as an ongoing display of the fire that destroyed the cities. That fire also pointed beyond itself to the “continuous fire that has been prepared for the Devil and his messengers” (Matt 25:41, LSV). The cities are an example because their temporal destruction prefigures final judgment. Jesus made the same connection: “it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city” (Matt 10:15, LSV).

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ὑπέχω: “to undergo, suffer: δίκην, Ju 7 (Soph., Eur., al.).”↩︎

D. Original-Language Investigation

Greek Transliteration Basic meaning In context Notes
ὑπομιμνῄσκω hypomimnēskō remind “I intend to remind you” Calling to mind the known, not teaching the new.
εἰδότας eidotas knowing (perf. ptc. of οἶδα) “you once having known” Concessive: “although you know.”
ἅπαξ hapax once, once for all “once” Position varies in manuscripts (see deep dive).
Ἰησοῦς / κύριος Iēsous / kyrios Jesus / Lord “Jesus” Major variant (deep dive).
σῴζω sōzō save, deliver “having saved” Exodus salvation.
τὸ δεύτερον to deuteron the second time, afterward “secondly” Contrasts salvation and destruction.
ἀρχή archē beginning; rule, domain “principality” Assigned position and authority.
οἰκητήριον oikētērion dwelling, habitation “proper dwelling” Elsewhere only 2 Cor 5:2.
ἀΐδιος aidios everlasting “eternal bonds” Elsewhere only Rom 1:20. In later Greek not sharply distinct from αἰώνιος.48
ζόφος zophos gloom, deep darkness “under darkness” Homeric “gloom of the underworld”; also v. 13; 2 Pet 2:4, 17; Heb 12:18.
τηρέω tēreō keep, guard “did not keep … has kept” Wordplay.
ἐκπορνεύω ekporneuō give oneself to fornication “given themselves to whoredom” NT hapax; intensive.
σὰρξ ἑτέρα sarx hetera other/different flesh “other flesh” See deep dive on Sodom.
πρόκειμαι prokeimai be set forth, displayed “set before” Present tense: still displayed.
δεῖγμα deigma specimen, example “an example” NT hapax; 2 Pet 2:6 has ὑπόδειγμα.
δίκη dikē justice; penalty “the justice” Execution of a sentence.
ὑπέχω hypechō undergo, suffer “undergoing” NT hapax; with δίκην = “suffer punishment.”
αἰώνιος aiōnios eternal, age-long “continuous” LSV’s consistent rendering.

On “eternal” and “continuous.” The LSV’s “continuous” for αἰώνιος reflects a decision to translate the word by its root, αἰών (aiōn, “age”), rather than by the traditional “eternal.” Whether αἰώνιος in the New Testament means “unending” or “belonging to the age to come” has long been discussed, and the word can carry both ideas: the life and judgment of the coming age, which does not end. Readers should not build a doctrine of the duration of judgment on the LSV’s English choice alone, any more than on “eternal.” The theology must be built from the whole biblical witness.

Deep dive: “Jesus … saved a people out of Egypt” — the text of Jude 5

The Greek manuscripts of Jude 5 are a tangle. The two main points of variation are (a) the name of the one who saved the people and (b) the position of “once.”

The readings. According to the SBLGNT apparatus and its updated form citing NA28:49

Edition Reading of the key words
SBLGNT (2010), NA28 (2012) εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ πάντα ὅτι Ἰησοῦς λαὸν… (“knowing all things once, that Jesus…”)
NA27 (1993) …πάντα ὅτι ὁ κύριος ἅπαξ λαὸν… (“that the Lord, having once saved…”)
Westcott–Hort (1881), Tregelles …ἅπαξ πάντα ὅτι κύριος… (“that [the] Lord…”)
Robinson–Pierpont (Byzantine), TR εἰδότας ὑμᾶς ἅπαξ τοῦτο ὅτι ὁ κύριος… (“once knowing this, that the Lord…”)

The great majority of later Byzantine manuscripts read “the Lord.” According to the tallies in one modern edition, the Byzantine wording appears in about 69 percent of manuscripts and the wording with “Jesus” in a fraction of one percent.50 The earliest manuscripts, however, divide very differently. Here is what the manuscripts themselves read, checked against their published transcriptions:51

Manuscript Date Reading at Jude 5
P72 (papyrus) 3rd/4th c. θ(εὸ)ς χρ(ιστὸ)ς, “God Christ”
ℵ 01 Sinaiticus 4th c. κ(ύριο)ς, “Lord” (with ἅπαξ after it)
B 03 Vaticanus 4th c. ι(ησου)ς, “Jesus”
A 02 Alexandrinus 5th c. ι(ησου)ς, “Jesus”
C 04 Ephraemi 5th c. ὁ κ(ύριο)ς, “the Lord,” changed by a later corrector to ὁ θ(εὸ)ς, “God”
Ψ 044 9th/10th c. κ(ύριο)ς, “Lord”
K 018, L 020 9th c. ὁ κ(ύριο)ς, “the Lord” (with τοῦτο)
1739 10th c. ι(ησου)ς, “Jesus”

The abbreviations are the ancient nomina sacra: sacred names written in shortened form with a line above, ΙΣ for Ἰησοῦς and ΚΣ for κύριος.

How have editors decided? Westcott and Hort (1881) printed “Lord” but placed “Jesus” in their margin. The Nestle–Aland 27th edition printed “the Lord.” The SBLGNT (2010) and the Nestle–Aland 28th edition (2012) both print “Jesus.”52 The reading impressed earlier commentators too. Alfred Plummer wrote that “there is very strong evidence in favour of substituting ‘Jesus’ for ‘the Lord;’ a most remarkable reading, showing how, in Christian language, the Man Jesus had become identified with the Eternal Son.” J. E. Huther reported that the scholar Rudolf Stier called it “without example, and incomprehensibly strange.”53

The arguments.

For “Jesus”:

  1. Strong early attestation in important manuscripts and early translations.
  2. It is the harder reading. Scribes were more likely to change a surprising “Jesus” into an unproblematic “the Lord” than the reverse. A scribe copying “Jesus saved a people out of Egypt” might suppose that the historical Jesus was meant, find the statement impossible, and “correct” it.
  3. It explains the other readings. “Lord,” “God,” and “God Christ” can all be understood as attempts to resolve the difficulty of “Jesus.”
  4. A possible scribal mechanism. In manuscripts, sacred names were abbreviated: ΙΣ for “Jesus” and ΚΣ for “Lord.” These differ by one letter, so confusion in either direction was possible. This cuts both ways, though, and does not decide the question.

For “the Lord”:

  1. “Lord” is Jude’s usual word for God and Christ (vv. 4, 9, 14, 17, 21, 25). A reading that uses “Jesus” for the pre-existent Christ would be unusual.
  2. Some scholars judge that “Jesus” acting in the exodus is so unexpected that it is more likely a scribal slip (ΚΣ to ΙΣ) than an original reading.

Discussion continues. What can be said with confidence is that “Jesus” is now the reading of the most widely used critical editions, of the SBLGNT on which this book is based, and of the LSV, and that it is very well attested.

What does it mean? If Jude wrote “Jesus,” he identifies the one who saved Israel from Egypt with Jesus Christ. He does not imply that the man from Nazareth lived in the second millennium BC. Rather, the one who became incarnate as Jesus already existed and acted as Israel’s deliverer. Christian theology calls this the pre-existence of Christ. It is affirmed elsewhere in the New Testament (John 1:1–3; 8:58; Phil 2:6–7; Col 1:15–17; Heb 1:2), and 1 Cor 10:4, 9 apply it specifically to the wilderness. Some interpreters connect it further with the mysterious “Messenger” of Exodus who leads Israel and of whom God says, “My Name [is] in His heart” (Exod 23:21, LSV). Jude does not develop the idea. He simply states it, as if it were already familiar to his readers.

If Jude wrote “the Lord,” he almost certainly still meant to evoke the same God whose lordship is now exercised by Jesus. Note that Jude calls Jesus “our only Master and Lord” in the previous verse (v. 4). On either reading, the warning is the same: the Lord who saves can also judge those who, having been saved, refuse to believe.

Deep dive: angels and the judgment traditions

Who were the angels “who did not keep their own principality, but left their proper dwelling”? The Old Testament offers only one story that fits: Genesis 6:1–4.

1 And it comes to pass that mankind has begun to multiply on the face of the ground, and daughters have been born to them, 2 and the sons of God see that they, the daughters of men, [are] beautiful, and they take women for themselves of all whom they have chosen. … 4 The giants were in the earth in those days, and even afterward, when sons of God come in to the daughters of men, and they have borne to them those who [were] the mighty from of old, the men of renown.

— Gen 6:1–4, LSV

Genesis does not say that the “sons of God” were punished, or even that they were angels. By the time of Jude, however, an elaborate Jewish tradition had grown up around these verses. Its fullest surviving form is the “Book of the Watchers,” 1 Enoch 1–36, usually dated to the third century BC or earlier. In it, two hundred angels called “Watchers” descend to earth, take human wives, father the giants, and teach humanity forbidden arts. God then sends his archangels to bind them:

And again the Lord said to Raphael: ‘Bind Azâzêl hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness: and make an opening in the desert … and cast him therein. And place upon him rough and jagged rocks, and cover him with darkness, and let him abide there for ever, and cover his face that he may not see light. And on the day of the great judgement he shall be cast into the fire.’

— 1 Enoch 10:4–6 (trans. R. H. Charles)54

And to Michael:

‘Go, bind Semjâzâ and his associates who have united themselves with women so as to have defiled themselves with them in all their uncleanness. And when their sons have slain one another … bind them fast for seventy generations in the valleys of the earth, till the day of their judgement and of their consummation …’

— 1 Enoch 10:11–12 (trans. R. H. Charles)

The correspondences with Jude 6 are close:

Jude 6 1 Enoch
“did not keep their own principality, but left their proper dwelling” The Watchers abandon heaven for earth (1 Enoch 6–7; 12:4; 15:3, 7)
“in eternal bonds” “Bind … hand and foot”; “bind them fast” (10:4, 12)
“under darkness” “cast him into the darkness … cover him with darkness” (10:4–5)
“until [the] judgment of [the] great day” “on the day of the great judgement” (10:6); “till the day of their judgement” (10:12)

Jude quotes 1 Enoch explicitly in vv. 14–15, so there is little doubt that he knew this tradition and expected his readers to know it. Second Peter’s parallel adds the term “Tartarus,” the Greek name for the deepest prison of the underworld: “God did not spare messengers having sinned, but having cast [them] down to Tartarus with chains of deepest gloom, delivered [them], having been reserved to judgment” (2 Pet 2:4, LSV). First Peter’s mysterious reference to “the spirits in prison, who sometime [ago] disobeyed … in [the] days of Noah” (1 Pet 3:19–20, LSV) probably belongs to the same circle of ideas.

The tradition also appears in other Jewish writings of the period. The Testament of Naphtali, discussed below, pairs the Watchers with Sodom exactly as Jude does. Sirach says that God “was not pacified toward the old giants” (Sir 16:7, Brenton). Third Maccabees recalls that God destroyed “the giants, who trusted in their strength and hardihood” (3 Macc 2:4, Brenton). The fall of the Watchers was a standard example of judgment in Second Temple Judaism, and Jude uses it the way his contemporaries did.

Other interpretations. Later Christian interpreters moved away from the angelic reading of Genesis 6. Augustine argued that the “sons of God” were “according to the flesh the sons of Seth” who intermarried with the ungodly line of Cain, and he insisted that angels, being spiritual, could not father children.55 Many readers have followed him, and others have read Jude 6 as a reference to an original fall of Satan and his angels before creation (cf. Rev 12:7–9), unconnected with Genesis 6. Both views are defensible as readings of Genesis in its own right. They fit Jude less well, because Jude’s vocabulary tracks 1 Enoch’s account of the Watchers, his next verse compares the angels’ sin to Sodom’s sexual sin, and he quotes 1 Enoch a few lines later. Clement of Alexandria, an early commentator, read Jude 6 of angels who “left their own habitation, meaning, that is, the heaven and the stars,” and took the “chains” as “the loss of the honour in which they had stood.”56

What Jude affirms, and what he does not. Jude affirms that some heavenly beings rebelled, that they are under restraint, and that they await final judgment. He does not provide a full angelology, a description of their prison, or a timetable. He uses a story his readers knew to make a single point: even angels who abandoned their God-given place did not escape judgment. How much of the surrounding Enochic narrative Jude believed to be historical is a separate question, taken up in Chapter 8.

Deep dive: Sodom and Gomorrah

Sodom and Gomorrah became the Bible’s standard example of total destruction. Moses warns Israel that disobedience would leave the land “like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim” (Deut 29:23, LSV). Isaiah calls Jerusalem’s rulers “you rulers of Sodom” (Isa 1:10, LSV). Jesus says the coming of the Son of Man will be like the days of Lot, when “He rained fire and brimstone from the sky, and destroyed all” (Luke 17:29, LSV). Paul and Peter both cite the cities. But what, according to the Bible and early Jewish tradition, was Sodom’s sin?

The biblical evidence.

  • Genesis 18–19. The outcry against Sodom was already great before the angels arrived: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah—because great; and their sin—because exceedingly grievous” (Gen 18:20, LSV). The episode in Gen 19:4–5 shows the city’s character in action. The men of the city, “from young even to aged,” surround Lot’s house and demand that the visitors be brought out “and we know them” (LSV), that is, for sexual assault. The scene combines violent sexual aggression, the violation of guests whom hospitality required Lot to protect, and the fact that the guests were angels.
  • Ezekiel 16:49–50. Ezekiel names the sins of “your sister Sodom” as “Arrogancy, fullness of bread, and quiet ease,” the failure to strengthen “the hand of the afflicted and needy,” and adds, “they are haughty and do abomination before Me” (LSV). Ezekiel’s emphasis is on pride, complacent wealth, and neglect of the poor, with “abomination” as a further charge.
  • Isaiah 1:10 and Jeremiah 23:14 use Sodom as a byword for injustice and moral corruption in Jerusalem.

The Second Temple evidence. Jewish writers of Jude’s era gave the story different emphases:

  • Pride and insolence: God “abhorred them for their pride” (Sir 16:8, Brenton). God destroyed “the Sodomites, those workers of exceeding iniquity” for their pride and insolence (3 Macc 2:5).
  • Hostility to strangers and sexual practices: Josephus writes that “the Sodomites grew proud, on account of their riches and great wealth; they became unjust towards men, and impious towards God … they hated strangers, and abused themselves with Sodomitical practices.”57
  • Gluttony, debauchery, and same-sex relations: Philo of Alexandria describes Sodom as “full of innumerable iniquities, and especially of gluttony and debauchery,” and says that its men “not only … went mad after women, and defile[d] the marriage bed of others, but also those who were men lusted after one another.”58
  • Changing the order of nature, paired with the Watchers: The Testament of Naphtali urges its readers to recognize the Lord in creation, “that you become not as Sodom, which changed the order of its nature, in like manner also the Watchers changed the order of their nature, whom also the Lord cursed at the flood.”59

The last text is especially important for Jude, because it makes exactly Jude’s pairing. Sodom and the Watchers are linked as two instances of transgressing the order of nature God established. The Watchers crossed from heaven to earth to unite with human women. Sodom’s men sought to violate heavenly visitors. Jude’s “in like manner to these … having gone after other flesh” fits this pattern precisely.

What “other flesh” means in Jude. Three readings are found among interpreters:

  1. Angelic flesh. “Other” (ἑτέρα, hetera) means “of a different kind.” The men of Sodom pursued sexual union with beings who were not human, the counterpart of the angels’ pursuit of human women. This is the reading most modern critical commentators favor, because it makes the best sense of “in like manner to these” and of the Testament of Naphtali parallel.
  2. Same-sex relations. “Other” means “contrary to nature,” and Jude refers to homosexual acts, which Philo and Josephus associated with Sodom. This reading is traditional in much Christian interpretation.
  3. Sexual immorality in general, with the angelic and same-sex dimensions both included in the description of the city’s excess.

The first reading best explains Jude’s comparison, and this book adopts it as the primary sense. Two cautions follow from it. First, Jude 7 should not be made to carry more than it says. The phrase’s main reference is to the attempted violation of angels, and Jude does not address modern questions about committed same-sex relationships. Those questions are usually argued from other texts (for example Lev 18:22 and Rom 1:26–27), and readers should weigh those passages on their own terms. Second, the opposite overcorrection is equally mistaken: Jude clearly condemns sexual immorality (“having given themselves to whoredom”). Sodom in Jude is not merely a symbol of inhospitality, even though inhospitality and violence were part of its sin. Honest reading lets Jude say what he says and no more.

Why Sodom fits Jude’s argument. Jude’s three examples move from God’s people (Israel), to heavenly beings (angels), to pagan cities (Sodom). The circle widens to show that judgment reaches every order of creation. All three share one feature: they left the place God gave them. Israel left trust for unbelief, the angels left heaven for earth, and Sodom left the order of creation for the pursuit of “other flesh.” The intruders, Jude will say, do “in like manner” (v. 8).

E. The Historical and Cultural World

The exodus in Jewish memory. The exodus from Egypt was the central saving event of Israel’s story, recited at Passover, celebrated in the Psalms, and used by the prophets as the pattern for future deliverance. The wilderness generation’s failure was equally remembered, as a warning. Psalm 95, sung in synagogue and church, ends with God’s oath: “Forty years I am weary of the generation, … Where I swore in My anger” that they would not enter his rest (Ps 95:10–11, LSV). Jude’s readers would have known both sides of the story.

Angels in Second Temple Judaism. Jewish thought between the Testaments developed a rich angelology: named archangels (Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel), angelic hierarchies, guardian angels of nations, and fallen angels. The Dead Sea Scrolls, 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and other writings show how widely these ideas were held. Jude’s casual reference to rebellious angels and, in v. 9, to Michael the archangel shows that he and his readers shared this world of thought.

The Dead Sea region. The southern end of the Dead Sea, with its salt formations, bitumen, and barren landscape, was identified in antiquity with the destroyed cities of the plain. Wisdom 10:7, quoted above, speaks of its “waste land that smoketh” and its pillar of salt. Josephus also describes the region.60 For Jude’s readers, the “example” was not only a story but a place.

  1. Josephus, Jewish War 4.8.4 (Whiston): “there are still the remainders of that Divine fire, and the traces [or shadows] of the five cities are still to be seen, as well as the ashes growing in their fruits” (Project Gutenberg #2850). Of Lot’s wife’s pillar of salt Josephus writes, “I have seen it, and it remains at this day” (Antiquities 1.11.4, Gutenberg #2848).↩︎

F. Connections Across Scripture

1 Corinthians 10:1–11 (close thematic parallel). Paul’s use of the wilderness generation is the closest parallel to Jude 5. All Israel “passed through the sea … and all ate the same spiritual food,” yet “in the most of them God was not well pleased, for they were strewn in the wilderness” (1 Cor 10:1, 3, 5, LSV). Paul identifies the rock as “the Christ” (10:4) and warns against tempting “the Christ” (10:9). His conclusion, “these things happened to those persons as types, and they were written for our admonition” (10:11, LSV), is exactly Jude’s use of the story. The texts share a tradition of interpretation, but neither is likely quoting the other.

Hebrews 3:16–19 (close thematic parallel). “Was it not with those who sinned, whose carcasses fell in the wilderness? … they were not able to enter in because of unbelief” (Heb 3:17, 19, LSV). Hebrews stresses unbelief just as Jude does (“those not having believed”).

2 Peter 2:4–9 (literary parallel). Peter’s version lists angels, the flood, and Sodom, in biblical order. It adds Noah and Lot as examples of the righteous rescued and concludes: “the LORD has known to rescue [the] pious out of temptation, and to keep [the] unrighteous being punished to [the] day of judgment” (2 Pet 2:9, LSV). The relationship to Jude is discussed in the Introduction and Appendix C.

Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10 (shared theme). The “continuous fire that has been prepared for the Devil and his messengers” (Matt 25:41, LSV) connects the fate of rebellious angels and the fire of judgment, the same two ideas that Jude 6–7 places side by side.

Exodus 23:20–21 (possible background). The Messenger in whom God’s Name dwells and who leads Israel through the wilderness has been connected by some interpreters with Jude’s “Jesus” in v. 5. This is a suggestive connection, not a demonstrated allusion.

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. “Jesus” or “the Lord” in v. 5? Discussed in the deep dive. The reading “Jesus” is strongly attested and is now printed in the main critical editions, but a minority of scholars still prefers “the Lord.”

2. Can the redeemed be destroyed? Jude’s first example concerns people who were genuinely saved from Egypt and later destroyed for unbelief. Christian traditions read this differently. Some see in it a warning that those who were once part of the redeemed community can fall away. Others see it as a type: physical deliverance from Egypt was real, but not every member of the delivered people had saving faith, and so the warning targets those whose membership in the church is not matched by faith. Jude’s purpose is practical rather than systematic. He warns the readers not to trust in privilege, and he assures them that God is able to keep them (v. 24).

3. Does Jude endorse the Watcher story as history? Jude certainly uses the tradition, and his argument assumes its point. Whether he regarded every detail of 1 Enoch’s narrative as historical cannot be determined from his brief allusion. The question is discussed further in Chapter 8.

4. What was Sodom’s sin? Discussed in the deep dive. Jude’s own emphasis is on sexual immorality and the pursuit of “other flesh,” understood in light of the angel parallel. Other biblical texts emphasize pride, wealth, injustice, and inhospitality. A full biblical portrait includes all of these.

5. “Eternal” or “continuous” fire? The question of what αἰώνιος means, and of the nature and duration of final judgment, is a larger theological discussion that Jude’s verse alone cannot settle. Jude’s own point is that Sodom’s destruction is a visible, lasting example of judgment that should give the reader pause.

H. The Passage Within Jude

Verses 5–7 are the first of Jude’s “texts,” the evidence that the intruders’ condemnation was “written beforehand” (v. 4). The next verse begins “In like manner” (ὁμοίως, homoiōs) and applies the examples: “those dreaming indeed defile the flesh, and they disregard lordship, and they speak evil of glorious [ones]” (v. 8). The three sins of v. 8 correspond loosely to the three examples. Defiling the flesh corresponds to Sodom. Disregarding lordship corresponds to the angels who left their place and to Israel’s rebellion. Slandering glorious ones prepares for the contrast with Michael in v. 9.

The passage also develops the letter’s key word: “keep.” The angels “did not keep” and are “kept” (v. 6). The readers, “kept” by God (v. 1), will be urged to “keep” themselves (v. 21). The examples of vv. 5–7 are not only threats against the intruders. They are also mirrors for the readers, showing what it would mean to leave the place God has given.

I. Contemporary Understanding

These reflections are suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

Privilege is not protection. Jude’s first example is directed at people who belong to the community of the saved. Church membership, a dramatic conversion story, or a heritage of faith do not by themselves guarantee faithfulness. Jude’s warning may be most needed in communities that feel most secure.

The goodness of boundaries. All three examples involve leaving a God-given place. Modern culture often treats limits as obstacles to self-realization. Jude’s examples suggest that boundaries such as the place of trust, of creaturely station, and of the created order can be gifts that protect and do not merely restrict. This idea can be misused to justify unjust social hierarchies, which Jude does not address. Applied to the believer’s relationship with God, though, it invites reflection on the freedom found in remaining where God has placed us: in his love (v. 21).

Reading hard texts honestly. Jude 7 is often quoted in modern debates. Responsible readers will resist both the temptation to make it say more than it does and the temptation to make it say less. That discipline is itself a form of “contending for the faith.”

Christ in the whole story. If Jude 5 identifies Jesus as Israel’s deliverer, Christians may read the Old Testament as the story of the same Lord they know in the Gospels. That conviction has shaped Christian worship and interpretation from the beginning.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. Why do you think Jude began his examples with God’s own people rather than with pagan Sodom? What effect might that order have had on his readers?
  2. What difference does it make to your understanding of Jesus if Jude 5 says that Jesus saved Israel from Egypt?
  3. The angels “did not keep their own principality” and are now “kept” for judgment. How does this wordplay illuminate the relationship between faithfulness and security?
  4. Jude, Ezekiel, Josephus, and Philo describe Sodom’s sin differently. Why might different writers emphasize different aspects of the same story? What are the risks of focusing on only one?
  5. Jude says his readers already know these things but need reminding. What truths do you know well but most need to be reminded of?

Genesis 6

Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)

1 וַיְהִי כִּי־הֵחֵל הָאָדָם לָרֹב עַל־פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה וּבָנוֹת יֻלְּדוּ לָהֶם 2 וַיִּרְאוּ בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ 3 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה לֹא־יָדוֹן רוּחִי בָאָדָם לְעֹלָם בְּשַׁגַּם הוּא בָשָׂר וְהָיוּ יָמָיו מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה 4 הַנְּפִלִים הָיוּ בָאָרֶץ בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם וְגַם אַחֲרֵי־כֵן אֲשֶׁר יָבֹאוּ בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים אֶל־בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם וְיָלְדוּ לָהֶם הֵמָּה הַגִּבֹּרִים אֲשֶׁר מֵעוֹלָם אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם 5 וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם בָּאָרֶץ וְכָל־יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ רַק רַע כָּל־הַיּוֹם 6 וַיִּנָּחֶם יְהוָה כִּי־עָשָׂה אֶת־הָאָדָם בָּאָרֶץ וַיִּתְעַצֵּב אֶל־לִבּוֹ 7 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶמְחֶה אֶת־הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר־בָּרָאתִי מֵעַל פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה מֵאָדָם עַד־בְּהֵמָה עַד־רֶמֶשׂ וְעַד־עוֹף הַשָּׁמָיִם כִּי נִחַמְתִּי כִּי עֲשִׂיתִם 8 וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה 9 אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ נֹחַ אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים הָיָה בְּדֹרֹתָיו אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים הִתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹחַ 10 וַיּוֹלֶד נֹחַ שְׁלֹשָׁה בָנִים אֶת־שֵׁם אֶת־חָם וְאֶת־יָפֶת 11 וַתִּשָּׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים וַתִּמָּלֵא הָאָרֶץ חָמָס 12 וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָרֶץ וְהִנֵּה נִשְׁחָתָה כִּי־הִשְׁחִית כָּל־בָּשָׂר אֶת־דַּרְכּוֹ עַל־הָאָרֶץ 13 וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים לְנֹחַ קֵץ כָּל־בָּשָׂר בָּא לְפָנַי כִּי־מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ חָמָס מִפְּנֵיהֶם וְהִנְנִי מַשְׁחִיתָם אֶת־הָאָרֶץ 14 עֲשֵׂה לְךָ תֵּבַת עֲצֵי־גֹפֶר קִנִּים תַּעֲשֶׂה אֶת־הַתֵּבָה וְכָפַרְתָּ אֹתָהּ מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ בַּכֹּפֶר 15 וְזֶה אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתָהּ שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת אַמָּה אֹרֶךְ הַתֵּבָה חֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה רָחְבָּהּ וּשְׁלֹשִׁים אַמָּה קוֹמָתָהּ 16 צֹהַר תַּעֲשֶׂה לַתֵּבָה וְאֶל־אַמָּה תְּכַלֶנָּה מִלְמַעְלָה וּפֶתַח הַתֵּבָה בְּצִדָּהּ תָּשִׂים תַּחְתִּיִּם שְׁנִיִּם וּשְׁלִשִׁים תַּעֲשֶׂהָ 17 וַאֲנִי הִנְנִי מֵבִיא אֶת־הַמַּבּוּל מַיִם עַל־הָאָרֶץ לְשַׁחֵת כָּל־בָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ רוּחַ חַיִּים מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמָיִם כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־בָּאָרֶץ יִגְוָע 18 וַהֲקִמֹתִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי אִתָּךְ וּבָאתָ אֶל־הַתֵּבָה אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ וְאִשְׁתְּךָ וּנְשֵׁי־בָנֶיךָ אִתָּךְ 19 וּמִכָּל־הָחַי מִכָּל־בָּשָׂר שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל תָּבִיא אֶל־הַתֵּבָה לְהַחֲיֹת אִתָּךְ זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה יִהְיוּ 20 מֵהָעוֹף לְמִינֵהוּ וּמִן־הַבְּהֵמָה לְמִינָהּ מִכֹּל רֶמֶשׂ הָאֲדָמָה לְמִינֵהוּ שְׁנַיִם מִכֹּל יָבֹאוּ אֵלֶיךָ לְהַחֲיוֹת 21 וְאַתָּה קַח־לְךָ מִכָּל־מַאֲכָל אֲשֶׁר יֵאָכֵל וְאָסַפְתָּ אֵלֶיךָ וְהָיָה לְךָ וְלָהֶם לְאָכְלָה 22 וַיַּעַשׂ נֹחַ כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים כֵּן עָשָׂה

English (BSB)

1 Now when men began to multiply on the face of the earth and daughters were born to them, 2 the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose. 3 So the LORD said, “My Spirit will not contend with man forever, for he is mortal; his days shall be 120 years.” 4 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and afterward as well—when the sons of God had relations with the daughters of men. And they bore them children who became the mighty men of old, men of renown. 5 Then the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time. 6 And the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart. 7 So the LORD said, “I will blot out man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth—every man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air—for I am grieved that I have made them.” 8 Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD. 9 This is the account of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God. 10 And Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. 11 Now the earth was corrupt in the sight of God, and full of violence. 12 And God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt; for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways. 13 Then God said to Noah, “The end of all living creatures has come before Me, because through them the earth is full of violence. Now behold, I will destroy both them and the earth. 14 Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out. 15 And this is how you are to build it: The ark is to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. 16 You are to make a roof for the ark, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in the side of the ark, and build lower, middle, and upper decks. 17 And behold, I will bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that has the breath of life. Everything on the earth will perish. 18 But I will establish My covenant with you, and you will enter the ark—you and your sons and your wife and your sons’ wives with you. 19 And you are to bring two of every living creature into the ark—male and female—to keep them alive with you. 20 Two of every kind of bird and animal and crawling creature will come to you to be kept alive. 21 You are also to take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten and gather it as food for yourselves and for the animals.” 22 So Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.

English (WEB)

1 When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, 2 God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. 3 The LORD said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” 4 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children with them. Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown. 5 The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil. 6 The LORD was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart. 7 The LORD said, “I will destroy man whom I have created from the surface of the ground—man, along with animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky—for I am sorry that I have made them.” 8 But Noah found favor in the LORD’s eyes. 9 This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God. 10 Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. 11 The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. 12 God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. 13 God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth. 14 Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch. 15 This is how you shall make it. The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. 16 You shall make a roof in the ship, and you shall finish it to a cubit upward. You shall set the door of the ship in its side. You shall make it with lower, second, and third levels. 17 I, even I, will bring the flood of waters on this earth, to destroy all flesh having the breath of life from under the sky. Everything that is on the earth will die. 18 But I will establish my covenant with you. You shall come into the ship, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. 19 Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. 20 Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive. 21 Take with you some of all food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself; and it will be for food for you, and for them.” 22 Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him.

Genesis 13:10

Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)

10 וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹט אֶת־עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא אֶת־כָּל־כִּכַּר הַיַּרְדֵּן כִּי כֻלָּהּ מַשְׁקֶה לִפְנֵי שַׁחֵת יְהוָה אֶת־סְדֹם וְאֶת־עֲמֹרָה כְּגַן־יְהוָה כְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר

English (BSB)

10 And Lot looked out and saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)

English (WEB)

10 Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar.

Genesis 18

Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)

1 וַיֵּרָא אֵלָיו יְהוָה בְּאֵלֹנֵי מַמְרֵא וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב פֶּתַח־הָאֹהֶל כְּחֹם הַיּוֹם 2 וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה שְׁלֹשָׁה אֲנָשִׁים נִצָּבִים עָלָיו וַיַּרְא וַיָּרָץ לִקְרָאתָם מִפֶּתַח הָאֹהֶל וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ אָרְצָה 3 וַיֹּאמַר אֲדֹנָי אִם־נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ אַל־נָא תַעֲבֹר מֵעַל עַבְדֶּךָ 4 יֻקַּח־נָא מְעַט־מַיִם וְרַחֲצוּ רַגְלֵיכֶם וְהִשָּׁעֲנוּ תַּחַת הָעֵץ 5 וְאֶקְחָה פַת־לֶחֶם וְסַעֲדוּ לִבְּכֶם אַחַר תַּעֲבֹרוּ כִּי־עַל־כֵּן עֲבַרְתֶּם עַל־עַבְדְּכֶם וַיֹּאמְרוּ כֵּן תַּעֲשֶׂה כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתָּ 6 וַיְמַהֵר אַבְרָהָם הָאֹהֱלָה אֶל־שָׂרָה וַיֹּאמֶר מַהֲרִי שְׁלֹשׁ סְאִים קֶמַח סֹלֶת לוּשִׁי וַעֲשִׂי עֻגוֹת 7 וְאֶל־הַבָּקָר רָץ אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח בֶּן־בָּקָר רַךְ וָטוֹב וַיִּתֵּן אֶל־הַנַּעַר וַיְמַהֵר לַעֲשׂוֹת אֹתוֹ 8 וַיִּקַּח חֶמְאָה וְחָלָב וּבֶן־הַבָּקָר אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה וַיִּתֵּן לִפְנֵיהֶם וְהוּא־עֹמֵד עֲלֵיהֶם תַּחַת הָעֵץ וַיֹּאכֵלוּ 9 וַיֹּאמְרוּ אֵׄלָׄיׄוׄ אַיֵּה שָׂרָה אִשְׁתֶּךָ וַיֹּאמֶר הִנֵּה בָאֹהֶל 10 וַיֹּאמֶר שׁוֹב אָשׁוּב אֵלֶיךָ כָּעֵת חַיָּה וְהִנֵּה־בֵן לְשָׂרָה אִשְׁתֶּךָ וְשָׂרָה שֹׁמַעַת פֶּתַח הָאֹהֶל וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו 11 וְאַבְרָהָם וְשָׂרָה זְקֵנִים בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים חָדַל לִהְיוֹת לְשָׂרָה אֹרַח כַּנָּשִׁים 12 וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ לֵאמֹר אַחֲרֵי בְלֹתִי הָיְתָה־לִּי עֶדְנָה וַאדֹנִי זָקֵן 13 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל־אַבְרָהָם לָמָּה זֶּה צָחֲקָה שָׂרָה לֵאמֹר הַאַף אֻמְנָם אֵלֵד וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי 14 הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר לַמּוֹעֵד אָשׁוּב אֵלֶיךָ כָּעֵת חַיָּה וּלְשָׂרָה בֵן 15 וַתְּכַחֵשׁ שָׂרָה לֵאמֹר לֹא צָחַקְתִּי כִּי יָרֵאָה וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא כִּי צָחָקְתְּ 16 וַיָּקֻמוּ מִשָּׁם הָאֲנָשִׁים וַיַּשְׁקִפוּ עַל־פְּנֵי סְדֹם וְאַבְרָהָם הֹלֵךְ עִמָּם לְשַׁלְּחָם 17 וַיהֹוָה אָמָר הַמְכַסֶּה אֲנִי מֵאַבְרָהָם אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה 18 וְאַבְרָהָם הָיוֹ יִהְיֶה לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם וְנִבְרְכוּ בוֹ כֹּל גּוֹיֵי הָאָרֶץ 19 כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת־בָּנָיו וְאֶת־בֵּיתוֹ אַחֲרָיו וְשָׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה לַעֲשׂוֹת צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט לְמַעַן הָבִיא יְהוָה עַל־אַבְרָהָם אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר עָלָיו 20 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה כִּי־רָבָּה וְחַטָּאתָם כִּי כָבְדָה מְאֹד 21 אֵרֲדָה־נָּא וְאֶרְאֶה הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ הַבָּאָה אֵלַי עָשׂוּ כָּלָה וְאִם־לֹא אֵדָעָה 22 וַיִּפְנוּ מִשָּׁם הָאֲנָשִׁים וַיֵּלְכוּ סְדֹמָה וְאַבְרָהָם עוֹדֶנּוּ עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי יְהוָה 23 וַיִּגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וַיֹּאמַר הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה צַדִּיק עִם־רָשָׁע 24 אוּלַי יֵשׁ חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִם בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה וְלֹא־תִשָּׂא לַמָּקוֹם לְמַעַן חֲמִשִּׁים הַצַּדִּיקִם אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבָּהּ 25 חָלִלָה לְּךָ מֵעֲשֹׂת כַּדָּבָר הַזֶּה לְהָמִית צַדִּיק עִם־רָשָׁע וְהָיָה כַצַּדִּיק כָּרָשָׁע חָלִלָה לָּךְ הֲשֹׁפֵט כָּל־הָאָרֶץ לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפָּט 26 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אִם־אֶמְצָא בִסְדֹם חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִם בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר וְנָשָׂאתִי לְכָל־הַמָּקוֹם בַּעֲבוּרָם 27 וַיַּעַן אַבְרָהָם וַיֹּאמַר הִנֵּה־נָא הוֹאַלְתִּי לְדַבֵּר אֶל־אֲדֹנָי וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר 28 אוּלַי יַחְסְרוּן חֲמִשִּׁים הַצַּדִּיקִם חֲמִשָּׁה הֲתַשְׁחִית בַּחֲמִשָּׁה אֶת־כָּל־הָעִיר וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא אַשְׁחִית אִם־אֶמְצָא שָׁם אַרְבָּעִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה 29 וַיֹּסֶף עוֹד לְדַבֵּר אֵלָיו וַיֹּאמַר אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם אַרְבָּעִים וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא אֶעֱשֶׂה בַּעֲבוּר הָאַרְבָּעִים 30 וַיֹּאמֶר אַל־נָא יִחַר לַאדֹנָי וַאֲדַבֵּרָה אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם שְׁלֹשִׁים וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא אֶעֱשֶׂה אִם־אֶמְצָא שָׁם שְׁלֹשִׁים 31 וַיֹּאמֶר הִנֵּה־נָא הוֹאַלְתִּי לְדַבֵּר אֶל־אֲדֹנָי אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם עֶשְׂרִים וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא אַשְׁחִית בַּעֲבוּר הָעֶשְׂרִים 32 וַיֹּאמֶר אַל־נָא יִחַר לַאדֹנָי וַאֲדַבְּרָה אַךְ־הַפַּעַם אוּלַי יִמָּצְאוּן שָׁם עֲשָׂרָה וַיֹּאמֶר לֹא אַשְׁחִית בַּעֲבוּר הָעֲשָׂרָה 33 וַיֵּלֶךְ יְהוָה כַּאֲשֶׁר כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר אֶל־אַבְרָהָם וְאַבְרָהָם שָׁב לִמְקֹמוֹ

English (BSB)

1 Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent. 2 And Abraham looked up and saw three men standing nearby. When he saw them, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed low to the ground. 3 “My lord,” said Abraham, “if I have found favor in your sight, please do not pass your servant by. 4 Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree. 5 And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves. This is why you have passed your servant’s way. After that, you may continue on your way.” “Yes,” they replied, “you may do as you have said.” 6 So Abraham hurried into the tent and said to Sarah, “Quick! Prepare three seahs of fine flour, knead it, and bake some bread.” 7 Meanwhile, Abraham ran to the herd, selected a tender and choice calf, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it. 8 Then Abraham brought curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and he set them before the men and stood by them under the tree as they ate. 9 “Where is your wife Sarah?” they asked. “There, in the tent,” he replied. 10 Then the LORD said, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” Now Sarah was behind him, listening at the entrance to the tent. 11 And Abraham and Sarah were already old and well along in years; Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. 12 So she laughed to herself, saying, “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” 13 And the LORD asked Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh and say, ‘Can I really bear a child when I am old?’ 14 Is anything too difficult for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you—in about a year—and Sarah will have a son.” 15 But Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.” “No,” replied the LORD, “but you did laugh.” 16 When the men got up to leave, they looked out over Sodom, and Abraham walked along with them to see them off. 17 And the LORD said, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? 18 Abraham will surely become a great and powerful nation, and through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed. 19 For I have chosen him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just, in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what He has promised.” 20 Then the LORD said, “The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great. Because their sin is so grievous, 21 I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. If not, I will find out.” 22 And the two men turned away and went toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD. 23 Abraham stepped forward and said, “Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked? 24 What if there are fifty righteous ones in the city? Will You really sweep it away and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous ones who are there? 25 Far be it from You to do such a thing—to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked are treated alike. Far be it from You! Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” 26 So the LORD replied, “If I find fifty righteous ones within the city of Sodom, on their account I will spare the whole place.” 27 Then Abraham answered, “Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord—though I am but dust and ashes— 28 suppose the fifty righteous ones lack five. Will You destroy the whole city for the lack of five?” He replied, “If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it.” 29 Once again Abraham spoke to the LORD, “Suppose forty are found there?” He answered, “On account of the forty, I will not do it.” 30 Then Abraham said, “May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak further. Suppose thirty are found there?” He replied, “If I find thirty there, I will not do it.” 31 And Abraham said, “Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, suppose twenty are found there?” He answered, “On account of the twenty, I will not destroy it.” 32 Finally, Abraham said, “May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?” And He answered, “On account of the ten, I will not destroy it.” 33 When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home.

English (WEB)

1 The LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. 2 He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, 3 and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. 4 Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. 5 I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart. After that you may go your way, now that you have come to your servant.” They said, “Very well, do as you have said.” 6 Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.” 7 Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it. 8 He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate. 9 They asked him, “Where is Sarah, your wife?” He said, “There, in the tent.” 10 He said, “I will certainly return to you at about this time next year; and behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.” Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him. 11 Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. 12 Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” 13 The LORD said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Will I really bear a child when I am old?’ 14 Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes around, and Sarah will have a son.” 15 Then Sarah denied it, saying, “I didn’t laugh,” for she was afraid. He said, “No, but you did laugh.” 16 The men rose up from there, and looked toward Sodom. Abraham went with them to see them on their way. 17 The LORD said, “Will I hide from Abraham what I do, 18 since Abraham will surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him? 19 For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that the LORD may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.” 20 The LORD said, “Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous, 21 I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know.” 22 The men turned from there, and went toward Sodom, but Abraham stood yet before the LORD. 23 Abraham came near, and said, “Will you consume the righteous with the wicked? 24 What if there are fifty righteous within the city? Will you consume and not spare the place for the fifty righteous who are in it? 25 May it be far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” 26 The LORD said, “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare the whole place for their sake.” 27 Abraham answered, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes. 28 What if there will lack five of the fifty righteous? Will you destroy all the city for lack of five?” He said, “I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there.” 29 He spoke to him yet again, and said, “What if there are forty found there?” He said, “I will not do it for the forty’s sake.” 30 He said, “Oh don’t let the Lord be angry, and I will speak. What if there are thirty found there?” He said, “I will not do it if I find thirty there.” 31 He said, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord. What if there are twenty found there?” He said, “I will not destroy it for the twenty’s sake.” 32 He said, “Oh don’t let the Lord be angry, and I will speak just once more. What if ten are found there?” He said, “I will not destroy it for the ten’s sake.” 33 The LORD went his way as soon as he had finished communing with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.

Chapter 4. Dreamers, Authority, and the Archangel’s Restraint (Jude 8–10)

A. The Text

The Greek text

8 Ὁμοίως μέντοι καὶ οὗτοι ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι σάρκα μὲν μιαίνουσιν, κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετοῦσιν, δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν. 9 ὁ δὲ Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος, ὅτε τῷ διαβόλῳ διακρινόμενος διελέγετο περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος, οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας, ἀλλὰ εἶπεν· Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος. 10 οὗτοι δὲ ὅσα μὲν οὐκ οἴδασιν βλασφημοῦσιν, ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται.

B. Plain-English Orientation

Having set out three examples of judgment, Jude now applies them. The intruders behave “in like manner.” Relying on their dreams, they do three things: they defile the flesh, they reject authority, and they slander heavenly beings.

To expose the arrogance of the third charge, Jude tells a story his readers evidently knew. When Michael, the greatest of the archangels, disputed with the Devil over Moses’ body, he did not presume to pronounce judgment on his adversary on his own authority. He left that to God: “The LORD rebuke you!”

The intruders show no such restraint. They mock what they do not understand. Meanwhile, the things they do understand, their instincts and appetites, are understood the way animals understand them, and those very things are destroying them.

The passage turns on a contrast between presumption and reverence. The intruders claim special insight through dreams, yet they are ignorant of spiritual realities and governed by animal instinct. Michael, who stands in the presence of God, knows the limits of his authority.

C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

Ὁμοίως μέντοι (Homoiōs mentoi) — ‘yet in the same way’

The opening Ὁμοίως μέντοι καὶ οὗτοι (Homoiōs mentoi kai houtoi), literally “In the same way, however, these also,” ties the intruders to the examples of vv. 5–7. The particle μέντοι (mentoi), “nevertheless, yet,” adds a note of surprise or protest. In spite of these well-known examples of judgment, the intruders do the same things. This is the first of the letter’s “these” applications.

καὶ οὗτοι ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι (kai houtoi enypniazomenoi) — ‘these too, dreaming’

The participle ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι (enypniazomenoi), “dreaming,” stands as the description of the intruders that governs all three of the following verbs. The LSV’s “those dreaming indeed defile the flesh” preserves this: the dreaming is the source of the behavior.

What does Jude mean? Some interpreters take it figuratively, as if the intruders lived in a dream world of self-delusion or fantasized about immorality. The background of the word points elsewhere. In the Greek Old Testament, the same verb describes the false prophet of Deuteronomy 13: “When a prophet or a dreamer of a dream arises in your midst … saying, Let us go after other gods … you do not listen to the words of that prophet or to that dreamer of the dream” (Deut 13:1–3, LSV). The Septuagint uses ἐνυπνιαζόμενος, Jude’s word, for that “dreamer of a dream.”61 Jeremiah denounces prophets “who prophesy falsehood in My Name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed” (Jer 23:25, LSV), and God says, “I [am] against the prophets of false dreams” (Jer 23:32, LSV).

Dreams were not suspect in themselves. Joel promised that in the last days “Your old men dream dreams” (Joel 2:28, LSV), and Peter announced the fulfillment of that promise at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). The problem was dreams claimed as divine revelation that led people away from God’s revealed will. Jude’s intruders seem to have claimed visions or revelations that authorized their conduct. That would explain why Jude stresses that the faith was delivered “once” (v. 3). No new revelation can overturn it.

  1. LXX Deut 13:2 (Eng. 13:1): Ἐὰν δὲ ἀναστῇ ἐν σοὶ προφήτης ἢ ἐνυπνιαζόμενος τὸ ἐνύπνιον; also 13:4, 6 (Brenton’s Greek Septuagint, eBible.org). The same participle appears in LXX Jer 34:9 (Eng. 27:9) of those who mislead the people.↩︎

σάρκα μὲν μιαίνουσιν (sarka men miainousin) — ‘defile the flesh’

The first of three charges, σάρκα μὲν μιαίνουσιν (sarka men miainousin), uses the verb μιαίνω (miainō), “to stain, defile, soil,” in a moral sense.62 “The flesh” here means the body. The charge corresponds to Sodom’s sexual immorality (v. 7) and to the intruders’ turning grace into “licentiousness” (v. 4).

The three charges are linked by the Greek particles μέν … δέ … δέ (men … de … de), “on the one hand … on the other … and.” The LSV’s “indeed … and … and” reflects this. The construction holds the three together as aspects of a single pattern of life.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. μιαίνω: “to stain, defile, soil; in physical sense; in moral sense: Tit 1:15, He 12:15, Ju 8.”↩︎

κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετοῦσιν (kyriotēta de athetousin) — ‘reject lordship’

The second charge, κυριότητα δὲ ἀθετοῦσιν (kyriotēta de athetousin), uses ἀθετέω (atheteō), “to set aside, reject, nullify,”63 with the object κυριότης (kyriotēs), “lordship, dominion.” What lordship do they reject?

  1. The lordship of the Lord. The word is derived from κύριος (kyrios, “lord”), and Jude has just said that the intruders deny “our only Master and Lord—Jesus Christ” (v. 4). Rejecting “lordship” would then mean rejecting the authority of Christ. Clement of Alexandria read it this way: “despise dominion … that is, the only Lord, who is truly our Lord, Jesus Christ.”64
  2. Angelic powers. In Eph 1:21 and Col 1:16, “lordship” (κυριότης) is one of a list of angelic ranks: “principality, and authority, and might, and lordship” (Eph 1:21, LSV). Since the next charge concerns “glorious [ones],” Jude might mean angelic authorities here too.
  3. Human church leaders. Some have suggested that the intruders despised the leadership of the community.

The first interpretation fits the immediate context best, since it echoes v. 4. It also fits the contrast with the angels of v. 6, who left their place under God’s authority. The singular “lordship,” without an article, may also suggest an abstract principle: the intruders reject the very idea of being under authority.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ἀθετέω: “properly, to make ἄθετον, or do away with what has been laid down … to reject: … Ju 8.”↩︎

  2. Clement of Alexandria, Adumbrationes on Jude 8, ANF 2. Clement adds: “They speak evil of majesty, that is, of the angels.”↩︎

δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν (doxas de blasphēmousin) — ‘and slander glorious ones’

The third charge is the most puzzling. The verb βλασφημέω (blasphēmeō) means “to slander, revile, speak abusively of.” The object δόξας (doxas), literally “glories,” refers to glorious beings, almost certainly angels. The LSV’s bracketed “[ones]” signals that the Greek has only the plural noun. Second Peter’s parallel confirms the angelic reference: “they are not afraid to speak evil of glorious ones, whereas messengers, being greater in strength and power, do not bear a slanderous judgment against them before the LORD” (2 Pet 2:10–11, LSV).

Why would anyone slander angels? Jude does not say, and scholars have proposed several explanations:

  • Disparaging the angels as guardians of the moral law. Jewish and early Christian tradition held that the Law of Moses was given “through messengers” (Gal 3:19; Acts 7:53; Heb 2:2). If the intruders taught that grace freed them from the moral law, they might have belittled the angels associated with that law. This is a suggestion drawn from the biblical evidence just cited, not a fact recorded in Jude.65
  • Mocking evil powers. If the “glorious ones” include fallen angels (some argue this from the Michael example, where the slander concerns the Devil), the intruders may have treated spiritual evil with contempt, claiming that their spiritual status put them beyond its reach.
  • General irreverence toward the whole unseen order of God’s creation.

The example that follows, Michael’s restraint toward the Devil, suggests that Jude’s main point is the intruders’ presumption. Whatever beings they slandered, they spoke with an authority they did not possess.

  1. The texts are Gal 3:19; Acts 7:53; Heb 2:2; compare LXX Deut 33:2. Older commentators read the “glories” variously. Clement of Alexandria took them as angels (Adumbrationes on Jude 8). The Pulpit Commentary and others discuss both angelic and human authorities (on Jude 8).↩︎

ὁ δὲ Μιχαὴλ ὁ ἀρχάγγελος (ho de Michaēl ho archangelos) — ‘but Michael the archangel’

Michael is one of only two angels named in the Protestant canon of Scripture; the other is Gabriel. In Daniel he is “Michael, first of the chief heads” and “the great head, who is standing up for the sons of your people” (Dan 10:13; 12:1, LSV), the guardian of Israel. In Revelation, “Michael and his messengers warred against the dragon” (Rev 12:7, LSV). Jude calls him ὁ ἀρχάγγελος (ho archangelos), “the archangel,” literally “the chief messenger,” as the LSV renders it. The only other New Testament use of the word is in 1 Thess 4:16, “with the voice of a chief-messenger” (LSV).

The choice of Michael heightens the contrast. If anyone had the standing to condemn the Devil, it was the commander of heaven’s armies.

ὅτε τῷ διαβόλῳ διακρινόμενος διελέγετο περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος (hote tō diabolō diakrinomenos dielegeto peri tou Mōuseōs sōmatos) — ‘when, contending with the devil, he argued about the body of Moses’

Two legal or debating verbs describe the encounter. διακρινόμενος (diakrinomenos) means “contending, disputing,” often in a judicial sense. διελέγετο (dielegeto) means “was arguing, debating.” The scene is a dispute, perhaps a kind of court case, “about the body of Moses” (περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος, peri tou Mōyseōs sōmatos), over who had rights to it.

The Old Testament says only this about Moses’ death: “Moses, servant of the Lord, dies there in the land of Moab, according to the command of YHWH; and He buries him in a valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-Peor, and no man has known his burying place to this day” (Deut 34:5–6, LSV). The mysterious burial, done by God himself in an unknown place, invited speculation, and a tradition grew up that angels were involved. Jude’s version, the only surviving ancient form of the story that names a dispute between Michael and the Devil, is explored in the deep dive below.

οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας (ouk etolmēsen krisin epenenkein blasphēmias) — ‘did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment’

The key phrase οὐκ ἐτόλμησεν κρίσιν ἐπενεγκεῖν βλασφημίας (ouk etolmēsen krisin epenenkein blasphēmias) can be read in two ways.

  1. “He did not dare to pronounce a slanderous (or abusive) judgment against him.” The genitive βλασφημίας (blasphēmias) describes the kind of judgment: an insulting, reviling condemnation. Michael did not abuse the Devil, even though the Devil deserved condemnation. He left judgment to God. This is the traditional reading (“durst not bring against him a railing accusation,” WBS) and the one most translations follow.
  2. “He did not presume to condemn him for slander.” The genitive names the charge: Michael did not pronounce a verdict of “slander” against the Devil. On this reading, which draws on an ancient Greek fragment preserved in a catena (a chain of excerpts from early commentators) and on the lost ending of the Testament of Moses (see the deep dive), the Devil had slandered Moses by calling him a murderer. Michael, though in the right, did not presume to judge the Devil for this slander and appealed to God instead.66

Both readings reach the same point. Michael, though an archangel and in the right, recognized that judgment over a fellow spiritual being belonged to God alone. The intruders, mere humans, pass judgment freely on beings far above them.

The verb ἐτόλμησεν (etolmēsen), “he dared,” is important. Jude does not say Michael was unable to condemn the Devil, or that the Devil deserved no condemnation. He says Michael did not dare. The restraint was reverence, not weakness.

  1. J. B. Mayor, Expositor’s Greek Testament (1910), on Jude 9, quoting the catena fragment (see n. 14) and R. H. Charles’s summary in his edition of the Assumption of Moses (1897). Public domain; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/jude/1.htm.↩︎

ἀλλὰ εἶπεν· Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος (alla eipen: Epitimēsai soi kyrios) — ‘but said: may the Lord rebuke you’

Michael’s words, Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος (Epitimēsai soi kyrios), use the optative of wish: “May the Lord rebuke you!” This is the second optative in Jude, after “be multiplied” in v. 2. The LSV prints “LORD” in capitals, indicating that the reference is to the God of Israel.

The words echo Zechariah’s vision of Joshua the high priest, accused by Satan before the angel of the LORD: “And YHWH says to Satan: ‘YHWH pushes against you, O Satan, / Indeed, YHWH pushes against you’” (Zech 3:2, LSV). The Greek Septuagint renders the same words as Ἐπιτιμήσαι Κύριος ἐν σοί, διάβολε, “May the Lord rebuke you, O Devil,” nearly identical to Jude.67 In both scenes, a heavenly figure facing the accuser leaves the rebuke to God.

Zechariah 3 will return in Jude 23: the high priest Joshua is “a brand delivered from fire” and is “clothed with filthy garments” (Zech 3:2–3, LSV), images that reappear in Jude’s call to snatch others “out of fire” and to hate the “coat having been stained from the flesh.”

  1. LXX Zech 3:2: Καὶ εἶπε Κύριος πρὸς τὸν διάβολον, Ἐπιτιμήσαι Κύριος ἐν σοὶ διάβολε (Brenton’s Greek Septuagint).↩︎

οὗτοι δὲ ὅσα μὲν οὐκ οἴδασιν βλασφημοῦσιν (houtoi de hosa men ouk oidasin blasphēmousin) — ‘but these people slander whatever they do not understand’

Verse 10 returns to the intruders, “these” (οὗτοι, houtoi), with a pointed contrast built on two verbs of knowing:

  • ὅσα μὲν οὐκ οἴδασιν βλασφημοῦσιν (hosa men ouk oidasin blasphēmousin), “whatever they do not know, they slander.” The verb οἶδα (oida) here refers to knowledge of spiritual realities, the unseen world of angels and authority. Those who claimed revelatory dreams are, in Jude’s judgment, ignorant of the very realm they speak about.

ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐπίστανται, ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται (hosa de physikōs hōs ta aloga zōa epistantai, en toutois phtheirontai) — ‘and what they know by instinct, like irrational animals, is what destroys them’

  • ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα ἐπίστανται (hosa de physikōs hōs ta aloga zōa epistantai), “whatever they understand by instinct, like unreasoning animals.” The second verb, ἐπίσταμαι (epistamai), means “to understand, know how.” The adverb φυσικῶς (physikōs), “naturally, by nature,”68 found only here in the New Testament, describes knowledge that comes from instinct, not reason or revelation. The phrase τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα (ta aloga zōa), “the irrational animals,” literally “the creatures without logos,” without reason or speech, was a stock expression for brute beasts.

Then the verdict: ἐν τούτοις φθείρονται (en toutois phtheirontai), “by these things they are destroyed” or “in these they are corrupted.” The verb φθείρω (phtheirō) means both “to corrupt” and “to destroy, ruin,” and Jude may intend both: the appetites they follow corrupt them morally and are leading them to destruction.

The irony is sharp. The intruders claim higher knowledge through dreams. In reality they are ignorant of spiritual things, and the only knowledge they truly possess is the instinctive knowledge of appetite, which they share with animals and which is ruining them. Clement of Alexandria paraphrased: “He means that they eat, and drink, and indulge in uncleanness, and says that they do other things that are common to them with animals, devoid of reason.”69 Paul’s description of those whose “god [is] the belly, and whose glory [is] in their shame” (Phil 3:19, LSV) is similar.

  2. Clement of Alexandria, Adumbrationes on Jude 10, ANF 2.↩︎

D. Original-Language Investigation

Greek Transliteration Basic meaning In context Notes

βλασφημέω / βλασφημία blasphēmeō / blasphēmia slander, revile / slander “speak evil of” / “slander” Not only against God; any abusive speech.

διαλέγομαι dialegomai argue, discuss “reasoning”
