A note on διάβολος. The Greek word for “Devil” means “slanderer” or “accuser.” There is a quiet irony in the scene. Michael refuses to slander the Slanderer, while the intruders slander even “glorious ones.” The term diabolos is used in the Septuagint of Zech 3:1–2 for the accuser (Hebrew haśśāṭān, “the adversary”), which strengthens the connection between Jude 9 and Zechariah 3.

A note on διακρίνομαι. The verb describing Michael’s dispute will reappear in v. 22 for those who are “doubting” or “wavering.” It is a good example of a word whose sense depends entirely on context: “dispute” in v. 9, “doubt” or “waver” (or perhaps “dispute” again) in v. 22. Chapter 12 explores the possibility that Jude intends a link.

Deep dive: Michael the archangel and the body of Moses

Jude’s reference to a dispute over Moses’ body is one of the most intriguing puzzles in the New Testament. The Old Testament contains no such story. Where did it come from?

What the Bible says. Deuteronomy 34:5–6 records that Moses died “according to the command of YHWH” (literally “at the mouth of YHWH”) and that “He buries him … and no man has known his burying place to this day” (LSV). God himself buried Moses, and the grave was unknown. That combination of divine burial and hidden grave naturally invited questions. Who carried out the burial? Why was the grave hidden? Was there opposition?

What early Christians said about Jude’s source. Several early Christian writers connected Jude 9 to a specific Jewish book:

  • Clement of Alexandria (c. 200), commenting on Jude 9, writes: “Here he confirms the assumption of Moses.”70 The Latin translation preserves the phrase assumptionem Moysi, which may refer either to a book (the Assumption of Moses) or to the event of Moses’ being “taken up.”
  • Origen (c. 230), in On First Principles, refers to “the work entitled The Ascension of Moses (a little treatise, of which the Apostle Jude makes mention in his Epistle),” in which “the archangel Michael, when disputing with the devil regarding the body of Moses, says that the serpent, being inspired by the devil, was the cause of Adam and Eve’s transgression.”71
  • Later writers also refer to this work. Didymus the Blind (fourth century), in his exposition of Jude, says that some doubted the canonicity of the letter because of this quotation from an apocryphal book. Gelasius of Cyzicus quotes the Assumption in a way that later enabled scholars to identify a surviving manuscript.72

What survives. In the mid-nineteenth century Antonio Ceriani discovered in the Ambrosian Library in Milan a single, incomplete sixth-century Latin manuscript of a Jewish work in which Moses, before his death, prophesies Israel’s history to Joshua. Ceriani published it in 1861 and identified it, through its agreement with a quotation in Gelasius, as the Assumption of Moses. R. H. Charles later argued that the surviving text is better called the Testament of Moses, since it contains Moses’ farewell speech but no account of his being taken up, and that the testament and the assumption may originally have been distinct works or parts of a combined one. The manuscript breaks off before Moses’ death. The dispute between Michael and the Devil does not appear in what survives, and it may have stood in the lost ending.73

Reconstructing the story. The most important clue survives in Greek. In a catena, a medieval chain of excerpts from early commentators, the story is told this way: when Moses had died on the mountain, “Michael is sent to remove the body; then, when the devil slandered Moses and proclaimed him a murderer because he struck the Egyptian, the angel, not bearing the slander against him, said to the devil, ‘May God rebuke you.’” (The Greek reads ὁ Μιχαὴλ ἀποστέλλεται μεταθήσων τὸ σῶμα, εἶτα τοῦ διαβόλου κατὰ τοῦ Μωυσέως βλασφημοῦντος καὶ φονέα ἀναγορεύοντος διὰ τὸ πατάξαι τὸν Αἰγύπτιον, οὐκ ἐνεγκὼν τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ βλασφημίαν ὁ ἄγγελος, Ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι ὁ Θεός, πρὸς τὸν διάβολον ἔφη.) R. H. Charles summarized the surviving fragments: Michael is commissioned to bury Moses, and Satan opposes the burial on two grounds. First, he claims to be the lord of matter, so the body belongs to him; Michael answers, “The Lord rebuke thee, for it was God’s spirit which created the world and all mankind.” Second, he brings the charge of murder against Moses, who had killed an Egyptian (Exod 2:11–12).74 The tenth-century commentator Oecumenius reports a similar tradition.75 Because the original ending is lost, every reconstruction is provisional. Even the old Cambridge commentary cautioned that such later traditions “may have grown out of the words of St Jude instead of being the foundation on which they rested.”

How did Jude use the story? Jude uses it as he uses the examples of vv. 5–7: as a known story with a clear moral point. He assumes his readers know it, mentions only what he needs, and draws a single lesson. He does not quote a book by name or introduce the story as Scripture.

Did Jude believe the event happened? Interpreters answer this differently.

  • Some hold that Jude, writing under the guidance of the Spirit, affirmed a true event preserved in Jewish tradition. Calvin, for example, judged that since “the Jews at that time had many things from the traditions of the fathers,” it was not unreasonable to say “that Jude referred to what had already been handed down for many ages.”76
  • Others hold that Jude used a familiar story as an illustration, much as a modern preacher might cite a well-known parable or a classic novel, without endorsing its historicity. On this view the authority lies in the moral point, not in the narrative details.
  • Still others think the question cannot be settled and is not essential to understanding Jude’s argument.

All agree on the point Jude draws: if the archangel Michael did not presume to pronounce judgment on the Devil, how much less should mere humans slander heavenly beings? Readers may hold different views about the story’s origin and still receive its lesson.

Why did the story matter in Jude’s world? A story about angels disputing over Moses’ body would have resonated with Jewish readers for whom Moses was the supreme prophet and lawgiver, and for whom the hidden grave was a sign of his unique relationship with God. In a community debating authority, revelation, and the moral law, a story in which even the great archangel deferred to God’s authority over the body of the lawgiver was a pointed choice.

E. The Historical and Cultural World

Angels and the law. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at Sinai and mediated the giving of the Law (Deut 33:2 LXX; Jubilees 1:27–29; Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19; Heb 2:2). Stephen speaks of Israel as those “who received the Law by arrangement of messengers” (Acts 7:53, LSV). If the intruders rejected the moral authority of the law of God, it would be natural for them to speak disparagingly of the angels associated with it.

Dreams and revelation in the ancient world. Throughout the ancient Mediterranean, dreams were widely regarded as a channel of divine communication. Jewish tradition accepted that God could speak through dreams, as with Joseph and Daniel, but also warned against dreamers who led people astray (Deut 13; Jer 23). Early Christianity valued prophecy and visions while insisting on testing them (1 Cor 14:29; 1 Thess 5:19–21; 1 John 4:1). The Didache warned that a prophet’s claims were to be judged by his “ways,” his conduct.77 Jude’s “dreamers” fall under this kind of judgment.

Testaments and “assumptions.” Jewish literature of the period included many “testaments,” farewell discourses of patriarchs before death (the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, the Testament of Moses), and stories of figures “taken up” to heaven (Enoch, Elijah, and in some traditions Moses). Jude’s references to Moses’ body and to Enoch (vv. 14–15) show that he and his readers were at home in this literature.

  1. Didache 11.8, ANF 7: “from their ways shall the false prophet and the prophet be known.”↩︎

F. Connections Across Scripture

Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Jeremiah 23:25–32 (background for “dreaming”). The “dreamer of a dream” who leads people to “go after other gods” (Deut 13:1–2, LSV) is the clearest Old Testament background for Jude’s term. The verbal link is strongest in the Greek Old Testament, where Jude’s word appears. This is probably a deliberate echo, though Jude does not quote the passage.

Zechariah 3:1–4 (direct allusion). Michael’s words in Jude 9 match the Septuagint of Zech 3:2 almost exactly. Since Zechariah 3 also supplies the imagery of Jude 23, Jude, or his source, seems to have known the whole scene well.

2 Peter 2:10–12 (literary parallel). Second Peter generalizes Jude’s example: “messengers, being greater in strength and power, do not bear a slanderous judgment against them before the LORD” (2 Pet 2:11, LSV). It omits the names of Michael and Moses and the specific story, perhaps because the story came from a non-canonical source. It also expands Jude’s comparison to animals: “as irrational natural beasts, made to be caught and destroyed” (2 Pet 2:12, LSV).

Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1; Revelation 12:7–9 (Michael). These passages establish Michael as Israel’s guardian and the leader of the heavenly forces against the dragon. Jude’s portrait of a Michael who refuses to presume is all the more striking against that background.

Matthew 4:10 (shared theme). When Jesus dismisses Satan in the wilderness, he does so by appealing to Scripture: “it has been written” (Matt 4:10, LSV). Like Michael, he grounds his response in God’s authority rather than his own.

Romans 1:22–24; Philippians 3:19 (shared theme). Paul’s description of those who, “professing to be wise, … were made fools” (Rom 1:22, LSV) and were given up to their desires parallels Jude’s portrait of people who claim higher knowledge yet live by animal appetite.

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. What is the source of the Michael story, and what does its use imply? Discussed in the deep dive. The source is most likely a lost ending of the Testament or Assumption of Moses. Christians have drawn different conclusions about what Jude’s use of the story implies about its historical truth.

2. What is “lordship,” and who are the “glorious ones”? Discussed above. The most likely readings are the Lord’s authority and angels, respectively. Alternatives are noted.

3. What does “a judgment of slander” mean? “A slanderous judgment” (traditional) or “a condemnation for slander” (reconstructed setting). Both lead to the same point.

4. Should Christians “rebuke the Devil”? Some modern Christian practices encourage believers to address and rebuke Satan directly in prayer. Jude 9 has been cited on both sides of this question. Some read it as a model, since Michael’s words are a form of rebuke spoken in God’s name. Others read it as a caution, since Michael refused to pronounce judgment himself and appealed to God. Jude’s own point concerns slander and presumption, not techniques of spiritual warfare. The verse most clearly teaches humility: whatever believers say about spiritual evil should be said in dependence on God’s authority, not their own.

H. The Passage Within Jude

Verse 8 is the first application in the letter’s alternating pattern of text and application. Verses 5–7 supplied the text, and v. 8 says “In like manner … those dreaming.” Verse 9 then introduces a second “text,” the Michael story, and v. 10 applies it: “But these…”

The passage also prepares for what follows. The animal comparison of v. 10 anticipates the woe on those who follow Cain, Balaam, and Korah (v. 11). The theme of slanderous speech anticipates the “harsh [words]” of v. 15 and the “swollen words” of v. 16. The phrase “they understand naturally” anticipates the description of the intruders in v. 19 as ψυχικοί (psychikoi), “natural” people “not having the Spirit.” In Jude’s view, the intruders’ claimed spirituality is in fact the opposite of spirituality.

I. Contemporary Understanding

Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

Testing claimed revelations. Movements in every generation claim new revelations, special dreams, or private words from God that set aside the received faith or its moral teaching. Jude, like Deuteronomy and the Didache, suggests a test. Does the claimed revelation lead toward the faith “once delivered” and toward holiness, or away from them? Christian traditions differ on the place of ongoing prophecy in the church. They can agree that no experience authorizes a believer to “defile the flesh” or reject the lordship of Christ.

Reverence in speech about spiritual realities. Michael’s restraint may challenge both careless mockery of spiritual realities and presumptuous bravado toward them. Christians may speak about evil truthfully and confidently, yet without contempt or self-reliance, leaving final judgment to God.

The danger of contempt. Jude’s charge is that the intruders “speak evil of” what they do not understand. Contempt for what one has not understood is a common failing in religious and political disputes today. Jude’s example invites believers to examine their own speech, including their speech about the people Jude warns against.

Appetite and identity. Jude’s picture of people who know their appetites “like the irrational beasts” may prompt reflection on how far modern life is shaped by instinctive desire, often deliberately cultivated by commerce and media, and on how Christian discipleship offers a different kind of knowledge and freedom.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. Jude describes the intruders as “dreaming,” probably meaning that they claimed revelations that justified their behavior. How can individuals and communities test claims to spiritual experience today?
  2. Why do you think Jude chose a story about Michael and the Devil to make his point about slander? What would be lost if he had simply said, “Do not slander angels”?
  3. Michael “did not dare” to pronounce judgment, even on the Devil. What does this suggest about the attitude believers should have toward those they consider enemies of God?
  4. Jude contrasts two kinds of knowledge: ignorance of spiritual realities and instinctive knowledge of appetite. Where do you see these two kinds of “knowing” in your own life or culture?
  5. How do you respond to the fact that Jude draws on a story not found in the Old Testament? Does it affect how you read the letter? Why or why not?

לֹא־יְדַעְתָּם וְנָעָבְדֵם 3 [13:4] לֹא תִשְׁמַע אֶל־דִּבְרֵי הַנָּבִיא הַהוּא אוֹ אֶל־חוֹלֵם הַחֲלוֹם הַהוּא כִּי מְנַסֶּה יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֶתְכֶם לָדַעַת הֲיִשְׁכֶם אֹהֲבִים אֶת־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁכֶם 4 [13:5] אַחֲרֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם תֵּלֵכוּ וְאֹתוֹ תִירָאוּ וְאֶת־מִצְוֺתָיו תִּשְׁמֹרוּ וּבְקֹלוֹ תִשְׁמָעוּ וְאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹדוּ וּבוֹ תִדְבָּקוּן 5 [13:6] וְהַנָּבִיא הַהוּא אוֹ חֹלֵם הַחֲלוֹם הַהוּא יוּמָת כִּי דִבֶּר־סָרָה עַל־יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הַמּוֹצִיא אֶתְכֶם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וְהַפֹּדְךָ מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים לְהַדִּיחֲךָ מִן־הַדֶּרֶךְ אֲשֶׁר צִוְּךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לָלֶכֶת בָּהּ וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ 6 [13:7] כִּי יְסִיתְךָ אָחִיךָ בֶן־אִמֶּךָ אוֹ־בִנְךָ אוֹ־בִתְּךָ אוֹ אֵשֶׁת חֵיקֶךָ אוֹ רֵעֲךָ אֲשֶׁר כְּנַפְשְׁךָ בַּסֵּתֶר לֵאמֹר נֵלְכָה וְנַעַבְדָה אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַעְתָּ אַתָּה וַאֲבֹתֶיךָ 7 [13:8] מֵאֱלֹהֵי הָעַמִּים אֲשֶׁר סְבִיבֹתֵיכֶם הַקְּרֹבִים אֵלֶיךָ אוֹ הָרְחֹקִים מִמֶּךָּ מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ וְעַד־קְצֵה הָאָרֶץ 8 [13:9] לֹא־תֹאבֶה לוֹ וְלֹא תִשְׁמַע אֵלָיו וְלֹא־תָחוֹס עֵינְךָ עָלָיו וְלֹא־תַחְמֹל וְלֹא־תְכַסֶּה עָלָיו 9 [13:10] כִּי הָרֹג תַּהַרְגֶנּוּ יָדְךָ תִּהְיֶה־בּוֹ בָרִאשׁוֹנָה לַהֲמִיתוֹ וְיַד כָּל־הָעָם בָּאַחֲרֹנָה 10 [13:11] וּסְקַלְתּוֹ בָאֲבָנִים וָמֵת כִּי בִקֵּשׁ לְהַדִּיחֲךָ מֵעַל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ הַמּוֹצִיאֲךָ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם מִבֵּית עֲבָדִים 11 [13:12] וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵל יִשְׁמְעוּ וְיִרָאוּן וְלֹא־יוֹסִפוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כַּדָּבָר הָרָע הַזֶּה בְּקִרְבֶּךָ 12 [13:13] כִּי־תִשְׁמַע בְּאַחַת עָרֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ נֹתֵן לְךָ לָשֶׁבֶת שָׁם לֵאמֹר 13 [13:14] יָצְאוּ אֲנָשִׁים בְּנֵי־בְלִיַּעַל מִקִּרְבֶּךָ וַיַּדִּיחוּ אֶת־יֹשְׁבֵי עִירָם לֵאמֹר נֵלְכָה וְנַעַבְדָה אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יְדַעְתֶּם 14 [13:15] וְדָרַשְׁתָּ וְחָקַרְתָּ וְשָׁאַלְתָּ הֵיטֵב וְהִנֵּה אֱמֶת נָכוֹן הַדָּבָר נֶעֶשְׂתָה הַתּוֹעֵבָה הַזֹּאת בְּקִרְבֶּךָ 15 [13:16] הַכֵּה תַכֶּה אֶת־יֹשְׁבֵי הָעִיר ההוא לְפִי־חָרֶב הַחֲרֵם אֹתָהּ וְאֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־בָּהּ וְאֶת־בְּהֶמְתָּהּ לְפִי־חָרֶב 16 [13:17] וְאֶת־כָּל־שְׁלָלָהּ תִּקְבֹּץ אֶל־תּוֹךְ רְחֹבָהּ וְשָׂרַפְתָּ בָאֵשׁ אֶת־הָעִיר וְאֶת־כָּל־שְׁלָלָהּ כָּלִיל לַיהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ וְהָיְתָה תֵּל עוֹלָם לֹא תִבָּנֶה עוֹד 17 [13:18] וְלֹא־יִדְבַּק בְּיָדְךָ מְאוּמָה מִן־הַחֵרֶם לְמַעַן יָשׁוּב יְהוָה מֵחֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ וְנָתַן־לְךָ רַחֲמִים וְרִחַמְךָ וְהִרְבֶּךָ כַּאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּע לַאֲבֹתֶיךָ 18 [13:19] כִּי תִשְׁמַע בְּקוֹל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־כָּל־מִצְוֺתָיו אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹת הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ

English (BSB)

1 If a prophet or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder to you, 2 and if the sign or wonder he has spoken to you comes about, but he says, “Let us follow other gods (which you have not known) and let us worship them,” 3 you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul. 4 You are to follow the LORD your God and fear Him. Keep His commandments and listen to His voice; serve Him and hold fast to Him. 5 Such a prophet or dreamer must be put to death, because he has advocated rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery; he has tried to turn you from the way in which the LORD your God has commanded you to walk. So you must purge the evil from among you. 6 If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you, saying, “Let us go and worship other gods” (which neither you nor your fathers have known, 7 the gods of the peoples around you, whether near or far, whether from one end of the earth or the other), 8 you must not yield to him or listen to him. Show him no pity, and do not spare him or shield him. 9 Instead, you must surely kill him. Your hand must be the first against him to put him to death, and then the hands of all the people. 10 Stone him to death for trying to turn you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. 11 Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing among you. 12 If, regarding one of the cities the LORD your God is giving you to inhabit, you hear it said 13 that wicked men have arisen from among you and have led the people of their city astray, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods” (which you have not known), 14 then you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly. And if it is established with certainty that this abomination has been committed among you, 15 you must surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword. Devote to destruction all its people and livestock. 16 And you are to gather all its plunder in the middle of the public square, and completely burn the city and all its plunder as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. The city must remain a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt. 17 Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands, so that the LORD will turn from His fierce anger, grant you mercy, show you compassion, and multiply you as He swore to your fathers, 18 because you obey the LORD your God, keeping all His commandments I am giving you today and doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD your God.

English (WEB)

1 If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, 2 and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying, “Let’s go after other gods” (which you have not known) “and let’s serve them,” 3 you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or to that dreamer of dreams; for the LORD your God is testing you, to know whether you love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul. 4 You shall walk after the LORD your God, fear him, keep his commandments, and obey his voice. You shall serve him, and cling to him. 5 That prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to draw you aside out of the way which the LORD your God commanded you to walk in. So you shall remove the evil from among you. 6 If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying, “Let’s go and serve other gods”—which you have not known, you, nor your fathers; 7 of the gods of the peoples who are around you, near to you, or far off from you, from the one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth— 8 you shall not consent to him nor listen to him; neither shall your eye pity him, neither shall you spare, neither shall you conceal him; 9 but you shall surely kill him. Your hand shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterwards the hands of all the people. 10 You shall stone him to death with stones, because he has sought to draw you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. 11 All Israel shall hear, and fear, and shall not do any more wickedness like this among you. 12 If you hear about one of your cities, which the LORD your God gives you to dwell there, that 13 certain wicked fellows have gone out from among you and have drawn away the inhabitants of their city, saying, “Let’s go and serve other gods,” which you have not known, 14 then you shall inquire, investigate, and ask diligently. Behold, if it is true, and the thing certain, that such abomination was done among you, 15 you shall surely strike the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword, destroying it utterly, with all that is therein and its livestock, with the edge of the sword. 16 You shall gather all its plunder into the middle of its street, and shall burn with fire the city, with all of its plunder, to the LORD your God. It shall be a heap forever. It shall not be built again. 17 Nothing of the devoted thing shall cling to your hand, that the LORD may turn from the fierceness of his anger and show you mercy, and have compassion on you and multiply you, as he has sworn to your fathers, 18 when you listen to the LORD your God’s voice, to keep all his commandments which I command you today, to do that which is right in the LORD your God’s eyes.

Jeremiah 23

Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)

1 הוֹי רֹעִים מְאַבְּדִים וּמְפִצִים אֶת־צֹאן מַרְעִיתִי נְאֻם־יְהוָה 2 לָכֵן כֹּה־אָמַר יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל־הָרֹעִים הָרֹעִים אֶת־עַמִּי אַתֶּם הֲפִצֹתֶם אֶת־צֹאנִי וַתַּדִּחוּם וְלֹא פְקַדְתֶּם אֹתָם הִנְנִי פֹקֵד עֲלֵיכֶם אֶת־רֹעַ מַעַלְלֵיכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה 3 וַאֲנִי אֲקַבֵּץ אֶת־שְׁאֵרִית צֹאנִי מִכֹּל הָאֲרָצוֹת אֲשֶׁר־הִדַּחְתִּי אֹתָם שָׁם וַהֲשִׁבֹתִי אֶתְהֶן עַל־נְוֵהֶן וּפָרוּ וְרָבוּ 4 וַהֲקִמֹתִי עֲלֵיהֶם רֹעִים וְרָעוּם וְלֹא־יִירְאוּ עוֹד וְלֹא־יֵחַתּוּ וְלֹא יִפָּקֵדוּ נְאֻם־יְהוָה 5 הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם־יְהוָה וַהֲקִמֹתִי לְדָוִד צֶמַח צַדִּיק וּמָלַךְ מֶלֶךְ וְהִשְׂכִּיל וְעָשָׂה מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה בָּאָרֶץ 6 בְּיָמָיו תִּוָּשַׁע יְהוּדָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח וְזֶה־שְּׁמוֹ אֲשֶׁר־יִקְרְאוֹ יְהוָה צִדְקֵנוּ 7 לָכֵן הִנֵּה־יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם־יְהוָה וְלֹא־יֹאמְרוּ עוֹד חַי־יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלָה אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם 8 כִּי אִם־חַי־יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱלָה וַאֲשֶׁר הֵבִיא אֶת־זֶרַע בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ צָפוֹנָה וּמִכֹּל הָאֲרָצוֹת אֲשֶׁר הִדַּחְתִּים שָׁם וְיָשְׁבוּ עַל־אַדְמָתָם 9 לַנְּבִאִים נִשְׁבַּר לִבִּי בְקִרְבִּי רָחֲפוּ כָּל־עַצְמוֹתַי הָיִיתִי כְּאִישׁ שִׁכּוֹר וּכְגֶבֶר עֲבָרוֹ יָיִן מִפְּנֵי יְהוָה וּמִפְּנֵי דִּבְרֵי קָדְשׁוֹ 10 כִּי מְנָאֲפִים מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ כִּי־מִפְּנֵי אָלָה אָבְלָה הָאָרֶץ יָבְשׁוּ נְאוֹת מִדְבָּר וַתְּהִי מְרוּצָתָם רָעָה וּגְבוּרָתָם לֹא־כֵן 11 כִּי־גַם־נָבִיא גַם־כֹּהֵן חָנֵפוּ גַּם־בְּבֵיתִי מָצָאתִי רָעָתָם נְאֻם־יְהוָה 12 לָכֵן יִהְיֶה דַרְכָּם לָהֶם כַּחֲלַקְלַקּוֹת בָּאֲפֵלָה יִדַּחוּ וְנָפְלוּ בָהּ כִּי־אָבִיא עֲלֵיהֶם רָעָה שְׁנַת פְּקֻדָּתָם נְאֻם־יְהוָה 13 וּבִנְבִיאֵי שֹׁמְרוֹן רָאִיתִי תִפְלָה הִנַּבְּאוּ בַבַּעַל וַיַּתְעוּ אֶת־עַמִּי אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל 14 וּבִנְבִאֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם רָאִיתִי שַׁעֲרוּרָה נָאוֹף וְהָלֹךְ בַּשֶּׁקֶר וְחִזְּקוּ יְדֵי מְרֵעִים לְבִלְתִּי־שָׁבוּ אִישׁ מֵרָעָתוֹ הָיוּ־לִי כֻלָּם כִּסְדֹם וְיֹשְׁבֶיהָ כַּעֲמֹרָה 15 לָכֵן כֹּה־אָמַר יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת עַל־הַנְּבִאִים הִנְנִי מַאֲכִיל אוֹתָם לַעֲנָה וְהִשְׁקִתִים מֵי־רֹאשׁ כִּי מֵאֵת נְבִיאֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם יָצְאָה חֲנֻפָּה לְכָל־הָאָרֶץ 16 כֹּה־אָמַר יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת אַל־תִּשְׁמְעוּ עַל־דִּבְרֵי הַנְּבִאִים הַנִּבְּאִים לָכֶם מַהְבִּלִים הֵמָּה אֶתְכֶם חֲזוֹן לִבָּם יְדַבֵּרוּ לֹא מִפִּי יְהוָה 17 אֹמְרִים אָמוֹר לִמְנַאֲצַי דִּבֶּר יְהוָה שָׁלוֹם יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וְכֹל הֹלֵךְ בִּשְׁרִרוּת לִבּוֹ אָמְרוּ לֹא־תָבוֹא עֲלֵיכֶם רָעָה 18 כִּי מִי עָמַד בְּסוֹד יְהוָה וְיֵרֶא וְיִשְׁמַע אֶת־דְּבָרוֹ מִי־הִקְשִׁיב דברי וַיִּשְׁמָע 19 הִנֵּה סַעֲרַת יְהוָה חֵמָה יָצְאָה וְסַעַר מִתְחוֹלֵל עַל רֹאשׁ רְשָׁעִים יָחוּל 20 לֹא יָשׁוּב אַף־יְהוָה עַד־עֲשֹׂתוֹ וְעַד־הֲקִימוֹ מְזִמּוֹת לִבּוֹ בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים תִּתְבּוֹנְנוּ בָהּ בִּינָה 21 לֹא־שָׁלַחְתִּי אֶת־הַנְּבִאִים וְהֵם רָצוּ לֹא־דִבַּרְתִּי אֲלֵיהֶם וְהֵם נִבָּאוּ 22 וְאִם־עָמְדוּ בְּסוֹדִי וְיַשְׁמִעוּ דְבָרַי אֶת־עַמִּי וִישִׁבוּם מִדַּרְכָּם הָרָע וּמֵרֹעַ מַעַלְלֵיהֶם 23 הַאֱלֹהֵי מִקָּרֹב אָנִי נְאֻם־יְהוָה וְלֹא אֱלֹהֵי מֵרָחֹק 24 אִם־יִסָּתֵר אִישׁ בַּמִּסְתָּרִים וַאֲנִי לֹא־אֶרְאֶנּוּ נְאֻם־יְהוָה הֲלוֹא אֶת־הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת־הָאָרֶץ אֲנִי מָלֵא נְאֻם־יְהוָה 25 שָׁמַעְתִּי אֵת אֲשֶׁר־אָמְרוּ הַנְּבִאִים הַנִּבְּאִים בִּשְׁמִי שֶׁקֶר לֵאמֹר חָלַמְתִּי חָלָמְתִּי 26 עַד־מָתַי הֲיֵשׁ בְּלֵב הַנְּבִאִים נִבְּאֵי הַשָּׁקֶר וּנְבִיאֵי תַּרְמִת לִבָּם 27 הַחֹשְׁבִים לְהַשְׁכִּיחַ אֶת־עַמִּי שְׁמִי בַּחֲלוֹמֹתָם אֲשֶׁר יְסַפְּרוּ אִישׁ לְרֵעֵהוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׁכְחוּ אֲבוֹתָם אֶת־שְׁמִי בַּבָּעַל 28 הַנָּבִיא אֲשֶׁר־אִתּוֹ חֲלוֹם יְסַפֵּר חֲלוֹם וַאֲשֶׁר דְּבָרִי אִתּוֹ יְדַבֵּר דְּבָרִי אֱמֶת מַה־לַתֶּבֶן אֶת־הַבָּר נְאֻם־יְהוָה 29 הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ נְאֻם־יְהוָה וּכְפַטִּישׁ יְפֹצֵץ סָלַע 30 לָכֵן הִנְנִי עַל־הַנְּבִאִים נְאֻם־יְהוָה מְגַנְּבֵי דְבָרַי אִישׁ מֵאֵת רֵעֵהוּ 31 הִנְנִי עַל־הַנְּבִיאִם נְאֻם־יְהוָה הַלֹּקְחִים לְשׁוֹנָם וַיִּנְאֲמוּ נְאֻם 32 הִנְנִי עַל־נִבְּאֵי חֲלֹמוֹת שֶׁקֶר נְאֻם־יְהוָה וַיְסַפְּרוּם וַיַּתְעוּ אֶת־עַמִּי בְּשִׁקְרֵיהֶם וּבְפַחֲזוּתָם וְאָנֹכִי לֹא־שְׁלַחְתִּים וְלֹא צִוִּיתִים וְהוֹעֵיל לֹא־יוֹעִילוּ לָעָם־הַזֶּה נְאֻם־יְהוָה 33 וְכִי־יִשְׁאָלְךָ הָעָם הַזֶּה אוֹ־הַנָּבִיא אוֹ־כֹהֵן לֵאמֹר מַה־מַשָּׂא יְהוָה וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵיהֶם אֶת־מַה־מַשָּׂא וְנָטַשְׁתִּי אֶתְכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה 34 וְהַנָּבִיא וְהַכֹּהֵן וְהָעָם אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר מַשָּׂא יְהוָה וּפָקַדְתִּי עַל־הָאִישׁ הַהוּא וְעַל־בֵּיתוֹ 35 כֹּה תֹאמְרוּ אִישׁ עַל־רֵעֵהוּ וְאִישׁ אֶל־אָחִיו מֶה־עָנָה יְהוָה וּמַה־דִּבֶּר יְהוָה 36 וּמַשָּׂא יְהוָה לֹא תִזְכְּרוּ־עוֹד כִּי הַמַּשָּׂא יִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ דְּבָרוֹ וַהֲפַכְתֶּם אֶת־דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת אֱלֹהֵינוּ 37 כֹּה תֹאמַר אֶל־הַנָּבִיא מֶה־עָנָךְ יְהוָה וּמַה־דִּבֶּר יְהוָה 38 וְאִם־מַשָּׂא יְהוָה תֹּאמֵרוּ לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה יַעַן אֲמָרְכֶם אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה מַשָּׂא יְהוָה וָאֶשְׁלַח אֲלֵיכֶם לֵאמֹר לֹא תֹאמְרוּ מַשָּׂא יְהוָה 39 לָכֵן הִנְנִי וְנָשִׁיתִי אֶתְכֶם נָשֹׁא וְנָטַשְׁתִּי אֶתְכֶם וְאֶת־הָעִיר אֲשֶׁר נָתַתִּי לָכֶם וְלַאֲבוֹתֵיכֶם מֵעַל פָּנָי 40 וְנָתַתִּי עֲלֵיכֶם חֶרְפַּת עוֹלָם וּכְלִמּוּת עוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר לֹא תִשָּׁכֵחַ

English (BSB)

1 “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” declares the LORD. 2 Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the shepherds who tend My people: “You have scattered My flock and driven them away, and have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds, declares the LORD. 3 Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them, and I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply. 4 I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing, declares the LORD. 5 Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land. 6 In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness. 7 So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they will no longer say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.’ 8 Instead they will say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.’ Then they will dwell once more in their own land.” 9 As for the prophets: My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble. I have become like a drunkard, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD, because of His holy words. 10 For the land is full of adulterers— because of the curse, the land mourns and the pastures of the wilderness have dried up— their course is evil and their power is misused. 11 “For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness,” declares the LORD. 12 “Therefore their path will become slick; they will be driven away into the darkness and fall into it. For I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD. 13 “Among the prophets of Samaria I saw an offensive thing: They prophesied by Baal and led My people Israel astray. 14 And among the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: They commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns his back on wickedness. They are all like Sodom to Me; the people of Jerusalem are like Gomorrah.” 15 Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says concerning the prophets: “I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has spread throughout the land.” 16 This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD. 17 They keep saying to those who despise Me, ‘The LORD says that you will have peace,’ and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart, ‘No harm will come to you.’ 18 But which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word? Who has given heed to His word and obeyed it? 19 Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked. 20 The anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart. In the days to come you will understand this clearly. 21 I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message; I did not speak to them, yet they have prophesied. 22 But if they had stood in My council, they would have proclaimed My words to My people and turned them back from their evil ways and deeds.” 23 “Am I only a God nearby,” declares the LORD, “and not a God far away?” 24 “Can a man hide in secret places where I cannot see him?” declares the LORD. “Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” declares the LORD. 25 “I have heard the sayings of the prophets who prophesy lies in My name: ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’ 26 How long will this continue in the hearts of these prophets who prophesy falsehood, these prophets of the delusion of their own minds? 27 They suppose the dreams that they tell one another will make My people forget My name, just as their fathers forgot My name through the worship of Baal. 28 Let the prophet who has a dream retell it, but let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” declares the LORD. 29 “Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?” 30 “Therefore behold,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who steal from one another words they attribute to Me.” 31 “Yes,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who wag their own tongues and proclaim, ‘The LORD declares it.’” 32 “Indeed,” declares the LORD, “I am against those who prophesy false dreams and retell them to lead My people astray with their reckless lies. It was not I who sent them or commanded them, and they are of no benefit at all to these people,” declares the LORD. 33 “Now when this people or a prophet or priest asks you, ‘What is the burden of the LORD?’ you are to say to them, ‘What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD.’ 34 As for the prophet or priest or anyone who claims, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ I will punish that man and his household. 35 This is what each man is to say to his friend and to his brother: ‘What has the LORD answered?’ or ‘What has the LORD spoken?’ 36 But refer no more to the burden of the LORD, for each man’s word becomes the burden, so that you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of Hosts, our God. 37 Thus you are to say to the prophet: ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and ‘What has the LORD spoken?’ 38 But if you claim, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ then this is what the LORD says: Because you have said, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ and I specifically told you not to make this claim, 39 therefore I will surely forget you and will cast you out of My presence, both you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers. 40 And I will bring upon you everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation that will never be forgotten.”

English (WEB)

1 “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” says the LORD. 2 Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says against the shepherds who feed my people: “You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and have not visited them. Behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings,” says the LORD. 3 “I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they will be fruitful and multiply. 4 I will set up shepherds over them who will feed them. They will no longer be afraid or dismayed, neither will any be lacking,” says the LORD. 5 “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will raise to David a righteous Branch; and he will reign as king and deal wisely, and will execute justice and righteousness in the land. 6 In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell safely. This is his name by which he will be called: The LORD our righteousness. 7 “Therefore, behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that they will no more say, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt;’ 8 but, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up and who led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country, and from all the countries where I had driven them.’ Then they will dwell in their own land.” 9 Concerning the prophets: My heart within me is broken. All my bones shake. I am like a drunken man, and like a man whom wine has overcome, because of the LORD, and because of his holy words. 10 “For the land is full of adulterers; for because of the curse the land mourns. The pastures of the wilderness have dried up. Their course is evil, and their might is not right; 11 for both prophet and priest are profane. Yes, in my house I have found their wickedness,” says the LORD. 12 Therefore their way will be to them as slippery places in the darkness. They will be driven on, and fall therein; for I will bring evil on them, even the year of their visitation,” says the LORD. 13 “I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria. They prophesied by Baal, and caused my people Israel to err. 14 In the prophets of Jerusalem I have also seen a horrible thing: they commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one returns from his wickedness. They have all become to me as Sodom, and its inhabitants as Gomorrah.” 15 Therefore the LORD of Armies says concerning the prophets: “Behold, I will feed them with wormwood, and make them drink poisoned water; for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has gone out into all the land.” 16 The LORD of Armies says, “Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They teach you vanity. They speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD. 17 They say continually to those who despise me, ‘The LORD has said, “You will have peace;”’ and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart they say, ‘No evil will come on you.’ 18 For who has stood in the council of the LORD, that he should perceive and hear his word? Who has listened to my word, and heard it? 19 Behold, the LORD’s storm, his wrath, has gone out. Yes, a whirling storm! It will burst on the head of the wicked. 20 The LORD’s anger will not return until he has executed and performed the intents of his heart. In the latter days, you will understand it perfectly. 21 I didn’t send these prophets, yet they ran. I didn’t speak to them, yet they prophesied. 22 But if they had stood in my council, then they would have caused my people to hear my words, and would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings. 23 “Am I a God at hand,” says the LORD, “and not a God afar off? 24 Can anyone hide himself in secret places so that I can’t see him?” says the LORD. “Don’t I fill heaven and earth?” says the LORD. 25 “I have heard what the prophets have said, who prophesy lies in my name, saying, ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’ 26 How long will this be in the heart of the prophets who prophesy lies, even the prophets of the deceit of their own heart? 27 They intend to cause my people to forget my name by their dreams which they each tell his neighbor, as their fathers forgot my name because of Baal. 28 The prophet who has a dream, let him tell a dream; and he who has my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the straw to the wheat?” says the LORD. 29 “Isn’t my word like fire?” says the LORD; “and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces? 30 “Therefore behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who each steal my words from his neighbor. 31 Behold, I am against the prophets,” says the LORD, “who use their tongues, and say, ‘He says.’ 32 Behold, I am against those who prophesy lying dreams,” says the LORD, “who tell them, and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their vain boasting; yet I didn’t send them or command them. They don’t profit this people at all,” says the LORD. 33 “When this people, or the prophet, or a priest, asks you, saying, ‘What is the message from the LORD?’ Then you shall tell them, ‘“What message? I will cast you off,” says the LORD.’ 34 As for the prophet, the priest, and the people, who say, ‘The message from the LORD,’ I will even punish that man and his household. 35 You will say everyone to his neighbor, and everyone to his brother, ‘What has the LORD answered?’ and, ‘What has the LORD said?’ 36 You will mention the message from the LORD no more, for every man’s own word has become his message; for you have perverted the words of the living God, of the LORD of Armies, our God. 37 You will say to the prophet, ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and, ‘What has the LORD spoken?’ 38 Although you say, ‘The message from the LORD,’ therefore the LORD says: ‘Because you say this word, “The message from the LORD,” and I have sent to you, telling you not to say, “The message from the LORD,” 39 therefore behold, I will utterly forget you, and I will cast you off with the city that I gave to you and to your fathers, away from my presence. 40 I will bring an everlasting reproach on you, and a perpetual shame, which will not be forgotten.’”

Jeremiah 34:9

Chapter 5. The Way of Cain, the Error of Balaam, the Rebellion of Korah (Jude 11)

A. The Text

The Greek text

11 οὐαὶ αὐτοῖς, ὅτι τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Κάϊν ἐπορεύθησαν, καὶ τῇ πλάνῃ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ μισθοῦ ἐξεχύθησαν, καὶ τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κόρε ἀπώλοντο.

— Jude 11, SBLGNT

What the earliest manuscripts read

Where the manuscripts differ in a way that affects translation, the table gives each reading and the manuscripts that have it. B. Plain-English Orientation

Jude now speaks as a prophet. He pronounces a “woe” over the intruders, an announcement of coming judgment mixed with lament. He gives the reason by comparing them to three notorious figures from Israel’s scriptures:

  • Cain, the first murderer, who killed his brother out of envy;
  • Balaam, the prophet-for-hire, who led Israel into immorality and idolatry for profit;
  • Korah, the Levite who rebelled against the leadership God had appointed and was swallowed by the earth.

Each figure stands for a kind of sin that Jude sees in the intruders. The three verbs also trace a progression: they went in Cain’s way, they abandoned themselves to Balaam’s error, and they perished in Korah’s rebellion. Jude speaks of their destruction as if it had already happened, because in his view it is as certain as Korah’s was.

C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

οὐαὶ αὐτοῖς (ouai autois) — ‘woe to them’

The interjection οὐαί (ouai), “woe!” or “alas!”, is the classic opening of a prophetic oracle of judgment. Isaiah pronounces a series of them: “Woe [to] those saying to evil ‘good,’ and to good ‘evil’” (Isa 5:20, LSV). Habakkuk, Amos, and other prophets use the same form. Jesus pronounced woes on the rich and on the scribes and Pharisees (Luke 6:24–26; Matt 23:13–36). The Epistle of Enoch, part of 1 Enoch that Jude knew, contains long series of woes against sinners: “Woe to those who build unrighteousness and oppression / And lay deceit as a foundation; / For they shall be suddenly overthrown” (1 Enoch 94:6, trans. Charles).78

Outside the Gospels and Revelation, the word “woe” appears in the New Testament only twice: in Paul’s “woe is to me if I may not proclaim good news” (1 Cor 9:16, LSV) and here.79 Jude’s is the only woe pronounced against others in the New Testament letters. It marks this verse as the emotional and prophetic climax of the first half of his argument.

A woe is not a curse that the speaker wishes on someone. It is a solemn announcement that judgment is coming. It often carries a note of grief. The English “alas” catches some of that tone.

  1. 1 Enoch 94:6, trans. R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917), Wikisource. Woes continue through chs. 94–100.↩︎

  2. Computed from MorphGNT/SBLGNT: οὐαί occurs in Matthew (13), Mark (2), Luke (15), 1 Corinthians (1, at 9:16), Jude (1), and Revelation (14).↩︎

ὅτι τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Κάϊν ἐπορεύθησαν (hoti tē hodō tou Kain eporeuthēsan) — ‘for they went the way of Cain’

The first verb, ἐπορεύθησαν (eporeuthēsan), “they went, walked,” pictures a course of life, a “way” (ὁδός, hodos) followed by choice. To walk in someone’s way is to follow that person’s example. The phrase τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Κάϊν (tē hodō tou Kain), “the way of Cain,” does not refer only to one act of murder. It refers to the kind of life Cain represents.

What did Cain represent? Genesis tells the bare story: Cain’s offering was not accepted, he became angry, and he killed his brother Abel. When God asked where Abel was, Cain replied, “I have not known; am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen 4:9, LSV). The deep dive below shows how Jewish and Christian interpreters filled out the picture. For Jude’s purpose, three features are most likely in view:

  • Envy and hatred of a brother. First John draws exactly this lesson: “not as Cain—he was of the evil one, and he slew his brother. And for [what] reason did he slay him? Because his works were evil, and those of his brother [were] righteous” (1 John 3:12, LSV). Jude’s intruders are divisive (v. 19), and they sit at the love feasts while betraying their meaning (v. 12).
  • Cynicism about judgment. Jewish tradition remembered Cain as the first person to deny that God judges. In the Targum’s retelling, Cain says to Abel, “There is neither judgment nor Judge, nor another world; nor will good reward be given to the righteous, nor vengeance be taken of the wicked.”80 Jude’s intruders, the “scoffers” of v. 18, live as if judgment were not real.
  • Corrupting others. Josephus describes Cain after his exile as one who “excited his acquaintance to procure pleasures and spoils by robbery, and became a great leader of men into wicked courses.”81 Jude’s intruders lead others astray.

Jude does not say which aspect he means. He may intend the whole tradition. Cain is the first person in Scripture to turn against God’s order and against his brother, the father of a “way” that others follow.

  2. Josephus, Antiquities 1.2.2 (Whiston), Project Gutenberg #2848.↩︎

καὶ τῇ πλάνῃ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ μισθοῦ ἐξεχύθησαν (kai tē planē tou Balaam misthou exechythēsan) — ‘and for pay they poured themselves into the error of Balaam’

The second verb is vivid. ἐξεχύθησαν (exechythēsan) is the passive of ἐκχέω (ekcheō), “to pour out.” Used of people it means “they were poured out,” that is, they gave themselves up wholly or abandoned themselves.82 The LSV’s “rushed” catches the headlong motion. The ASV has “ran riotously” (ASV), Webster “run greedily” (WBS), and the BSB “rushed headlong” (BSB). The intruders did not drift into Balaam’s error. They threw themselves into it.

“The deceit of Balaam” translates τῇ πλάνῃ τοῦ Βαλαάμ (tē planē tou Balaam). The noun πλάνη (planē) means “error, wandering, deception,” the state of going astray and leading others astray. It belongs to the same word family as the “stars going astray” (ἀστέρες πλανῆται, asteres planētai) of v. 13.

The phrase μισθοῦ (misthou), “for reward” or “for pay,” is a genitive of price: they abandoned themselves to error for wages. Balaam was famous for being hired. Moab’s king Balak sent elders “with divinations in their hand,” payment for the seer’s services (Num 22:7, LSV), and promised to honor him greatly (Num 22:17). Deuteronomy remembers that Moab “hired against you Balaam son of Beor … to revile you” (Deut 23:4, LSV). Second Peter summarizes: Balaam “loved a reward of unrighteousness” (2 Pet 2:15, LSV).

Balaam’s “error” was more than greed. According to Numbers, after he failed to curse Israel, it was “through the word of Balaam” that the Israelites were led “to cause a trespass against YHWH in the matter of Peor” (Num 31:16, LSV), the episode in which Israelite men engaged in sexual immorality with Moabite and Midianite women and joined in the worship of their gods (Num 25:1–3). Revelation puts the tradition plainly: Balaam “taught Balak to cast a stumbling-block before the sons of Israel, to eat idol-sacrifices, and to commit whoredom” (Rev 2:14, LSV). For Jude’s readers, Balaam was the prophet who, for profit, taught God’s people that immorality was permissible. The parallel with the intruders, who turn grace into licentiousness (v. 4) and flatter people “for the sake of profit” (v. 16), is exact.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ἐκχέω: “pass., of persons (like Lat. effundor), to give oneself up to (RV, ran riotously in): Ju 11.”↩︎

καὶ τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κόρε ἀπώλοντο (kai tē antilogia tou Kore apōlonto) — ‘and perished in the rebellion of Korah’

The third clause turns to rebellion. “Controversy” translates ἀντιλογίᾳ (antilogia), literally “speaking against,” hence “contradiction, dispute, rebellion.”83 The LSV’s “controversy” is literal. Most translations have “rebellion” (WEB, BSB) or “gainsaying” (ASV, WBS).

The word carries an echo that Jude’s Greek-reading audience may have heard. In the Septuagint, ἀντιλογία is the word used for the “water of contention” at Meribah, where Israel quarreled with Moses and God: Τοῦτο τὸ ὕδωρ Ἀντιλογίας, ‘This is the water of Contention’ (Num 20:13 LXX; also Num 27:14; Deut 32:51; 33:8). It is also used for legal disputes brought before judges (Exod 18:16; Deut 17:8; 19:17).84 The word suggests a challenge to God-given authority.

Korah’s story is told in Numbers 16. A Levite, already privileged to serve at the tabernacle, he led two hundred and fifty leaders of the congregation against Moses and Aaron. His slogan sounded spiritual and egalitarian: “Enough of you! For all the congregation—all of them [are] holy, and YHWH [is] in their midst; and why do you lift yourselves up above the assembly of YHWH?” (Num 16:3, LSV). Moses saw through it: “is it little to you that the God of Israel has separated you … and you have also sought the priesthood! Therefore, you and all your congregation are meeting against YHWH” (Num 16:9–11, LSV). The judgment was spectacular: “the earth opens her mouth and swallows them … and they go down—they and all that they have—alive to Sheol … and they perish from the midst of the assembly” (Num 16:32–33, LSV), while fire consumed the two hundred and fifty who offered incense (16:35).

The verb ἀπώλοντο (apōlonto), “they perished,” is in the aorist, a past tense. Jude speaks of the intruders as if they had already perished. Grammarians sometimes call this a “prophetic” use of the past tense: a future event is described as already accomplished because it is so certain. In a sense they perished when they joined Korah’s rebellion, as Korah’s company was doomed the moment it set itself against God. The word ἀπόλλυμι (apollymi) also links back to v. 5, where Jesus “destroyed” (ἀπώλεσεν, apōlesen) the unbelieving wilderness generation.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. ἀντιλογία: “[in LXX chiefly for רִיב] gain-saying, strife.”↩︎

  2. Brenton’s Greek Septuagint: Num 20:13; 27:14; Deut 32:51; 33:8 (the “water of contention”); Exod 18:16; Deut 17:8; 19:17; 21:5; 25:1 (legal disputes).↩︎

The progression of the three verbs

Read in sequence, the three verbs describe a downward path:

Verb Figure Stage
ἐπορεύθησαν, “they went” Cain Setting out on a way of life
ἐξεχύθησαν, “they rushed / abandoned themselves” Balaam Throwing oneself into it wholeheartedly
ἀπώλοντο, “they perished” Korah Reaching its end

The sins also escalate. Cain’s sin was personal: hatred, murder, and contempt for judgment. Balaam’s sin led others into sin for profit. Korah’s sin openly defied God’s appointed order. The intruders, Jude suggests, embody all three.

D. Original-Language Investigation

Greek Transliteration Basic meaning In context Notes
οὐαί ouai woe, alas “woe” Prophetic oracle of judgment; only woe against others in the NT letters.
πορεύομαι poreuomai go, walk, proceed “went on” Way of life; also vv. 16, 18.
ὁδός hodos way, road “the way of Cain” Pattern of life.
Κάϊν Kain Cain “Cain”
ἐκχέω (pass.) ekcheō pour out; (of persons) abandon oneself “rushed” Passive used reflexively.
πλάνη planē error, deception, wandering “deceit” Related to πλανῆται (v. 13).
Βαλαάμ Balaam Balaam “Balaam”
μισθός misthos wages, reward “for reward” Genitive of price.
ἀντιλογία antilogia contradiction, dispute, rebellion “controversy” LXX: Meribah “water of contention”; legal disputes.
Κόρε Kore Korah “Korah” Only here in the NT.
ἀπόλλυμι apollymi destroy; (mid.) perish “they perished” Aorist describing certain doom; links to v. 5.

A caution about “prophetic aorist.” Not every past tense in prophecy is a “prophetic aorist.” Here, though, the context makes the category apt. Jude has just said the intruders’ judgment is “written beforehand” (v. 4) and is about to quote Enoch’s prophecy of judgment in the past tense: “Behold, the LORD has come” (v. 14). The past tense expresses certainty.

Deep dive: Cain, Balaam, and Korah in Scripture and tradition

The three figures had rich afterlives in Jewish and Christian interpretation, and Jude’s readers would have heard his brief allusions against that background.

Cain.

  • In Genesis (4:1–16), Cain is the firstborn of Adam and Eve and a tiller of the ground. His offering is not accepted. God warns him that sin is crouching at the door but that he must rule over it (4:7). He kills Abel, denies responsibility, and is sentenced to be “a wanderer, even a trembling one” (4:12, LSV), though God marks him for protection.
  • In the New Testament, Cain is the archetype of hatred: “not as Cain—he was of the evil one” (1 John 3:12, LSV). Hebrews contrasts Abel’s faith with Cain’s lack of it: “By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice to God than Cain” (Heb 11:4, LSV). Jesus speaks of “all the righteous blood … from the blood of Abel the righteous” (Matt 23:35, LSV).
  • In Jewish tradition, Cain became the prototype of several vices. Josephus portrays him as “wholly intent upon getting,” the inventor of “measures and weights,” who “changed the world into cunning craftiness” and “became a great leader of men into wicked courses.”85 The Palestinian Targums turn the brothers’ conversation in the field into a theological argument, with Cain denying that there is “judgment” or a “Judge” or “another world,” and Abel affirming them, before Cain kills him.86 (The Targums as we have them were written down later than Jude, though they preserve older traditions. Their witness here is to a line of interpretation, not proof of what Jude had read.)

Any of these portraits could stand behind Jude’s “way of Cain.” Jealous hatred fits the divisions in v. 19. Leading others into sin and greed fit vv. 11–12 and 16. Denial of judgment fits the “scoffers” of v. 18. Jude’s brevity leaves the allusion open, and that openness allows it to cover the full range of the intruders’ behavior.

Balaam.

  • In Numbers 22–24, Balaam is a non-Israelite seer from Pethor on the Euphrates whom Balak, king of Moab, hires to curse Israel. Repeatedly, he insists, “If Balak gives to me the fullness of his house of silver and gold, I am not able to pass over the command of YHWH” (Num 24:13, LSV), and he ends up blessing Israel. His donkey sees the angel that he cannot see and speaks to him (22:21–35). Read by itself, the story is ambiguous. Balaam obeys God’s word in the end, but his eagerness to go, and God’s anger at his going (22:22), suggest mixed motives.
  • The rest of Scripture resolves the ambiguity negatively. Numbers 31:16 blames Balaam’s counsel for the apostasy at Peor. Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, and Joshua remember him as hired to curse Israel and as “the diviner” killed among Israel’s enemies (Deut 23:4–5; Neh 13:2; Josh 13:22). Micah calls Israel to “remember … What Balaam son of Beor answered” Balak (Mic 6:5, LSV).
  • In Jewish tradition, Josephus has Balaam advise the Midianites to send their most beautiful daughters to the Israelite camp to seduce the young men into abandoning their law and worshipping other gods, “for by this means God will be angry at them.”87
  • In the New Testament, Balaam becomes the type of the false teacher who is motivated by money and leads believers into immorality and idolatry (2 Pet 2:15–16; Rev 2:14).

Jude’s two words, “error” and “reward,” compress this whole tradition. The intruders are teachers who, for personal gain, mislead God’s people into sexual immorality while claiming spiritual authority.

Korah.

  • In Numbers 16, Korah, a Levite of the clan of Kohath, joined with the Reubenites Dathan, Abiram, and On to challenge Moses’ leadership and Aaron’s priesthood. God vindicated Moses: the earth swallowed the rebels, and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty incense-offerers. Afterward, God confirmed Aaron’s priesthood by making his rod blossom, so that “the murmurings of the sons of Israel” would cease (Num 17:5, LSV).
  • Elsewhere in Scripture, Korah’s rebellion is remembered as “striving against YHWH” (Num 26:9, LSV) and as envy: “they are envious of Moses in the camp, / Of Aaron, YHWH’s holy one” (Ps 106:16, LSV). Ben Sira recalls how “the congregation of Core” maligned Aaron “with fury and wrath” and were “consumed … with the fiery flame” (Sir 45:18–19, Brenton). Remarkably, “the sons of Korah did not die” (Num 26:11, LSV). Their descendants became temple singers, and several psalms bear their name.
  • In Jewish tradition, Korah became the archetype of the schismatic who challenges legitimate authority under the guise of spiritual equality.

Korah’s slogan, “all the congregation—all of them [are] holy,” sounds like something the New Testament itself might say, and in a sense it does (1 Pet 2:9). That is what makes him a fitting type for the intruders. Their rejection of authority (v. 8) may have been dressed in the language of spiritual freedom and equality. Korah shows that true statements can be used to justify rebellion against God’s order.

Why these three? All three are figures who opposed God’s purposes while associated in some way with God’s people or God’s word: a son of Adam, a prophet, and a Levite. All three led others, or tried to lead others, with them. All three met judgment. Together they show that the intruders’ danger lies not only in their own sin but in their influence on others.

E. The Historical and Cultural World

Prophetic speech in the early church. Early Christian communities recognized prophets alongside apostles and teachers (Acts 13:1; 1 Cor 12:28; Eph 4:11). Jude’s woe oracle shows him speaking with prophetic authority, in the tradition of Israel’s prophets and of Jesus. His opponents, the “dreamers,” may also have claimed prophetic gifts. Jude answers prophecy with prophecy, but his prophecy is anchored in Scripture.

Paid religious teachers. In the Greco-Roman world, philosophers and religious specialists often taught for fees, and critics of the time routinely mocked them for greed. Early Christians debated how traveling ministers should be supported. Paul defended the right to support but often declined it so as not to burden or mislead (1 Cor 9:3–18; 1 Thess 2:5–9). The Didache warns that a traveling apostle who “ask[s] money” is a false prophet.88 Balaam was a fitting type for teachers whose message bent to their income.

Interpreting Israel’s stories as types. Jewish and early Christian teachers commonly read figures from Israel’s history as patterns (Greek τύποι, typoi, “types”) for the present. Paul says of the wilderness stories, “these things happened to those persons as types, and they were written for our admonition” (1 Cor 10:11, LSV). Jude’s three figures are used in exactly this way.

  1. Didache 11.6, ANF 7.↩︎

F. Connections Across Scripture

1 John 3:11–12 (shared tradition). John’s use of Cain as the antithesis of brotherly love is the closest New Testament parallel to Jude’s reference. Both writers assume that their readers know Cain as a type of the person who belongs to the evil one.

2 Peter 2:15–16 (literary parallel). Peter expands Jude’s Balaam reference, mentioning Balaam’s love of “a reward of unrighteousness” and the “mute donkey” that “forbid the madness of the prophet” (LSV). He omits Cain and Korah.

Revelation 2:14 (shared tradition). The letter to Pergamum names “those holding the teaching of Balaam,” which Revelation defines as eating idol-sacrifices and committing sexual immorality. The parallel shows that Balaam had become a standard type of the antinomian teacher in early Christianity.

Numbers 16; Psalm 106:16–18; Sirach 45:18–19 (Korah). The core narrative and its later echoes. The theme of envy in Ps 106:16 parallels the grumbling of Jude 16.

Isaiah 5; Luke 6:24–26; Matthew 23 (woes). The prophetic and dominical woes provide the form of Jude’s oracle.

1 Corinthians 10:1–11 (method). Paul’s typological reading of the wilderness narratives, including the warning “neither murmur, as also some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor 10:10, LSV), parallels Jude’s method and some of his material.

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. Which aspect of Cain does Jude intend? Interpreters differ. Some emphasize hatred and murder (following 1 John), some the corruption of others (following Josephus), and some the denial of judgment (following the Targums). J. B. Mayor noted that for Philo, Cain is “the type of selfishness,” and that 1 John names him “as a type of jealous hate.”89 The allusion may be deliberately broad.

2. Is the aorist “they perished” prophetic? Most commentators take it so. An alternative view holds that Jude regards the intruders’ fate as already sealed by their choice, in the way Korah’s company was doomed as soon as it set itself against Moses.

3. How does Jude’s use of Balaam relate to Numbers 22–24? Numbers 22–24 portrays Balaam ambiguously, and other passages (Num 31; Deut 23; Neh 13; Josh 13) portray him negatively. Jude relies on the latter. This shows that the New Testament writers read individual passages in light of the whole canon and of traditional interpretation.

4. Is authority itself sacred? Jude’s use of Korah could be misused to defend any human authority against criticism. Moses and Aaron’s authority in Numbers 16 was explicitly God-given and confirmed by God. Korah’s sin was rebellion against God’s appointment, not criticism of human leaders as such. The Bible elsewhere honors prophets who challenged corrupt leaders (Nathan, Elijah, Jeremiah). Applying Jude 11 requires discernment about whether authority is truly from God and exercised under God.

  1. J. B. Mayor, Expositor’s Greek Testament (1910), on Jude 11, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/egt/jude/1.htm.↩︎

H. The Passage Within Jude

Verse 11 is the climax of the section that began in v. 8. The “dreamers” of v. 8, who slander what they do not understand and are ruled by instinct (v. 10), are now placed in a line of biblical rebels. The woe also prepares for the dense metaphors of vv. 12–13, which open “These are…” and describe the intruders’ character and fate. The three verbs of v. 11, went, rushed, and perished, recall the movement of the earlier examples, from salvation to destruction (v. 5).

The three figures also connect with later verses. Balaam’s “reward” anticipates the intruders’ flattery “for the sake of profit” (v. 16). Korah’s “murmuring” (Num 16:11; 17:5) anticipates the “discontented grumblers” of v. 16. Cain’s “way” anticipates their “walking according to their own lusts” (vv. 16, 18).

I. Contemporary Understanding

Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

Three enduring temptations. Cain, Balaam, and Korah represent temptations that recur in every religious community: resentment and hatred toward fellow believers; using spiritual influence for personal gain; and rejecting God’s order while using spiritual language to justify it. Jude’s woe may invite communities to examine themselves before they examine others.

Religion and money. Balaam’s “reward” remains a live issue. Churches and ministries today face questions about how leaders are supported, how money shapes messages, and how marketing can bend teaching. Jude does not condemn all payment for ministry; other New Testament writers defend it. He does condemn error embraced for profit.

Equality as a cover for rebellion. Korah’s slogan, “all the congregation—all of them [are] holy,” was true and yet was used to justify defiance of God’s appointment. Believers may need discernment to recognize when good principles are being used for self-promotion, while remaining open to legitimate challenges to leaders who abuse their position.

The weight of influence. All three figures harmed others. Teachers, parents, leaders, and anyone with influence may consider that their “way” becomes a path others walk.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. Why do you think Jude chose a “woe” rather than a simple warning? How does the form of a prophetic oracle change the effect of his words?
  2. Which of the three figures (Cain, Balaam, Korah) seems most relevant to the challenges facing Christians today? Why?
  3. Korah’s slogan was that “all the congregation” is holy. How can a community tell the difference between a legitimate challenge to leaders and a Korah-like rebellion?
  4. Balaam’s error was embraced “for reward.” In what subtle ways can financial or social rewards shape what religious leaders say, or what congregations want to hear?
  5. Jude’s three verbs describe a downward progression: going, rushing, perishing. Where might a person or community notice the early stages of such a path, and turn back?

יֹדַעַת אִישׁ לְמִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הֲרֹגוּ 18 וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם 19 וְאַתֶּם חֲנוּ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים כֹּל הֹרֵג נֶפֶשׁ וְכֹל נֹגֵעַ בֶּחָלָל תִּתְחַטְּאוּ בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי אַתֶּם וּשְׁבִיכֶם 20 וְכָל־בֶּגֶד וְכָל־כְּלִי־עוֹר וְכָל־מַעֲשֵׂה עִזִּים וְכָל־כְּלִי־עֵץ תִּתְחַטָּאוּ 21 וַיֹּאמֶר אֶלְעָזָר
