1 Corinthians 12

Greek (SBLGNT)

1 Περὶ δὲ τῶν πνευματικῶν, ἀδελφοί, οὐ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν. 2 οἴδατε ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦτε πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ ἄφωνα ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε ἀπαγόμενοι. 3 διὸ γνωρίζω ὑμῖν ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἐν πνεύματι θεοῦ λαλῶν λέγει· Ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦς, καὶ οὐδεὶς δύναται εἰπεῖν· Κύριος Ἰησοῦς εἰ μὴ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ. 4 Διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσίν, τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα· 5 καὶ διαιρέσεις διακονιῶν εἰσιν, καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς κύριος· 6 καὶ διαιρέσεις ἐνεργημάτων εἰσίν, ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς θεός, ὁ ἐνεργῶν τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν. 7 ἑκάστῳ δὲ δίδοται ἡ φανέρωσις τοῦ πνεύματος πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον. 8 ᾧ μὲν γὰρ διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος δίδοται λόγος σοφίας, ἄλλῳ δὲ λόγος γνώσεως κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, 9 ἑτέρῳ πίστις ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ πνεύματι, ἄλλῳ χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ πνεύματι, 10 ἄλλῳ ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων, ἄλλῳ προφητεία, 1ἄλλῳ διακρίσεις πνευμάτων, ἑτέρῳ γένη γλωσσῶν, 2ἄλλῳ ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν· 11 πάντα δὲ ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ καθὼς βούλεται. 12 Καθάπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα ἕν ἐστιν καὶ μέλη πολλὰ ἔχει, πάντα δὲ τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος πολλὰ ὄντα ἕν ἐστιν σῶμα, οὕτως καὶ ὁ Χριστός· 13 καὶ γὰρ ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι ἡμεῖς πάντες εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν, εἴτε Ἰουδαῖοι εἴτε Ἕλληνες, εἴτε δοῦλοι εἴτε ἐλεύθεροι, καὶ πάντες ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν. 14 Καὶ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα οὐκ ἔστιν ἓν μέλος ἀλλὰ πολλά. 15 ἐὰν εἴπῃ ὁ πούς· Ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ χείρ, οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ σώματος, οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ σώματος; 16 καὶ ἐὰν εἴπῃ τὸ οὖς· Ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ ὀφθαλμός, οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ σώματος, οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ σώματος· 17 εἰ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ὀφθαλμός, ποῦ ἡ ἀκοή; εἰ ὅλον ἀκοή, ποῦ ἡ ὄσφρησις; 18 νυνὶ δὲ ὁ θεὸς ἔθετο τὰ μέλη, ἓν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν, ἐν τῷ σώματι καθὼς ἠθέλησεν. 19 εἰ δὲ ἦν τὰ πάντα ἓν μέλος, ποῦ τὸ σῶμα; 20 νῦν δὲ πολλὰ μὲν μέλη, ἓν δὲ σῶμα. 21 οὐ δύναται δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς εἰπεῖν τῇ χειρί· Χρείαν σου οὐκ ἔχω, ἢ πάλιν ἡ κεφαλὴ τοῖς ποσίν· Χρείαν ὑμῶν οὐκ ἔχω· 22 ἀλλὰ πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὰ δοκοῦντα μέλη τοῦ σώματος ἀσθενέστερα ὑπάρχειν ἀναγκαῖά ἐστιν, 23 καὶ ἃ δοκοῦμεν ἀτιμότερα εἶναι τοῦ σώματος, τούτοις τιμὴν περισσοτέραν περιτίθεμεν, καὶ τὰ ἀσχήμονα ἡμῶν εὐσχημοσύνην περισσοτέραν ἔχει, 24 τὰ δὲ εὐσχήμονα ἡμῶν οὐ χρείαν ἔχει. ἀλλὰ ὁ θεὸς συνεκέρασεν τὸ σῶμα, τῷ ὑστεροῦντι περισσοτέραν δοὺς τιμήν, 25 ἵνα μὴ ᾖ σχίσμα ἐν τῷ σώματι, ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη. 26 καὶ εἴτε πάσχει ἓν μέλος, συμπάσχει πάντα τὰ μέλη· εἴτε δοξάζεται μέλος, συγχαίρει πάντα τὰ μέλη. 27 Ὑμεῖς δέ ἐστε σῶμα Χριστοῦ καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους. 28 καὶ οὓς μὲν ἔθετο ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ πρῶτον ἀποστόλους, δεύτερον προφήτας, τρίτον διδασκάλους, ἔπειτα δυνάμεις, ἔπειτα χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων, ἀντιλήμψεις, κυβερνήσεις, γένη γλωσσῶν. 29 μὴ πάντες ἀπόστολοι; μὴ πάντες προφῆται; μὴ πάντες διδάσκαλοι; μὴ πάντες δυνάμεις; 30 μὴ πάντες χαρίσματα ἔχουσιν ἰαμάτων; μὴ πάντες γλώσσαις λαλοῦσιν; μὴ πάντες διερμηνεύουσιν; 31 ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ μείζονα. καὶ ἔτι καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν ὑμῖν δείκνυμι.

English (BSB)

1 Now about spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. 2 You know that when you were pagans, you were influenced and led astray to mute idols. 3 Therefore I inform you that no one who is speaking by the Spirit of God says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit. 4 There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. 5 There are different ministries, but the same Lord. 6 There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. 7 Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. 8 To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, 10 to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. 11 All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines. 12 The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ. 13 For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink. 14 For the body does not consist of one part, but of many. 15 If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be? If the whole body were an ear, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But in fact, God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design. 19 If they were all one part, where would the body be? 20 As it is, there are many parts, but one body. 21 The eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need you.” Nor can the head say to the feet, “I do not need you.” 22 On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, 23 and the parts we consider less honorable, we treat with greater honor. And our unpresentable parts are treated with special modesty, 24 whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body and has given greater honor to the parts that lacked it, 25 so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another. 26 If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it. 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it. 28 And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues. 29 Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? 30 Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? 31 But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.

English (WEB)

1 Now concerning spiritual things, brothers, I don’t want you to be ignorant. 2 You know that when you were heathen, you were led away to those mute idols, however you might be led. 3 Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.” No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit. 4 Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. 5 There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. 6 There are various kinds of workings, but the same God who works all things in all. 7 But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all. 8 For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, 9 to another faith by the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healings by the same Spirit, 10 and to another workings of miracles, and to another prophecy, and to another discerning of spirits, to another different kinds of languages, and to another the interpretation of languages. 11 But the one and the same Spirit produces all of these, distributing to each one separately as he desires. 12 For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ. 13 For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit. 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot would say, “Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,” it is not therefore not part of the body. 16 If the ear would say, “Because I’m not the eye, I’m not part of the body,” it’s not therefore not part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be? 18 But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired. 19 If they were all one member, where would the body be? 20 But now they are many members, but one body. 21 The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.” 22 No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary. 23 Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant modesty, 24 while our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part, 25 that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. 26 When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. 27 Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually. 28 God has set some in the assembly: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracle workers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and various kinds of languages. 29 Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all miracle workers? 30 Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak with various languages? Do all interpret? 31 But earnestly desire the best gifts. Moreover, I show a most excellent way to you.

1 Corinthians 13

Greek (SBLGNT)

1 Ἐὰν ταῖς γλώσσαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων λαλῶ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον. 2 καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω προφητείαν καὶ εἰδῶ τὰ μυστήρια πάντα καὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γνῶσιν, καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω πᾶσαν τὴν πίστιν ὥστε ὄρη μεθιστάναι, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, οὐθέν εἰμι. 3 καὶ ἐὰν ψωμίσω πάντα τὰ ὑπάρχοντά μου, καὶ ἐὰν παραδῶ τὸ σῶμά μου, ἵνα καυθήσομαι, ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, οὐδὲν ὠφελοῦμαι. 4 Ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ, χρηστεύεται ἡ ἀγάπη, οὐ ζηλοῖ ἡ ἀγάπη, οὐ περπερεύεται, οὐ φυσιοῦται, 5 οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ, οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς, οὐ παροξύνεται, οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν, 6 οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ, συγχαίρει δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· 7 πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει. 8 Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε πίπτει. εἴτε δὲ προφητεῖαι, καταργηθήσονται· εἴτε γλῶσσαι, παύσονται· εἴτε γνῶσις, καταργηθήσεται. 9 ἐκ μέρους γὰρ γινώσκομεν καὶ ἐκ μέρους προφητεύομεν· 10 ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται. 11 ὅτε ἤμην νήπιος, ἐλάλουν ὡς νήπιος, ἐφρόνουν ὡς νήπιος, ἐλογιζόμην ὡς νήπιος· ὅτε γέγονα ἀνήρ, κατήργηκα τὰ τοῦ νηπίου. 12 βλέπομεν γὰρ ἄρτι δι’ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι, τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον· ἄρτι γινώσκω ἐκ μέρους, τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ἐπεγνώσθην. 13 νυνὶ δὲ μένει πίστις, ἐλπίς, ἀγάπη· τὰ τρία ταῦτα, μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη.

English (BSB)

1 If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. 3 If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing. 4 Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. 5 It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. 6 Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. 7 It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part, 10 but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away. 11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways. 12 Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. 13 And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.

English (WEB)

1 If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. 2 If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing. 3 If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing. 4 Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, 5 doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil; 6 doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; 7 bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things. 8 Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with. 9 For we know in part and we prophesy in part; 10 but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with. 11 When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things. 12 For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known. 13 But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.

1 Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε. 2 ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ ἀλλὰ θεῷ, οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει, πνεύματι δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια· 3 ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παραμυθίαν. 4 ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ ἑαυτὸν οἰκοδομεῖ· ὁ δὲ προφητεύων ἐκκλησίαν οἰκοδομεῖ. 5 θέλω δὲ πάντας ὑμᾶς λαλεῖν γλώσσαις, μᾶλλον δὲ ἵνα προφητεύητε· μείζων δὲ ὁ προφητεύων ἢ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσαις, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ διερμηνεύῃ, ἵνα ἡ ἐκκλησία οἰκοδομὴν λάβῃ. 6 Νῦν δέ, ἀδελφοί, ἐὰν ἔλθω πρὸς ὑμᾶς γλώσσαις λαλῶν, τί ὑμᾶς ὠφελήσω, ἐὰν μὴ ὑμῖν λαλήσω ἢ ἐν ἀποκαλύψει ἢ ἐν γνώσει ἢ ἐν προφητείᾳ ἢ ἐν διδαχῇ; 7 ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν διδόντα, εἴτε αὐλὸς εἴτε κιθάρα, ἐὰν διαστολὴν τοῖς φθόγγοις μὴ δῷ, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ αὐλούμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον; 8 καὶ γὰρ ἐὰν ἄδηλον φωνὴν σάλπιγξ δῷ, τίς παρασκευάσεται εἰς πόλεμον; 9 οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς γλώσσης ἐὰν μὴ εὔσημον λόγον δῶτε, πῶς γνωσθήσεται τὸ λαλούμενον; ἔσεσθε γὰρ εἰς ἀέρα λαλοῦντες. 10 τοσαῦτα εἰ τύχοι γένη φωνῶν εἰσιν ἐν κόσμῳ, καὶ οὐδὲν ἄφωνον· 11 ἐὰν οὖν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος. 12 οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς, ἐπεὶ ζηλωταί ἐστε πνευμάτων, πρὸς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ζητεῖτε ἵνα περισσεύητε. 13 Διὸ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ. 14 ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμά μου προσεύχεται, ὁ δὲ νοῦς μου ἄκαρπός ἐστιν. 15 τί οὖν ἐστιν; προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ· ψαλῶ τῷ πνεύματι, ψαλῶ δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ· 16 ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ; ἐπειδὴ τί λέγεις οὐκ οἶδεν· 17 σὺ μὲν γὰρ καλῶς εὐχαριστεῖς, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἕτερος οὐκ οἰκοδομεῖται. 18 εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ· 19 ἀλλὰ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ θέλω πέντε λόγους τῷ νοΐ μου λαλῆσαι, ἵνα καὶ ἄλλους κατηχήσω, ἢ μυρίους λόγους ἐν γλώσσῃ. 20 Ἀδελφοί, μὴ παιδία γίνεσθε ταῖς φρεσίν, ἀλλὰ τῇ κακίᾳ νηπιάζετε, ταῖς δὲ φρεσὶν τέλειοι γίνεσθε. 21 ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται ὅτι Ἐν ἑτερογλώσσοις καὶ ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέρων λαλήσω τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ, καὶ οὐδ’ οὕτως εἰσακούσονταί μου, λέγει κύριος. 22 ὥστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖόν εἰσιν οὐ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις, ἡ δὲ προφητεία οὐ τοῖς ἀπίστοις ἀλλὰ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν. 23 ἐὰν οὖν συνέλθῃ ἡ ἐκκλησία ὅλη ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ πάντες λαλῶσιν γλώσσαις, εἰσέλθωσιν δὲ ἰδιῶται ἢ ἄπιστοι, οὐκ ἐροῦσιν ὅτι μαίνεσθε; 24 ἐὰν δὲ πάντες προφητεύωσιν, εἰσέλθῃ δέ τις ἄπιστος ἢ ἰδιώτης, ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων, 25 τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας αὐτοῦ φανερὰ γίνεται, καὶ οὕτως πεσὼν ἐπὶ πρόσωπον προσκυνήσει τῷ θεῷ, ἀπαγγέλλων ὅτι Ὄντως ὁ θεὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστιν. 26 Τί οὖν ἐστιν, ἀδελφοί; ὅταν συνέρχησθε, ἕκαστος ψαλμὸν ἔχει, διδαχὴν ἔχει, ἀποκάλυψιν ἔχει, γλῶσσαν ἔχει, ἑρμηνείαν ἔχει· πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γινέσθω. 27 εἴτε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, κατὰ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος, καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω· 28 ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ᾖ διερμηνευτής, σιγάτω ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἑαυτῷ δὲ λαλείτω καὶ τῷ θεῷ. 29 προφῆται δὲ δύο ἢ τρεῖς λαλείτωσαν, καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι διακρινέτωσαν· 30 ἐὰν δὲ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ καθημένῳ, ὁ πρῶτος σιγάτω. 31 δύνασθε γὰρ καθ’ ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν, ἵνα πάντες μανθάνωσιν καὶ πάντες παρακαλῶνται 32 (καὶ πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται, 33 οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἀκαταστασίας ὁ θεὸς ἀλλὰ εἰρήνης), ὡς ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις τῶν ἁγίων. 34 Αἱ γυναῖκες ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν, οὐ γὰρ ἐπιτρέπεται αὐταῖς λαλεῖν· ἀλλὰ ὑποτασσέσθωσαν, καθὼς καὶ ὁ νόμος λέγει. 35 εἰ δέ τι μαθεῖν θέλουσιν, ἐν οἴκῳ τοὺς ἰδίους ἄνδρας ἐπερωτάτωσαν, αἰσχρὸν γάρ ἐστιν γυναικὶ λαλεῖν ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ. 36 ἢ ἀφ’ ὑμῶν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξῆλθεν, ἢ εἰς ὑμᾶς μόνους κατήντησεν; 37 Εἴ τις δοκεῖ προφήτης εἶναι ἢ πνευματικός, ἐπιγινωσκέτω ἃ γράφω ὑμῖν ὅτι κυρίου ἐστίν· 38 εἰ δέ τις ἀγνοεῖ, ἀγνοεῖται. 39 ὥστε, ἀδελφοί μου, ζηλοῦτε τὸ προφητεύειν, καὶ τὸ λαλεῖν μὴ κωλύετε γλώσσαις· 40 πάντα δὲ εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν γινέσθω.

English (BSB)

1 Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy. 2 For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit. 3 But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. 4 The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church. 5 I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified. 6 Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? 7 Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct? 8 Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle? 9 So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air. 10 Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning. 11 If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me. 12 It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church. 13 Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. 14 For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. 15 What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind. 16 Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? 17 You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified. 18 I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. 19 But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue. 20 Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature. 21 It is written in the Law: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.” 22 Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers. 23 So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds? 24 But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all, 25 and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, “God is truly among you!” 26 What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church. 27 If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret. 28 But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God. 29 Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said. 30 And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop. 31 For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged. 32 The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. 33 For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace—as in all the churches of the saints. 34 Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. 35 If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church. 36 Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached? 37 If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command. 38 But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored. 39 So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. 40 But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.

English (WEB)

1 Follow after love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. 2 For he who speaks in another language speaks not to men, but to God, for no one understands, but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries. 3 But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation. 4 He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly. 5 Now I desire to have you all speak with other languages, but even more that you would prophesy. For he is greater who prophesies than he who speaks with other languages, unless he interprets, that the assembly may be built up. 6 But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking with other languages, what would I profit you unless I speak to you either by way of revelation, or of knowledge, or of prophesying, or of teaching? 7 Even lifeless things that make a sound, whether pipe or harp, if they didn’t give a distinction in the sounds, how would it be known what is piped or harped? 8 For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war? 9 So also you, unless you uttered by the tongue words easy to understand, how would it be known what is spoken? For you would be speaking into the air. 10 There are, it may be, so many kinds of languages in the world, and none of them is without meaning. 11 If then I don’t know the meaning of the language, I would be to him who speaks a foreigner, and he who speaks would be a foreigner to me. 12 So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound to the building up of the assembly. 13 Therefore let him who speaks in another language pray that he may interpret. 14 For if I pray in another language, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful. 15 What should I do? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also. 16 Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the “Amen” at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say? 17 For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up. 18 I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all. 19 However, in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language. 20 Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature. 21 In the law it is written, “By men of strange languages and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people. They won’t even listen to me that way, says the Lord.” 22 Therefore other languages are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelieving; but prophesying is for a sign, not to the unbelieving, but to those who believe. 23 If therefore the whole assembly is assembled together and all speak with other languages, and unlearned or unbelieving people come in, won’t they say that you are crazy? 24 But if all prophesy, and someone unbelieving or unlearned comes in, he is reproved by all, and he is judged by all. 25 And thus the secrets of his heart are revealed. So he will fall down on his face and worship God, declaring that God is among you indeed. 26 What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, or has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up. 27 If any man speaks in another language, let there be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret. 28 But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself and to God. 29 Let two or three of the prophets speak, and let the others discern. 30 But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent. 31 For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be exhorted. 32 The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets, 33 for God is not a God of confusion but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints. 34 Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking except in submission, as the law also says, 35 if they desire to learn anything. “Let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a wife to be talking in the assembly.” 36 What!? Was it from you that the word of God went out? Or did it come to you alone? 37 If any man thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize the things which I write to you, that they are the commandment of the Lord. 38 But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant. 39 Therefore, brothers, desire earnestly to prophesy, and don’t forbid speaking with other languages. 40 Let all things be done decently and in order.

Chapter 11. Building, Praying, Keeping, Waiting (Jude 20–21)

A. The Text

B. Plain-English Orientation

After the long exposure of the intruders, Jude finally tells his readers what to do. He began by urging them to “fight for the faith” (v. 3). Here is what that fight consists of. It is not, first of all, an attack on the intruders. It is a way of life:

  • building one another up on the foundation of the holy faith;
  • praying in the power of the Holy Spirit;
  • keeping themselves in God’s love;
  • waiting with hope for the mercy of Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.

The grammar shows what matters most. There is one main command, “keep yourselves in the love of God,” and three supporting activities expressed as participles: building, praying, and waiting. These are the means by which believers remain in the love that God has already shown them (v. 1).

The passage also has a striking shape. It mentions the Holy Spirit, God (the Father), and the Lord Jesus Christ, and it gathers faith, love, and hope, the three great Christian virtues. In two verses Jude sketches the whole Christian life.

C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

ὑμεῖς δέ, ἀγαπητοί (hymeis de, agapētoi) — ‘but you, beloved’

For the third and last time, Jude addresses his readers as “beloved” (vv. 3, 17, 20). The emphatic Ὑμεῖς δέ (Hymeis de), “But you,” repeats the turn of v. 17 and sets the readers against the intruders just described. The intruders are “not having the Spirit” (v. 19). The readers pray “in the Holy Spirit” (v. 20). The contrast could hardly be sharper.

ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ὑμῶν πίστει (epoikodomountes heautous tē hagiōtatē hymōn pistei) — ‘building yourselves up on your most holy faith’

The participle ἐποικοδομοῦντες (epoikodomountes), “building up on,” comes from the language of construction: οἰκοδομέω (oikodomeō), “to build a house,” with the prefix ἐπί (epi), “upon.” The New Testament uses this image often for the growth of believers and of the church. Paul writes: “I have laid a foundation, and another builds on [it], for no one is able to lay another foundation except that which is laid, which is Jesus the Christ” (1 Cor 3:10–11, LSV). Believers are “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being chief corner-[stone]” (Eph 2:20, LSV), and are to be “rooted and built up in Him, and confirmed in the faith” (Col 2:7, LSV).

“Yourselves” (ἑαυτούς, heautous) is a reflexive pronoun. In the plural it often has a reciprocal sense, “one another.” Paul uses the same pronoun when he tells the Colossians to be “teaching and admonishing each other” (νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς, Col 3:16, LSV), and the Ephesians to be “forgiving one another” (χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς, Eph 4:32, LSV).149 Jude is not describing private self-improvement. He is describing a community building each other up: “build up one another, as also you do” (1 Thess 5:11, LSV).

“On your most holy faith” (τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ὑμῶν πίστει, tē hagiōtatē hymōn pistei). The foundation is “the faith,” the same faith “once delivered to the holy ones” that Jude urged his readers to contend for in v. 3. The phrase “your most holy faith” ties the end of the letter to its beginning. Contending for the faith (v. 3) and building on the faith (v. 20) are the same activity seen from two sides.

The adjective ἁγιωτάτῃ (hagiōtatē), “most holy,” is the superlative of ἅγιος (hagios), “holy.” It is the only superlative of that adjective in the New Testament.150 Jude chooses the strongest possible word. The faith is not a human tradition to be adjusted to taste. It is “most holy,” set apart by God and belonging to him. The intruders have turned grace into licentiousness (v. 4). The readers build on a faith that is holy through and through.

The Byzantine text puts the words in a different order, “on your most holy faith building yourselves up,” but the meaning is the same.151

  1. SBLGNT Col 3:16: διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς; Eph 4:32: χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς. The LSV renders these “teaching and admonishing each other” and “forgiving one another.”↩︎

  2. Computed from MorphGNT/SBLGNT: the only superlative form of ἅγιος in the New Testament is ἁγιωτάτῃ in Jude 20.↩︎

  3. SBLGNT apparatus: “ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ὑμῶν πίστει WH Treg NIV ] τῇ ἁγιωτάτῃ ὑμῶν πίστει ἐποικοδομοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς RP.”↩︎

ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ προσευχόμενοι (en pneumati hagiō proseuchomenoi) — ‘praying in the Holy Spirit’

The second participle, προσευχόμενοι (proseuchomenoi), “praying,” is qualified by ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ (en pneumati hagiō), “in the Holy Spirit.” See the deep dive below. In brief, it describes prayer that the Holy Spirit inspires, empowers, and guides. That is the opposite of the intruders, who are “not having the Spirit” (v. 19), and of their “dreaming” (v. 8), which Jude regards as false spirituality.

ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ τηρήσατε (heautous en agapē theou tērēsate) — ‘keep yourselves in the love of God’

Here is the main verb of the sentence and the central command of the letter: ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ τηρήσατε (heautous en agapē theou tērēsate), “keep yourselves in the love of God.” The aorist imperative τηρήσατε (tērēsate) is the fifth and final use of τηρέω, “keep,” the word that runs through the whole letter:

  • the readers “having been kept in Jesus Christ” (v. 1);
  • the angels who “did not keep” their place (v. 6);
  • the angels whom God “has kept” in bonds (v. 6);
  • the darkness that “has been kept” for the wandering stars (v. 13);
  • and now, “keep yourselves” (v. 21).

The readers have been kept by God, and now they are to keep themselves. The angels did not keep their position. The readers must keep theirs. See the deep dive below.

“The love of God” (ἀγάπῃ θεοῦ, agapē theou) could grammatically mean either God’s love for us or our love for God. In Jude, the first is clearly primary. The readers are “having been loved in God [the] Father” (v. 1). To “keep yourselves in the love of God” is to remain in the place where God’s love has put you. Jesus said: “According as the Father loved Me, I also loved you, remain in My love; if you may keep My commands, you will remain in My love” (John 15:9–10, LSV). Responding love for God is implied, but the foundation is God’s love.

προσδεχόμενοι τὸ ἔλεος τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (prosdechomenoi to eleos tou kyriou hēmōn Iēsou Christou) — ‘waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ’

The third participle is προσδεχόμενοι (prosdechomenoi), “waiting for, expecting.” It is the word used of Simeon, who was “looking for the comforting of Israel” (Luke 2:25, LSV), and of believers “waiting for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13, LSV). It describes active, eager expectation, not passive delay.

What the readers wait for is “the mercy (ἔλεος, eleos) of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Mercy was the first gift Jude wished his readers (v. 2). Here it is the mercy they will receive at Christ’s coming, when he comes to judge (vv. 14–15). Paul prays for a friend, “may the LORD give to him to find kindness from the LORD in that day” (2 Tim 1:18, LSV), using the same Greek word, ἔλεος. The coming that means judgment for the ungodly (vv. 14–15) means mercy for those who wait for it.

εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (eis zōēn aiōnion) — ‘leading to eternal life’

The final phrase, εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (eis zōēn aiōnion), “into eternal life,” names the goal of the waiting. The LSV supplies “[resulting]” to show that the Greek preposition εἰς expresses direction or result. Christ’s mercy leads to eternal life. The LSV’s “continuous life” reflects its consistent rendering of αἰώνιος (aiōnios). In New Testament usage the phrase means both life without end and the life that belongs to the age to come.

The contrast with the intruders’ destiny is deliberate. For them, “the gloom of the darkness throughout the age has been kept” (v. 13) and “continuous fire” is the example (v. 7). For the readers, the same word αἰώνιος describes life. Two destinies are set before the readers, and Jude’s command is to remain in the love that leads to life.

The shape of vv. 20–21

The sentence has a clear structure:

Element Greek Relation
building yourselves up on your most holy faith ἐποικοδομοῦντες participle (means)
praying in the Holy Spirit προσευχόμενοι participle (means)
keep yourselves in the love of God τηρήσατε main imperative
waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ προσδεχόμενοι participle (accompanying attitude)
into eternal life εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον goal

Two further patterns appear:

  • A Trinitarian pattern: the Holy Spirit (v. 20), the love of God the Father (v. 21), and the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ (v. 21). Jude does not offer a doctrine of the Trinity, but he speaks naturally of Spirit, Father, and Son as together the source of the Christian’s life. Paul does the same in 2 Cor 13:14.
  • A pattern of faith, love, and hope: “your most holy faith” (v. 20), “the love of God” (v. 21), and “waiting” for mercy and eternal life (v. 21), which is hope. Paul’s famous triad is “faith, hope, love—these three” (1 Cor 13:13, LSV). He also speaks of “your work of faith, and the labor of the love, and the endurance of the hope” (1 Thess 1:3, LSV). Jude’s version may reflect a shared early Christian pattern.

Deep dive: Praying in the Holy Spirit

What does it mean to pray “in the Holy Spirit”? The phrase ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ can be read in several ways, and Christian traditions have emphasized different aspects.

The New Testament background. The closest parallel is Eph 6:18: “praying at all times in the Spirit, and in this, watching in all perseverance and supplication for all the holy ones” (LSV). Paul also describes the Spirit’s role in prayer:

  • The Spirit enables the most basic Christian prayer, the cry to God as Father: “you received [the] Spirit of adoption in which we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Rom 8:15, LSV); “God sent forth the Spirit of His Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Gal 4:6, LSV).
  • The Spirit helps believers in their weakness: “the Spirit helps our weaknesses; for what we may pray for, as it is necessary, we have not known, but [this] One—the Spirit—makes intercession for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom 8:26, LSV).
  • In 1 Corinthians, Paul speaks of praying “in an [unknown] tongue” and says, “I will pray [in] the spirit, and I will also pray [with] understanding” (1 Cor 14:14–15, LSV).

Jesus speaks of worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24), and Paul of “serving God by the Spirit” (Phil 3:3, LSV).

Interpretations.

  1. Prayer inspired and guided by the Spirit. Most interpreters understand Jude to mean prayer that is prompted, empowered, and shaped by the Holy Spirit, prayer that flows from the Spirit’s presence in the believer and the community. On this reading, the phrase describes all genuine Christian prayer, including the “Abba, Father” of adoption and the Spirit’s help in weakness.
  2. Charismatic or ecstatic prayer. Some interpreters, especially in Pentecostal and charismatic traditions, see in Jude 20 a reference to Spirit-inspired prayer of the kind described in 1 Corinthians 14, including prayer in tongues. That is a possible reading, since Jude’s communities, like Paul’s, were probably familiar with such phenomena. Nothing in Jude’s wording, however, requires it.
  3. Prayer within the sphere of the Spirit, as opposed to the “natural” sphere of v. 19. This reading emphasizes the contrast with the intruders. Whatever the intruders’ spiritual claims, true prayer happens in the realm of the Holy Spirit.

These readings are not exclusive. What is clear from the context is Jude’s contrast. The intruders appealed to “dreams” and claimed spiritual superiority, but in Jude’s judgment they were “not having the Spirit.” The readers’ answer is not to reject spiritual experience but to pray in the Spirit, inside the community, on the foundation of the faith, and in the love of God. In Jude’s view, genuine spirituality is marked by prayer, holiness, love, and humility, not by private revelations that license sin.

Prayer as part of contending. It is significant that prayer is one of the means by which believers “fight for the faith” (v. 3). Jude does not imagine that false teaching can be met only with arguments. A praying community, dependent on the Spirit, is itself a defense of the faith.

Deep dive: Keeping oneself in the love of God

Jude’s central command, “keep yourselves in the love of God,” raises a question that runs through the whole letter: how does the believer’s keeping relate to God’s keeping?

God’s keeping comes first. The letter opens by describing the readers as “having been kept in Jesus Christ” (v. 1), or, as the Greek dative may also mean, kept for him. The perfect participle describes a settled state. It closes with praise to “Him who is able to guard you without stumbling” (v. 24). The readers’ security rests on God’s action, which frames the whole letter.

The believer’s keeping is real. Between those two statements stands the command of v. 21: “keep yourselves.” It is not a suggestion. The negative examples in the letter show what failure to keep looks like: the wilderness generation that did not believe (v. 5) and the angels who “did not keep their own principality” (v. 6).

How the two fit together. Jude does not explain the relationship theoretically, but the structure of vv. 20–21 suggests a practical answer. The believer keeps himself or herself in God’s love not by heroic effort but by staying where God’s love is found: building on the faith, praying in the Spirit, and waiting for Christ’s mercy. These are not ways of earning God’s love. They are ways of remaining in it. Jesus’ words in John 15 offer a parallel: “remain in My love; if you may keep My commands, you will remain in My love” (John 15:9–10, LSV). The love comes first, and obedience is the way of abiding in it.

An image may help. The love of God is like a sheltered harbor. God has brought the readers into it (v. 1), and God is able to keep them there (v. 24). The command “keep yourselves in the love of God” means: do not sail out of the harbor. Build up the community, pray, wait for the Lord, and you will remain where you have been placed.

Different traditions, one command. As noted in Chapter 1, Christian traditions explain the relationship between divine preservation and human perseverance differently. All can agree on Jude’s practical point: the command to keep oneself in God’s love is meant seriously, and the means of obeying it are building, praying, and waiting.

D. Original-Language Investigation

Greek Transliteration Basic meaning In context Notes
ἐποικοδομέω epoikodomeō build upon “building yourselves up” Construction image (1 Cor 3:10–14; Eph 2:20; Col 2:7).
ἑαυτούς heautous yourselves; one another “yourselves” Plural reflexive can be reciprocal (Col 3:16; Eph 4:32).
ἁγιώτατος hagiōtatos most holy “most holy” Only superlative of ἅγιος in the NT.
πίστις pistis faith “faith” The faith of v. 3.
προσεύχομαι proseuchomai pray “praying”
ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ en pneumati hagiō in the Holy Spirit “in the Holy Spirit” See deep dive.
τηρέω tēreō keep “keep” Aorist imperative; fifth use.
ἀγάπη θεοῦ agapē theou love of God “the love of God” Primarily God’s love for believers.
προσδέχομαι prosdechomai wait for, expect “waiting for” Eager expectation (Luke 2:25; Titus 2:13).
ἔλεος eleos mercy “the mercy” Echoes v. 2.
ζωὴ αἰώνιος zōē aiōnios eternal life “continuous life” Life of the age to come.

A grammatical note on the participles. Greek participles that accompany an imperative often take on some of its force. Many translations therefore render vv. 20–21 as a series of commands: ‘build yourselves up … pray … keep yourselves … wait’ (compare the WEB and BSB). That is legitimate. It is still worth seeing that Jude subordinates building, praying, and waiting to the single command to keep oneself in God’s love. They are not three extra tasks. They are how the one task is done.

E. The Historical and Cultural World

Prayer in early Christian gatherings. From the beginning, prayer was central to Christian community life. The Jerusalem believers were “continuing steadfastly in … the prayers” (Acts 2:42, LSV). Paul’s letters are full of prayer reports and requests. The Didache provides texts of thanksgiving prayers and instructs believers to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times a day.152 Jude’s call to pray in the Spirit belongs to this common practice. Since the love feasts were also occasions of prayer, the instruction may have had a communal setting in mind.

Waiting for the Lord. The early Christians lived in expectation of Christ’s return. The Aramaic prayer Maranatha, usually understood as ‘Our Lord, come!’ (1 Cor 16:22; Didache 10.6), preserved this hope in the language of the earliest Palestinian believers. (The LSV renders it “The LORD has come!” in 1 Cor 16:22, reflecting a different way of dividing the Aramaic words.)153 Jude’s “waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” expresses the same expectation, colored by the judgment scene he has just quoted.

  1. Didache 8.2–3 (the Lord’s Prayer, “Thrice in the day thus pray”) and 9–10 (thanksgiving prayers), ANF 7 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0714.htm). The citation of chapter 8 is from the same New Advent text consulted for chapters 9–12.↩︎

  2. Didache 10.6 in the original Greek reads μαραναθά. The New Advent (ANF) translation renders the passage; the Aramaic term itself is also found at 1 Cor 16:22.↩︎

F. Connections Across Scripture

1 Corinthians 3:10–11; Ephesians 2:20–22; Colossians 2:7; Acts 20:32 (building imagery). The church as a building on the foundation of Christ and the apostolic faith. Jude’s “building yourselves up on your most holy faith” belongs to this family of images.

Ephesians 6:18; Romans 8:15–16, 26–27; Galatians 4:6 (prayer in the Spirit). The closest parallels to Jude’s “praying in the Holy Spirit.”

John 15:9–10; 1 John 4:16 (remaining in love). “God is love, and he who is remaining in love, remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16, LSV). The Johannine language of “remaining” in God’s love parallels Jude’s “keep yourselves in the love of God.”

Romans 5:5; 8:39 (the love of God). “The love of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom 5:5, LSV). Paul, like Jude, connects God’s love and the Spirit.

Titus 2:13; Luke 2:25 (waiting). The same verb of eager expectation.

1 Corinthians 13:13; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8 (faith, love, hope). The triad that Jude’s vv. 20–21 seem to echo.

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. Is the reference to the Holy Spirit Trinitarian? Jude’s mention of the Holy Spirit, God, and the Lord Jesus Christ in two verses is often noted as an early example of the threefold pattern that later Christian theology articulated as the doctrine of the Trinity. Jude does not reflect on the relationship among the three. His language reflects the experience of early Christians, who knew God as Father, Jesus as Lord, and the Spirit as present power.

2. What kind of prayer is “in the Holy Spirit”? See the deep dive. Interpretations range from all Spirit-led prayer to specifically charismatic forms.

3. Is “the love of God” God’s love or our love? God’s love is primary (v. 1), though a responding love is implied.

4. Is the “mercy” of v. 21 present or future? It is future, the mercy shown at Christ’s coming and judgment. The waiting has present effects: it shapes how believers live now.

H. The Passage Within Jude

Verses 20–21 are the positive counterpart to the whole central section. Each element answers something in the description of the intruders:

The intruders The readers
pervert grace into license (v. 4) build on the most holy faith (v. 20)
“dreaming” (v. 8); “not having the Spirit” (v. 19) praying in the Holy Spirit (v. 20)
stains (or reefs) at the love feasts (v. 12) keep themselves in the love of God (v. 21)
darkness kept for them forever (v. 13) waiting for mercy leading to eternal life (v. 21)

The passage also completes the frame that began in vv. 1–2. Love, keeping, mercy, God, and Jesus Christ all return. Verse 3’s call to contend for the faith is now explained: contending means building, praying, keeping, and waiting.

Finally, vv. 20–21 prepare for vv. 22–23. Those who are kept in God’s love and wait for Christ’s mercy are the ones who can show mercy to others. The movement is from receiving mercy to extending it.

I. Contemporary Understanding

Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

The positive shape of faithfulness. When Christians face false teaching or moral confusion, it is easy to define faithfulness only by what one opposes. Jude’s instructions are almost entirely positive: build, pray, keep, wait. Communities under pressure may find that their best defense is a deep, positive spiritual life rather than constant vigilance against enemies.

Community, not isolation. “Building yourselves up” is communal. Jude assumes that believers grow together, through shared teaching, worship, encouragement, and accountability. Modern individualism can make faith a private project. Jude’s grammar resists that.

Prayer as spiritual defense. Prayer in the Spirit is part of contending for the faith. Churches facing division or confusion might give prayer, honest and dependent, a central place in their response, not merely a ceremonial one.

Living from love toward hope. The passage moves from the love of God, already given, to the mercy of Christ, still awaited. The Christian life is lived between those two points, secure in love and leaning toward hope. That orientation may help believers handle both complacency and anxiety.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. Jude’s response to false teaching is mostly positive: build, pray, keep, wait. Why might that be more effective than a purely defensive strategy?
  2. How do you understand “praying in the Holy Spirit”? How has your tradition shaped your understanding?
  3. What practices help you, or your community, “keep” yourselves in the love of God? Which of Jude’s three activities (building, praying, waiting) is most neglected in your experience?
  4. Jude speaks of the faith as “most holy.” What does it mean to treat the faith as holy rather than as a human tradition to be adjusted?
  5. How does waiting for “the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” shape the way you think about the future and live in the present?

ἐμοῦ ἐστε.

English (BSB)

1 “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. 2 He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful. 3 You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you. 4 Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me. 5 I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing. 6 If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned. 7 If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. 8 This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples. 9 As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love. 10 If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept My Father’s commandments and remain in His love. 11 I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete. 12 This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends. 14 You are My friends if you do what I command you. 15 No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you. 16 You did not choose Me, but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit—fruit that will remain—so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. 17 This is My command to you: Love one another. 18 If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first. 19 If you were of the world, it would love you as its own. Instead, the world hates you, because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world. 20 Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘No servant is greater than his master.’ If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well. 21 But they will treat you like this because of My name, since they do not know the One who sent Me. 22 If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not be guilty of sin. Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin. 23 Whoever hates Me hates My Father as well. 24 If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin; but now they have seen and hated both Me and My Father. 25 But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’ 26 When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—He will testify about Me. 27 And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.

Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. 3 You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. 4 Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. 5 I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. 6 If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned. 7 If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you. 8 “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples. 9 Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. 10 If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. 11 I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full. 12 “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. 13 Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. 14 You are my friends if you do whatever I command you. 15 No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you. 16 You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you. 17 “I command these things to you, that you may love one another. 18 If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you. 19 If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. 20 Remember the word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his lord.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. 21 But they will do all these things to you for my name’s sake, because they don’t know him who sent me. 22 If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. 23 He who hates me, hates my Father also. 24 If I hadn’t done among them the works which no one else did, they wouldn’t have had sin. But now they have seen and also hated both me and my Father. 25 But this happened so that the word may be fulfilled which was written in their law, ‘They hated me without a cause.’ 26 “When the Counselor has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me. 27 You will also testify, because you have been with me from the beginning.

Chapter 12. Mercy for the Wavering, Rescue from the Fire (Jude 22–23)

A. The Text

B. Plain-English Orientation

Jude’s last instructions turn from the readers’ own spiritual life (vv. 20–21) to their responsibility toward others. Those who have been kept in God’s love and who wait for Christ’s mercy must now show mercy themselves. Jude names three kinds of people (on the most widely accepted reading of the text):

  1. Those who are wavering, unsettled by the intruders’ influence. Show them mercy.
  2. Those in immediate danger, already near the fire of judgment. Snatch them out.
  3. Others who are deeply compromised. Show them mercy too, but with fear, hating even the clothing stained by their sin.

These two verses transform the letter. After so much warning and condemnation, Jude’s last practical word is mercy. The readers are not to write off everyone touched by the intruders. They are to distinguish between people in different situations and to act toward each with compassion, urgency, and wisdom. Contending for the faith (v. 3) ends in rescue.

The Greek text of these verses is one of the most complicated in the New Testament. The manuscripts preserve two-clause and three-clause versions with different verbs. This chapter follows the three-clause text printed in the LSV, the SBLGNT, and NA28, and explains the alternatives in a deep dive.

C. Phrase-by-Phrase Exploration

καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεᾶτε (kai hous men eleate) — ‘and have mercy on some’

The command ἐλεᾶτε (eleate), “show mercy, have mercy,” is a present imperative of ἐλεάω (eleaō), a variant form of the more common ἐλεέω (eleeō). The Byzantine manuscripts read ἐλεεῖτε, the more familiar form.154 The word picks up the theme of mercy that frames the letter. Jude wished his readers mercy (v. 2), and they wait for Christ’s mercy (v. 21). Now they are to show mercy. Mercy received becomes mercy given.

The construction καὶ οὓς μὲν … οὓς δὲ … οὓς δὲ (kai hous men … hous de … hous de), “and some … others … others,” divides the people in view into groups. The LSV’s “and, indeed, … others … others” reflects it.

  1. SBLGNT apparatus for Jude 22–23: “ἐλεᾶτε WH NIV ] ἐλεεῖτε RP; ἐλέγχετε Treg.”↩︎

διακρινομένους (diakrinomenous) — ‘who are doubting’

The participle διακρινομένους (diakrinomenous) comes from διακρίνω (diakrinō), a verb with a wide range: “to separate, distinguish, judge,” and in the middle voice “to dispute” or “to doubt, waver.” Jude used the same verb in v. 9 for Michael “disputing” with the Devil. Here two meanings are possible:

  1. “Those who doubt” or “waver.” This is the sense the verb usually has in the New Testament when it describes a person’s inner state. Jesus says, “if you may have faith, and may not doubt” (Matt 21:21, LSV). James writes, “let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, for he who is doubting has been like a wave of the sea, driven by wind and tossed” (Jas 1:6, LSV). On this reading, Jude refers to believers who have been unsettled by the intruders and are uncertain whom to believe. They need mercy, patient and compassionate help, not condemnation.
  2. “Those who dispute.” This sense matches Jude’s own use in v. 9. It would refer to people who argue, perhaps those who have taken the intruders’ side. Some manuscripts read “convict” or “refute” (ἐλέγχετε, elenchete) instead of “show mercy” in this clause, which would give “refute those who dispute.”

Most translations and commentators prefer “doubt” or “waver.” The image in James of the doubter as “a wave of the sea” offers an interesting echo of Jude’s “wild waves” (v. 13). The intruders are wild waves, and those they unsettle are tossed by them. The wavering are not the enemy. They are the ones at risk.

The Byzantine text reads the nominative διακρινόμενοι (diakrinomenoi), which makes the participle describe the readers rather than the people they help. Webster’s revision of the traditional English Bible translates it “And of some have compassion, making a difference” (WBS), meaning that the readers should show compassion while discerning between cases. That reading also has a good sense, but the accusative form, referring to those who doubt, has stronger early support and is printed in the critical editions.155

  1. The Text-Critical Greek NT notes (eBible.org) record ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι in about 88% of manuscripts, ἐλέγχετε διακρινομένους in about 7% (including the reading of the Tyndale House GNT, marked “TH”), and ἐλεᾶτε διακρινομένους (NA28, SBLGNT, WH) in about 2%. Manuscript counts do not determine originality; the critical editions weigh the age and quality of witnesses.↩︎

οὓς δὲ σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες (hous de sōzete ek pyros harpazontes) — ‘save others, snatching them out of the fire’

The second group is in more urgent danger. The command σῴζετε (sōzete), “save, rescue,” is accompanied by the participle ἁρπάζοντες (harpazontes), “snatching, seizing.” The verb ἁρπάζω (harpazō) means “to seize by force, to grab.” Jesus uses it when he says that “no one will snatch them out of My hand” (John 10:28, LSV). Here it describes a rescuer pulling someone out of a burning building, an act of urgent, physical intervention.

The “fire” (πῦρ, pyr) recalls the “continuous fire” of Sodom (v. 7), the fire of judgment. These people are already, so to speak, in the flames, close to the fate of the intruders. They cannot be helped by gentle persuasion alone. They need decisive action.

The image comes from the prophets. In Zechariah’s vision, the LORD says of Joshua the high priest: “Is this not a brand delivered from fire?” (Zech 3:2, LSV), a burning stick pulled out of the fire before it is consumed. The Septuagint’s wording, δαλὸς ἐξεσπασμένος ἐκ πυρός (dalos exespasmenos ek pyros), “a brand snatched out of fire,” is close to Jude’s ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες (ek pyros harpazontes).156 Amos uses the same image in a passage that also recalls Sodom and Gomorrah: “I have overturned among you, / Like the overturn by God of Sodom and Gomorrah, / And you are as a brand delivered from a burning” (Amos 4:11, LSV). Jude’s readers, who have just heard about Sodom’s fire (v. 7), are called to be the hands that pull people from it.

Notice where this allusion comes from. Zechariah 3 also stood behind Michael’s words in v. 9: “The LORD rebuke you!” In that chapter, the accuser stands against Joshua, the LORD rebukes the accuser, Joshua is called “a brand delivered from fire,” and his filthy garments are removed (Zech 3:1–4). Jude draws on the same scene twice. In v. 9 it shows the restraint of the heavenly defender. In v. 23 it shows the rescue of the one accused.

  1. LXX Zech 3:2: οὐκ ἰδοὺ τοῦτο ὡς δαλὸς ἐξεσπασμένος ἐκ πυρός; (Brenton’s Greek Septuagint).↩︎

οὓς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ (hous de eleate en phobō) — ‘and on others have mercy with fear’

The third group also receives mercy, ἐλεᾶτε again, but now ἐν φόβῳ (en phobō), “in fear” or “with fear.” What kind of fear?

  1. Fear of God. Mercy must be shown with reverent awareness of God’s holiness and judgment. The readers must not treat sin lightly while showing mercy to sinners. Paul writes, “having known, therefore, the fear of the LORD, we persuade men” (2 Cor 5:11, LSV), and Hebrews calls believers to serve God “with reverence and fear, for our God [is] also a consuming fire” (Heb 12:28–29, LSV).
  2. Caution about contamination. Those who help people deeply involved in sin must take care not to be drawn into it themselves. Paul gives the same caution: “you who [are] spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of meekness, considering yourself—lest you also may be tempted” (Gal 6:1, LSV).

The two senses go together, and the next phrase explains the second.

μισοῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα (misountes kai ton apo tēs sarkos espilōmenon chitōna) — ‘hating even the tunic stained by the flesh’

The final phrase is vivid: μισοῦντες καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκὸς ἐσπιλωμένον χιτῶνα (misountes kai ton apo tēs sarkos espilōmenon chitōna), “hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.”

  • The χιτών (chitōn) was the basic garment of the ancient world, a tunic worn next to the skin under the outer cloak.
  • ἐσπιλωμένον (espilōmenon), “stained, spotted,” is the perfect passive participle of σπιλόω (spiloō), “to stain, defile.”157 It belongs to the same family as σπίλος, “stain,” and, on one reading, as the σπιλάδες of v. 12. If Jude intended the link, the intruders who were “stains” at the love feasts (LSV) have stained the garments of those they influenced.
  • “From the flesh” (ἀπὸ τῆς σαρκός, apo tēs sarkos) points to the source of the stain: sinful human nature, and especially the sexual sins Jude has repeatedly mentioned (vv. 4, 7–8).

The image is deliberately strong. The undergarment touched the body directly. To hate “even the coat” is to want nothing to do with the sin, not even with what has been in contact with it, while still reaching out to the person. Again Zechariah 3 is in the background: “Joshua was clothed with filthy garments,” and the LORD says, “Turn aside the filthy garments from off him. … See, I have caused your iniquity to pass away from off you, so as to clothe you with costly apparel” (Zech 3:3–4, LSV). The garment is not the person. The garment can be removed, and the person can be clothed afresh.

The phrase holds together two attitudes that are easily separated: mercy toward people and hatred of sin. Christians have often summarized the balance in the slogan “love the sinner, hate the sin.” Jude gives a more demanding picture. The mercy is real, but it is shown “in fear,” and the hatred of sin is strong enough to recoil from its slightest trace.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. σπιλόω: “to stain, spot, defile: c. acc., Ja 3:6, Ju 23.”↩︎

Deep dive: Showing mercy to those who doubt

Jude’s instruction to “show mercy to those who are doubting” is one of the most pastorally significant sentences in the letter, and it deserves reflection.

Who are the doubters? In Jude’s situation, they were probably believers who had been exposed to the intruders’ teaching and conduct and had become unsure. Perhaps the intruders’ visions impressed them, or their freedom seemed attractive. Perhaps they could not see why Jude and the other leaders objected. Such people were not yet committed to the intruders’ way of life, but they were wavering.

Why mercy? Jude could have told his readers to rebuke or exclude the doubters. Instead he tells them to show mercy. Several reasons emerge from the letter:

  • They have received mercy themselves (vv. 2, 21). Those who wait for Christ’s mercy cannot withhold mercy from others.
  • Doubt is not the same as rebellion. The intruders deliberately turn grace into license and reject authority. The doubters are uncertain. To treat uncertainty as rebellion would push the wavering toward the very people Jude warns against.
  • The goal is restoration. Jude’s whole letter aims to keep people in God’s love. Mercy toward the wavering serves that goal.

What does mercy look like? Jude does not spell it out, but the New Testament offers many models. Paul urges, “receive him who is weak in the faith—not to determinations of reasonings” (Rom 14:1, LSV). The Lord’s servant “must not quarrel, but to be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient under evil, instructing those opposing in meekness—if perhaps God may give to them conversion” (2 Tim 2:24–25, LSV). James promises that “he who turned back a sinner from the straying of his way will save a soul from death” (Jas 5:20, LSV). Jesus’ parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one gone astray ends, “it is not [the] will in [the] presence of your Father who is in the heavens that one of these little ones may perish” (Matt 18:14, LSV). Mercy to the doubting likely includes patience, gentle instruction, prayer, presence, and the steady testimony of a community that is building itself up in the faith (v. 20).

Discernment. Jude’s threefold distinction shows that mercy is not uniform. The wavering need patient compassion. Those near the fire need urgent rescue. The deeply compromised need mercy mixed with caution. Wise pastoral care pays attention to the person’s situation.

Doubt today. The word “doubt” covers many experiences: intellectual questions, emotional struggles, confusion caused by conflicting teachers, disappointment with the church. Not all of them are what Jude had in mind. His instruction, though, suggests a general principle. Communities that hold firmly to “the faith once delivered” should be the most merciful toward those who struggle to hold it. Firmness and mercy are not opposites in Jude. Both flow from being kept in God’s love.

Deep dive: The text of Jude 22–23

Few New Testament passages survive in as many forms as these two verses. The main forms can be grouped as follows (Greek simplified):158

Witness Text Structure
SBLGNT, NA28, Tregelles, NIV Greek text; LSV καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεᾶτε διακρινομένους, οὓς δὲ σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες, οὓς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ… Three groups: show mercy to the doubting / save others, snatching from fire / show mercy to others in fear
Tregelles (first verb), Tyndale House GNT (as reported) καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλέγχετε διακρινομένους… Three groups, but the first is “refute (or convict) those who dispute”
Westcott–Hort καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεᾶτε διακρινομένους σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες, οὓς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ… Two groups: “have mercy on some who doubt, saving them by snatching them from fire; and on others have mercy in fear”
Robinson–Pierpont, TR καὶ οὓς μὲν ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι, οὓς δὲ ἐν φόβῳ σῴζετε ἐκ (τοῦ) πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες… Two groups: “on some have compassion, making a difference; others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire”
P72 (early papyrus) οὓς μὲν ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάσατε, διακρινομένους δὲ ἐλεεῖτε ἐν φόβῳ… Two groups: “snatch some from the fire, but on those who doubt have mercy in fear”

The manuscripts themselves show the same spread. In the transcriptions of the earliest copies:159

Manuscript Date Form of vv. 22–23
P72 3rd/4th c. two clauses: οὓς μὲν ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάσατε, διακρινομένους δὲ ἐλεεῖτε ἐν φόβῳ (‘snatch some from fire, but on those who doubt have mercy in fear’)
ℵ 01 Sinaiticus 4th c. three clauses with ἐλεᾶτε … σῴζετε … ἐλεᾶτε (as SBLGNT)
B 03 Vaticanus 4th c. two clauses: ἐλεᾶτε διακρινομένους σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες, οὓς δὲ ἐλεᾶτε ἐν φόβῳ
A 02 Alexandrinus 5th c. three clauses, beginning ἐλέγχετε (‘convict’)
C 04 Ephraemi 5th c. ἐλέγχετε (corrected to ἐλεᾶτε) διακρινομένους, οὓς δὲ σῴζετε ἐκ πυρὸς ἁρπάζοντες ἐν φόβῳ (two clauses)
Ψ 044 9th/10th c. three clauses with ἐλεᾶτε
1739 10th c. three clauses, beginning ἐλέγχετε
K 018, L 020 9th c. Byzantine two-clause form: ἐλεεῖτε διακρινόμενοι, οὓς δὲ ἐν φόβῳ σῴζετε…

Early Christian writers knew different forms too. Clement of Alexandria paraphrased a two-part text: “But some, he says, save, plucking them from the fire; but of some have compassion in fear.”160

Why so many forms? The repetition of similar words (two forms of “show mercy,” and the series οὓς μὲν … οὓς δέ) made the passage easy to miscopy. Scribes may have dropped a clause by accident when the eye skipped from one οὓς δέ to the next, or they may have smoothed a difficult text. The verb διακρίνω, which can mean “doubt” or “dispute,” also invited different interpretations and therefore different verbs (“show mercy” or “refute”).

Which is original? Interpreters are divided. The three-clause text printed in the SBLGNT and NA28 is supported by Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus (with “convict”), Ψ, and 1739, and it can explain the two-clause forms as accidental omissions. The two-clause forms are supported by the oldest witness, P72, and by Vaticanus, in different shapes. A good case can therefore be made that a shorter text is original and that the three-clause text grew by expansion. Nineteenth-century commentators already struggled with the passage. The Cambridge commentary observed that “the MSS. present a strange variety of readings” and that those “of most authority give, Some rebuke (or convict) … when they debate with you.” Plummer, in Ellicott’s commentary, thought “the evidence is very strong in favour of” the reading “some indeed convict.” J. B. Mayor gave the problem one of the longest notes in his commentary.161

Does it matter? The core of the passage is the same in all forms: mercy toward some, urgent rescue of others from the fire, and caution about the defilement of sin. The differences affect how many groups Jude distinguishes and whether the first group receives mercy or rebuke. This book follows the three-clause text of the LSV and SBLGNT, while recognizing that certainty is not possible.

D. Original-Language Investigation

Greek Transliteration Basic meaning In context Notes
ἐλεάω / ἐλεέω eleaō / eleeō show mercy “show mercy” Present imperative; variant ἐλέγχετε, “convict.”
διακρίνομαι diakrinomai dispute; doubt, waver “those who are doubting” Same verb as v. 9; Jas 1:6.
σῴζω sōzō save, rescue “rescue”
ἁρπάζω harpazō seize, snatch “snatching” Urgent action; John 10:28.
πῦρ pyr fire “fire” Judgment fire (v. 7); Zech 3:2; Amos 4:11.
φόβος phobos fear, reverence “in fear” Fear of God and caution.
μισέω miseō hate “hating”
χιτών chitōn tunic, undergarment “the coat” Garment worn next to the skin.
σπιλόω spiloō stain, defile “stained” Perfect passive participle; cf. σπιλάδες (v. 12).
σάρξ sarx flesh “the flesh” Sinful human nature; cf. vv. 7–8.

E. The Historical and Cultural World

Clothing and purity. In the Jewish world, garments could become ritually impure through contact with bodily discharges or with unclean things (Lev 13–15), and purification involved washing clothes. The image of a defiled garment would have carried both ritual and moral overtones. Zechariah’s vision of the high priest’s filthy garments, which are removed and replaced with clean ones, provided a powerful picture of forgiveness and restoration.

Fire as judgment. In Jewish and early Christian thought, fire was the most common image of divine judgment: the fire of Sodom, the fire of Gehenna, the “continuous fire” of the final judgment. To snatch someone from the fire was to rescue them from judgment, by persuasion, intervention, or prayer, before it was too late.

Church discipline and restoration. Early Christian communities practiced various forms of discipline toward members who fell into serious sin (Matt 18:15–17; 1 Cor 5; 2 Thess 3:14–15). The goal was always restoration: “do not count as an enemy, but admonish as a brother” (2 Thess 3:15, LSV). Jude’s instructions belong to this pastoral tradition, though they do not describe formal procedures.

F. Connections Across Scripture

Zechariah 3:1–5 (allusion). The brand snatched from the fire and the filthy garments removed. This is the most important background for both images in v. 23, and the same chapter stands behind Michael’s words in v. 9.

Amos 4:11 (shared image). “A brand delivered from a burning,” in a passage that also mentions Sodom and Gomorrah.

James 1:6; 5:19–20 (shared themes). The doubter as a wave of the sea, and the saving of a sinner from death. James’s closing verses resemble Jude’s in spirit: both letters end by urging readers to restore those who wander.

Galatians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:24–26; Romans 14:1 (pastoral care). Gentle restoration with awareness of one’s own vulnerability.

Matthew 18:12–14 (the lost sheep). God’s will that none of the little ones perish.

Revelation 3:4; 2 Corinthians 7:1 (defiled garments; cleansing). “a few names even in Sardis who did not defile their garments” (Rev 3:4, LSV); “may we cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God” (2 Cor 7:1, LSV). Paul joins cleansing from defilement of the flesh with “the fear of God,” as Jude joins mercy “in fear” with hatred of the garment “stained from the flesh.”

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. Two groups or three? See the deep dive.

2. “Doubt” or “dispute”? Most interpreters prefer “doubt” or “waver,” following New Testament usage and the logic of showing mercy. The alternative (“dispute,” with “refute” or “convict”) has some manuscript support and matches Jude’s use of the verb in v. 9.

3. Who is in the fire? Probably people who have gone further than the doubters, adopting the intruders’ practices. Some interpreters think the intruders themselves might be included among those who could still be snatched from the fire. Jude’s harsh descriptions in vv. 4–19 do not encourage that reading, but his structure leaves the door open in a way that is worth noting.

4. What does “in fear” mean? Fear of God, caution about contamination, or both.

5. How do vv. 22–23 relate to the rest of the letter? Some readers find the shift from condemnation to mercy abrupt. It is better understood as the goal of the letter. Jude exposes the intruders in order to protect the community and rescue those at risk. The warnings serve the mercy.

H. The Passage Within Jude

Verses 22–23 complete the exhortation that began in v. 20. The readers who keep themselves in God’s love (v. 21) now extend that love to others. The letter’s three great themes come together here:

  • Mercy: wished for the readers (v. 2), awaited from Christ (v. 21), shown to others (vv. 22–23).
  • Fire and judgment: the fire of Sodom (v. 7), the coming judgment (vv. 14–15), and the fire from which people must be snatched (v. 23).
  • Defilement: the flesh defiled by the intruders (v. 8), the stains at the love feasts (v. 12), and the garment stained by the flesh (v. 23).

The passage also prepares for the doxology. The readers who rescue others from stumbling into the fire will themselves be kept “without stumbling” by the God who is able (v. 24).

I. Contemporary Understanding

Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

Mercy as the end of contending. Jude’s letter shows that contending for the faith does not end in triumph over opponents but in mercy toward the wavering and rescue of the endangered. Christians who are passionate about truth might ask whether their passion leads to the same place.

Differentiated care. Jude distinguishes among people in different situations. Pastoral care today might likewise distinguish between honest questioners, people in crisis, and people deeply entangled in harmful patterns, responding to each with appropriate compassion, urgency, and wisdom.

Mercy without naïveté. Showing mercy “in fear” and “hating even the coat” suggests that mercy does not mean ignoring danger. Those who help others out of destructive situations, whether addiction, abuse, or spiritual manipulation, often need to set boundaries and protect themselves. That is not a failure of mercy but part of it.

The garment can be changed. Zechariah’s vision, behind Jude’s words, ends with new clothes. Those who have been stained can be cleansed. Christians who show mercy do so in the hope that God will “turn aside the filthy garments” and clothe people afresh.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. Why do you think Jude ends his practical instructions with mercy rather than with further warnings? How does this change your reading of the whole letter?
  2. Think of people you know who are “wavering” in faith. What would it look like to show them mercy, in practical terms?
  3. Jude speaks of “snatching” some from the fire. Are there situations in which urgent intervention is more loving than patient waiting? How can one tell?
  4. What does it mean to show mercy “in fear”? How can believers help others without being drawn into the same patterns?
  5. The garment imagery comes from Zechariah 3, where filthy garments are removed and replaced. How does this picture of cleansing shape the way you think about people who have fallen into sin?
