E. The Historical and Cultural World

Doxologies in Jewish and Christian worship. Jewish prayer was rich in blessings and doxologies ascribing glory to God, and the five books of the Psalter each close with one (Pss 41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48; 150). Early Christians continued the practice, and doxologies often closed letters that would be read in worship (Rom 16:25–27; Phil 4:20; 1 Tim 1:17; 1 Pet 4:11; 5:11; 2 Pet 3:18). Jude’s letter, read aloud in the community, would end in worship.

“Savior” in the Roman world. Hellenistic kings and Roman emperors were often hailed as “savior” (σωτήρ) and “benefactor” in inscriptions and official language.175 When Christians called God “our Savior” and gave him “glory,” “power,” and “authority,” they were making a claim that implicitly relativized every human ruler. Jude’s doxology is not a political manifesto, but its language would not have been neutral in the first-century world.

Standing in the presence of a king. In the ancient Near East, to stand in the presence of a king was an honor reserved for those admitted to court. To be “set” before God’s glory “unblemished” and “in gladness” is the image of acceptance at the royal court of heaven.

  1. Abbott-Smith, s.v. σωτήρ (see n. 9).↩︎

F. Connections Across Scripture

Romans 16:25–27; Ephesians 3:20–21 (form). The closest parallels in form: “to Him who is able … to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to Him [be] glory” (Rom 16:25, 27, LSV). The parallel probably explains the addition of “wise” in some manuscripts of Jude.

1 Timothy 1:17; 1 Peter 4:11; 2 Peter 3:18 (doxologies). Other New Testament doxologies use similar vocabulary. Second Peter ends: “to Him [is] the glory both now, and to the day of the age! Amen” (2 Pet 3:18, LSV), a doxology to Christ that resembles Jude’s.

Psalms 121; 56:13; 116:8 (being kept from stumbling). The Old Testament roots of Jude’s promise.

Colossians 1:22; Ephesians 1:4; 5:27; 1 Thessalonians 3:13 (presentation unblemished). The goal of God’s work is a people presented holy and blameless before him.

1 Chronicles 29:10–13 (attributes). David’s blessing of God, ascribing greatness, power, glory, and kingdom to him.

John 17:5; 2 Timothy 1:9 (before time). “The glory that I had with You before the world was” (John 17:5, LSV); grace “given to us in Christ Jesus, before the times of the ages” (2 Tim 1:9, LSV). These texts share the critical text’s vision of glory before time.

G. Scholarly and Theological Questions

1. Which text of v. 25 is original? Most scholars accept the longer text of the critical editions, with “through Jesus Christ our Lord” and “before all time,” and without “wise.” The Byzantine form is shorter in two places and adds “wise,” probably from Rom 16:27. Readers of the LSV should know that their translation reflects the Byzantine form here.

2. Is the doxology addressed to God or to Christ? It is addressed to “the only God our Savior,” with glory ascribed “through Jesus Christ” (critical text). Some later doxologies are addressed directly to Christ (2 Pet 3:18; Rev 5:13). Jude’s is addressed to God through Christ, and that reflects the pattern of early Christian worship.

3. Does “able to guard you without stumbling” guarantee perseverance? As in Chapters 1 and 11, Christian traditions answer differently. All agree that the doxology expresses confidence in God’s power and faithfulness. Some read it as a guarantee that true believers will persevere. Others read it as a statement of God’s ability that believers must still respond to. Jude’s placement of the doxology after v. 21 suggests that he did not see the two as competing.

4. “Is” or “be”? The verbless Greek allows both. The LSV’s “[is]” emphasizes that glory already belongs to God. The traditional “be” emphasizes the worshipers’ acknowledgment.

H. The Passage Within Jude

The doxology completes the letter’s frame. The opening described the readers as “called, … loved … and … kept” (v. 1). The ending praises God who is “able to guard” them (v. 24). Between these two statements of God’s keeping lies everything else: the intruders, the examples of judgment, the woes, the images of disorder, the call to build, pray, keep, wait, and show mercy.

Every major theme of the letter is gathered in these two verses:

  • Keeping and guarding: “able to guard you” (v. 24), completing the τηρέω thread (vv. 1, 6, 13, 21).
  • Stumbling and falling: the danger shown by the wilderness generation, the angels, and the intruders, and averted by God’s power.
  • Blemish and purity: “unblemished” (v. 24), in contrast to the stains (v. 12) and the stained garment (v. 23).
  • Glory: the “glorious [ones]” slandered by the intruders (v. 8), and the true glory of God before which the readers will stand (vv. 24–25).
  • Joy: “in gladness” (v. 24), the final mood of a letter that began with mercy, peace, and love.
  • Salvation: “our common salvation” (v. 3) and “God our Savior” (v. 25).
  • Lordship: “our only Master and Lord—Jesus Christ” (v. 4) and ‘through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (v. 25, critical text).
  • Time: ancient examples, present dangers, and future judgment, all embraced by the eternal glory of God, ‘before all time, and now, and forever.’

Jude wanted to write about “our common salvation” (v. 3) and was forced to write a warning instead. In the doxology he finally gets to write about salvation, and he does it in praise.

I. Contemporary Understanding

Suggested applications, distinct from the original meaning.

Ending in worship. Jude ends a hard letter with praise. Christians facing conflict, confusion, or danger might learn from his example to return, finally, to the worship of God, not as an escape from difficulty but as the truest response to it.

Confidence that is not self-confidence. The doxology’s emphasis on God’s ability frees believers from depending on their own steadiness. That is good news for the wavering, the weary, and those who have stumbled before.

Joy as the end. The final picture is of believers standing before God’s glory “in gladness.” Christian faith, for all its seriousness about sin and judgment, aims at joy. Communities that have forgotten that may need Jude’s ending as much as his warnings.

Using the doxology. Jude 24–25 has long been used as a benediction at the close of Christian services. Its use may be enriched by remembering its context. It is spoken to people who face real dangers, by someone who knows those dangers well, in confidence that God is greater.

J. Reflection and Discussion

  1. How does reading the doxology after the rest of Jude change its meaning for you, compared with hearing it as a stand-alone benediction?
  2. What does “stumbling” look like in your life or community? How does the promise that God “is able to guard you” speak to that?
  3. Jude pictures believers standing before God’s glory “unblemished, in gladness.” What does that picture suggest about the goal of the Christian life?
  4. The critical text includes “before all time, and now, and forever.” What difference does it make to think of God’s glory as stretching back before creation?
  5. Jude both commands believers to keep themselves (v. 21) and praises God for keeping them (v. 24). How do you hold these together in your own life?

Psalm 73

Hebrew (Westminster Leningrad Codex)

1 מִזְמוֹר לְאָסָף אַךְ טוֹב לְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֱלֹהִים לְבָרֵי לֵבָב 2 וַאֲנִי כִּמְעַט נטוי רַגְלָי כְּאַיִן שפכה אֲשֻׁרָי 3 כִּי־קִנֵּאתִי בַּהוֹלְלִים שְׁלוֹם רְשָׁעִים אֶרְאֶה 4 כִּי אֵין חַרְצֻבּוֹת לְמוֹתָם וּבָרִיא אוּלָם 5 בַּעֲמַל אֱנוֹשׁ אֵינֵמוֹ וְעִם־אָדָם לֹא יְנֻגָּעוּ 6 לָכֵן עֲנָקַתְמוֹ גַאֲוָה יַעֲטָף־שִׁית חָמָס לָמוֹ 7 יָצָא מֵחֵלֶב עֵינֵמוֹ עָבְרוּ מַשְׂכִּיּוֹת לֵבָב 8 יָמִיקוּ וִידַבְּרוּ בְרָע עֹשֶׁק מִמָּרוֹם יְדַבֵּרוּ 9 שַׁתּוּ בַשָּׁמַיִם פִּיהֶם וּלְשׁוֹנָם תִּהֲלַךְ בָּאָרֶץ 10 לָכֵן ישיב עַמּוֹ הֲלֹם וּמֵי מָלֵא יִמָּצוּ לָמוֹ 11 וְאָמְרוּ אֵיכָה יָדַע־אֵל וְיֵשׁ דֵּעָה בְעֶלְיוֹן 12 הִנֵּה־אֵלֶּה רְשָׁעִים וְשַׁלְוֵי עוֹלָם הִשְׂגּוּ־חָיִל 13 אַךְ־רִיק זִכִּיתִי לְבָבִי וָאֶרְחַץ בְּנִקָּיוֹן כַּפָּי 14 וָאֱהִי נָגוּעַ כָּל־הַיּוֹם וְתוֹכַחְתִּי לַבְּקָרִים 15 אִם־אָמַרְתִּי אֲסַפְּרָה כְמוֹ הִנֵּה דוֹר בָּנֶיךָ בָגָדְתִּי 16 וָאֲחַשְּׁבָה לָדַעַת זֹאת עָמָל היא בְעֵינָי 17 עַד־אָבוֹא אֶל־מִקְדְּשֵׁי־אֵל אָבִינָה לְאַחֲרִיתָם 18 אַךְ בַּחֲלָקוֹת תָּשִׁית לָמוֹ הִפַּלְתָּם לְמַשּׁוּאוֹת 19 אֵיךְ הָיוּ לְשַׁמָּה כְרָגַע סָפוּ תַמּוּ מִן־בַּלָּהוֹת 20 כַּחֲלוֹם מֵהָקִיץ אֲדֹנָי בָּעִיר צַלְמָם תִּבְזֶה 21 כִּי יִתְחַמֵּץ לְבָבִי וְכִלְיוֹתַי אֶשְׁתּוֹנָן 22 וַאֲנִי־בַעַר וְלֹא אֵדָע בְּהֵמוֹת הָיִיתִי עִמָּךְ 23 וַאֲנִי תָמִיד עִמָּךְ אָחַזְתָּ בְּיַד־יְמִינִי 24 בַּעֲצָתְךָ תַנְחֵנִי וְאַחַר כָּבוֹד תִּקָּחֵנִי 25 מִי־לִי בַשָּׁמָיִם וְעִמְּךָ לֹא־חָפַצְתִּי בָאָרֶץ 26 כָּלָה שְׁאֵרִי וּלְבָבִי צוּר־לְבָבִי וְחֶלְקִי אֱלֹהִים לְעוֹלָם 27 כִּי־הִנֵּה רְחֵקֶיךָ יֹאבֵדוּ הִצְמַתָּה כָּל־זוֹנֶה מִמֶּךָּ 28 וַאֲנִי קִרֲבַת אֱלֹהִים לִי־טוֹב שַׁתִּי בַּאדֹנָי יְהֹוִה מַחְסִי לְסַפֵּר כָּל־מַלְאֲכוֹתֶיךָ

English (BSB)

1 Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. 2 But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped. 3 For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. 4 They have no struggle in their death; their bodies are well-fed. 5 They are free of the burdens others carry; they are not afflicted like other men. 6 Therefore pride is their necklace; a garment of violence covers them. 7 From their prosperity proceeds iniquity; the imaginations of their hearts run wild. 8 They mock and speak with malice; with arrogance they threaten oppression. 9 They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut across the earth. 10 So their people return to this place and drink up waters in abundance. 11 The wicked say, “How can God know? Does the Most High have knowledge?” 12 Behold, these are the wicked— always carefree as they increase their wealth. 13 Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands. 14 For I am afflicted all day long and punished every morning. 15 If I had said, “I will speak this way,” then I would have betrayed Your children. 16 When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight 17 until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end. 18 Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin. 19 How suddenly they are laid waste, completely swept away by terrors! 20 Like one waking from a dream, so You, O Lord, awaken and despise their form. 21 When my heart was grieved and I was pierced within, 22 I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You. 23 Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand. 24 You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory. 25 Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You. 26 My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. 27 Those far from You will surely perish; You destroy all who are unfaithful to You. 28 But as for me, it is good to draw near to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may proclaim all Your works.

English (WEB)

1 Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. 2 But as for me, my feet were almost gone. My steps had nearly slipped. 3 For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. 4 For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm. 5 They are free from burdens of men, neither are they plagued like other men. 6 Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck. Violence covers them like a garment. 7 Their eyes bulge with fat. Their minds pass the limits of conceit. 8 They scoff and speak with malice. In arrogance, they threaten oppression. 9 They have set their mouth in the heavens. Their tongue walks through the earth. 10 Therefore their people return to them, and they drink up waters of abundance. 11 They say, “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” 12 Behold, these are the wicked. Being always at ease, they increase in riches. 13 Surely I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocence, 14 For all day long I have been plagued, and punished every morning. 15 If I had said, “I will speak thus”, behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children. 16 When I tried to understand this, it was too painful for me— 17 until I entered God’s sanctuary, and considered their latter end. 18 Surely you set them in slippery places. You throw them down to destruction. 19 How they are suddenly destroyed! They are completely swept away with terrors. 20 As a dream when one wakes up, so, Lord, when you awake, you will despise their fantasies. 21 For my soul was grieved. I was embittered in my heart. 22 I was so senseless and ignorant. I was a brute beast before you. 23 Nevertheless, I am continually with you. You have held my right hand. 24 You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory. 25 Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you. 26 My flesh and my heart fails, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. 27 For, behold, those who are far from you shall perish. You have destroyed all those who are unfaithful to you. 28 But it is good for me to come close to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.

Afterword: Reading Jude Whole

We have walked through Jude phrase by phrase, stopping at reefs and clouds, angels and archangels, Enoch and the love feast. It is worth stepping back, as Jude’s first hearers would have done when the reading ended, and hearing the letter once more as a single word.

Jude wrote to people he loved about something he loved, “our common salvation.” What he found was a community in danger. People had slipped in who spoke impressively, claimed visions, sat at the common table, and taught that grace made holiness unnecessary. Jude did not respond with a treatise. He responded with memory. Remember the people saved from Egypt who did not believe. Remember the angels who left their place and Sodom’s fire. Remember Michael, who did not presume to judge even the Devil. Remember Cain, Balaam, and Korah. Remember what Enoch said and what the apostles told you. In each memory, Jude saw the present more clearly. The story of God’s people had seen this danger before, and God had not been defeated by it.

Yet the letter does not end in memory, and it certainly does not end in denunciation. It ends with a community building itself up on a most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keeping itself in the love of God, and waiting for the mercy of Jesus Christ. It ends with that community reaching out in mercy to the wavering, snatching the endangered from the fire, and showing compassion even where caution is needed. And it ends with praise to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling and to bring them, faultless and rejoicing, into the presence of his glory.

Three sentences may summarize what Jude asks of every generation that reads him:

Remember what God has done and said. The faith was delivered once for all. Its shape is known. Novelty is not the measure of truth.

Keep yourselves in the love of God. Faithfulness is not mainly a matter of fighting enemies but of remaining where God’s love has placed us, through building up one another, prayer, and hope.

Show mercy. Those who contend most earnestly for the faith should be the quickest to reach out to the doubting and the endangered, because they themselves live by mercy.

Around these three sentences stand the two great statements that frame the letter: you have been called, loved, and kept; and God is able to guard you without stumbling. Between them lies everything else, the danger, the warnings, and the work. Jude’s readers, then and now, are invited to live in the space those two statements define, in confidence that the one who kept them from the beginning will keep them to the end.

To Him be glory. Amen.

Reading across the rows shows the textual families. Tyndale, the Geneva Bible, Webster, and Young’s Literal Translation follow the Textus Receptus. The World English Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, and the Text-Critical English New Testament follow the Byzantine Majority Text. The Revised Version, Darby, the American Standard Version, the Translation for Translators, the Open English Bible, the Unlocked Literal Bible, the Free Bible Version, and the Berean Standard Bible follow critical texts, and Noyes mostly does. The Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate, which is why it reads “Jesus” in v. 5 and “reprove” in v. 22. The Literal Standard Version mixes readings from both traditions (see A.4).

A.3 Notes on the major units, with the manuscript evidence

Jude 1: “loved” or “sanctified.” ἠγαπημένοις, “loved,” is the reading of P72, ℵ, A, B, Ψ, and 1739; ἡγιασμένοις, “sanctified,” is the reading of K and L and of about 90% of all manuscripts. The critical editions all read “loved,” judging it the earlier and harder reading. “Sanctified in God the Father” looks like a scribal improvement of the unusual “loved in God the Father,” perhaps influenced by 1 Cor 1:2. See Chapter 1.

Jude 4: “only Master [God] and Lord.” The added θεόν, “God,” is absent from P72, P78, ℵ, A, B, C, and 1739, and present in the later manuscripts Ψ, K, and L. It appears in the Byzantine tradition and produced the traditional English rendering “denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ” (WBS). Since a single article governs the nouns, even the longer text most naturally refers all the titles to Jesus, as the WEB’s rendering of the Majority Text shows: “our only Master, God, and Lord, Jesus Christ.” See Chapter 2.

Jude 5: “Jesus” or “the Lord.” This is the most discussed variant in the letter. “Jesus” (written ΙΣ) is read by A, B, and 1739. “The Lord” (ΚΣ) is read by ℵ, the first hand of C, Ψ, K, and L, and by most later manuscripts; a corrector of C changed it to “God.” The early papyrus P72 has “God Christ.” The editors of NA28 adopted “Jesus,” reversing NA27, and the SBLGNT reads it too. The placement of “once” also varies. See the deep dive in Chapter 3.

Jude 15: “all the impious” or “every soul.” “Every soul” (πᾶσαν ψυχήν), the reading of NA28, is found in P72 and ℵ, and corresponds to 1 Enoch 1:9’s “all flesh” (Charles). “All the impious” (πάντας τοὺς ἀσεβεῖς), the reading of SBLGNT, is found in A, B, C, and Ψ, and matches Jude’s emphasis on “impious”; 1739 has “all impious people.” K and L add “their,” as the Byzantine text does. See Chapter 8.

Jude 19: “who cause divisions” or “who separate themselves.” The TR’s added ἑαυτούς creates the traditional English rendering “These are they who separate themselves” (WBS), suggesting withdrawal. Among the manuscripts checked, only C and a corrector of 1739 have it. The critical and Byzantine texts lack it, which gives “these are the ones who cause divisions.” See Chapter 10.

Jude 22–23: two groups or three? The manuscripts preserve at least six forms. ℵ and Ψ have three clauses (mercy, rescue, mercy with fear), as do the SBLGNT and NA28. A and 1739 also have three clauses but begin with “refute” (ἐλέγχετε) instead of “show mercy,” as do Tregelles and the Tyndale House Greek New Testament (as reported). B has two clauses, “have mercy on some who doubt, saving them by snatching them from fire; have mercy on others with fear,” the form printed by Westcott and Hort. C has two clauses beginning with “refute.” K and L have the two-clause Byzantine form, and P72 has a short two-clause form of its own (“snatch some from fire; on those who dispute have mercy with fear”). Clement of Alexandria’s paraphrase suggests a two-part text. See the deep dive in Chapter 12.

Jude 25: the shape of the doxology. “Through Jesus Christ our Lord” is present in every manuscript checked except K. “Before all time” is present in ℵ, A, B, C, Ψ, L, and 1739 (1739 without the article) and absent from P72 and K. Both phrases are absent from the Byzantine text and the TR, and so from the LSV and the other translations that follow them (see A.2). “Wise,” found here in K and L, is probably borrowed from Rom 16:27. See Chapter 13.

A.4 What the variants show about the LSV

The LSV states in its preface that its New Testament is based on the Textus Receptus and the Majority Text, departing from them “in certain, specific instances … where the evidence seems incontrovertible.”177 Jude illustrates this policy well. In vv. 1, 3, 4, 5, and 22–23 the LSV adopts readings of the critical editions against the Byzantine majority. In vv. 15 and 25 it keeps the Byzantine readings. Readers of this book should therefore keep in mind that the LSV’s English does not always correspond to a single printed Greek edition. The commentary notes every place where that matters.

  1. LSV preface, https://www.lsvbible.com/p/the-preface-to-literal-standard-version.html (accessed 7 November 2026).↩︎

A.5 How significant are these variants?

None of Jude’s variants affects any central Christian doctrine. Several affect how particular verses are read: whether Jesus is named as Israel’s deliverer (v. 5), how many groups the readers are to help (vv. 22–23), and whether glory is ascribed to God “through Jesus Christ” and ‘before all time’ (v. 25). Honest reading includes knowing where the text is uncertain, and good textual scholarship lets readers see how much of the text is secure. For Jude, by any measure, almost all of it is.

Appendix C. Jude and 2 Peter: The Parallel Passages

This appendix sets the parallel passages side by side, first in the Greek of the SBL Greek New Testament and then in two public-domain English translations, the Berean Standard Bible (BSB) and the World English Bible (WEB). The texts are generated directly from the source files by tools/make_parallels.py, so they are exact. Each verse of Jude is also given in eighteen free translations in section A of its chapter. For discussion of the relationship between the two letters, see the Historical and Literary Introduction, §8.

Summary of the evidence. The two letters share a sequence of themes, images, and rare words. Three Greek words occur in the New Testament only in these two letters: συνευωχέομαι (“feast together”), ὑπέρογκος (“swollen”), and ἐμπαίκτης (“scoffer”).178 Jude contains material not found in 2 Peter: the quotation of Enoch (vv. 14–15), the named dispute of Michael and the Devil over Moses’ body (v. 9), Cain and Korah (v. 11), the wild waves and wandering stars (v. 13), and the closing exhortations to mercy (vv. 20–23). 2 Peter adds the flood and Noah (2:5), Lot (2:7–8), Balaam’s donkey (2:16), and the scoffers’ question about Christ’s coming (3:4).

Observation: Intruders: Jude’s παρεισέδυσαν (“they slipped in”) and 2 Peter’s παρεισάξουσιν (“they will secretly bring in”). Both deny the Master (δεσπότης). Jude speaks of the past, 2 Peter of the future.

Material in Jude without a parallel in 2 Peter

  • The greeting’s description of believers as called, loved, and kept (v. 1).
  • The exodus example, with the reading Ἰησοῦς, “Jesus,” in the critical text (v. 5).
  • The story of Michael and the Devil over Moses’ body (v. 9).
  • Cain and Korah (v. 11).
  • Wild waves of the sea and wandering stars (v. 13).
  • The quotation from 1 Enoch (vv. 14–15).
  • “Grumblers” and flattery (v. 16).
  • Those who cause divisions, not having the Spirit (v. 19).
  • Building, praying in the Holy Spirit, keeping in God’s love (vv. 20–21).
  • Mercy for the doubting and rescue from the fire (vv. 22–23).

Texts Highlighted in This Appendix

Every passage cited or alluded to by reference in this appendix is printed here, original language first: Hebrew or Aramaic from the Westminster Leningrad Codex, Greek from the SBL Greek New Testament (the Septuagint for the Apocrypha), followed by two public-domain English translations, the Berean Standard Bible (BSB) and the World English Bible (WEB). 1 Enoch is given in R. H. Charles’s translation. A long passage already printed in full earlier in the book is linked rather than repeated.

2 Peter 2:1–4, 6–8, 10–13, 15–18

Greek (SBLGNT)

1 Ἐγένοντο δὲ καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐν τῷ λαῷ, ὡς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσονται ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι, οἵτινες παρεισάξουσιν αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας, καὶ τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς δεσπότην ἀρνούμενοι, ἐπάγοντες ἑαυτοῖς ταχινὴν ἀπώλειαν· 2 καὶ πολλοὶ ἐξακολουθήσουσιν αὐτῶν ταῖς ἀσελγείαις, δι’ οὓς ἡ ὁδὸς τῆς ἀληθείας βλασφημηθήσεται· 3 καὶ ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλαστοῖς λόγοις ὑμᾶς ἐμπορεύσονται· οἷς τὸ κρίμα ἔκπαλαι οὐκ ἀργεῖ, καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια αὐτῶν οὐ νυστάζει. 4 Εἰ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς ἀγγέλων ἁμαρτησάντων οὐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους, … 6 καὶ πόλεις Σοδόμων καὶ Γομόρρας τεφρώσας καταστροφῇ κατέκρινεν, ὑπόδειγμα μελλόντων ἀσεβέσιν τεθεικώς, 7 καὶ δίκαιον Λὼτ καταπονούμενον ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν ἀθέσμων ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς ἐρρύσατο— 8 βλέμματι γὰρ καὶ ἀκοῇ ὁ δίκαιος ἐγκατοικῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡμέραν ἐξ ἡμέρας ψυχὴν δικαίαν ἀνόμοις ἔργοις ἐβασάνιζεν— … 10 μάλιστα δὲ τοὺς ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμοῦ πορευομένους καὶ κυριότητος καταφρονοῦντας. Τολμηταί, αὐθάδεις, δόξας οὐ τρέμουσιν, βλασφημοῦντες, 11 ὅπου ἄγγελοι ἰσχύϊ καὶ δυνάμει μείζονες ὄντες οὐ φέρουσιν κατ’ αὐτῶν βλάσφημον κρίσιν. 12 οὗτοι δέ, ὡς ἄλογα ζῷα γεγεννημένα φυσικὰ εἰς ἅλωσιν καὶ φθοράν, ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσιν βλασφημοῦντες, ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ αὐτῶν καὶ φθαρήσονται, 13 ἀδικούμενοι μισθὸν ἀδικίας· ἡδονὴν ἡγούμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφήν, σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι ἐντρυφῶντες ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις αὐτῶν συνευωχούμενοι ὑμῖν, … 15 καταλιπόντες εὐθεῖαν ὁδὸν ἐπλανήθησαν, ἐξακολουθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ τοῦ Βοσὸρ ὃς μισθὸν ἀδικίας ἠγάπησεν 16 ἔλεγξιν δὲ ἔσχεν ἰδίας παρανομίας· ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον ἐκώλυσεν τὴν τοῦ προφήτου παραφρονίαν. 17 Οὗτοί εἰσιν πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι καὶ ὁμίχλαι ὑπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι, οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους τετήρηται. 18 ὑπέρογκα γὰρ ματαιότητος φθεγγόμενοι δελεάζουσιν ἐν ἐπιθυμίαις σαρκὸς ἀσελγείαις τοὺς ὀλίγως ἀποφεύγοντας τοὺς ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφομένους,

English (BSB)

1 Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves. 2 Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. 3 In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep. 4 For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment; … 6 if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly; 7 and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless 8 (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)— … 10 Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings. 11 Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord. 12 These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed. 13 The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. … 15 They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. 16 But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness. 17 These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. 18 With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.

English (WEB)

1 But false prophets also arose among the people, as false teachers will also be among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying even the Master who bought them, bringing on themselves swift destruction. 2 Many will follow their immoral ways, and as a result, the way of the truth will be maligned. 3 In covetousness they will exploit you with deceptive words: whose sentence now from of old doesn’t linger, and their destruction will not slumber. 4 For if God didn’t spare angels when they sinned, but cast them down to Tartarus, and committed them to pits of darkness to be reserved for judgment; … 6 and turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them to destruction, having made them an example to those who would live in an ungodly way, 7 and delivered righteous Lot, who was very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked 8 (for that righteous man dwelling among them was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds), … 10 but chiefly those who walk after the flesh in the lust of defilement and despise authority. Daring, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignitaries, 11 whereas angels, though greater in might and power, don’t bring a slanderous judgment against them before the Lord. 12 But these, as unreasoning creatures, born natural animals to be taken and destroyed, speaking evil in matters about which they are ignorant, will in their destroying surely be destroyed, 13 receiving the wages of unrighteousness; people who count it pleasure to revel in the daytime, spots and defects, reveling in their deceit while they feast with you; … 15 Forsaking the right way, they went astray, having followed the way of Balaam the son of Beor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing; 16 but he was rebuked for his own disobedience. A speechless donkey spoke with a man’s voice and stopped the madness of the prophet. 17 These are wells without water, clouds driven by a storm, for whom the blackness of darkness has been reserved forever. 18 For, uttering great swelling words of emptiness, they entice in the lusts of the flesh, by licentiousness, those who are indeed escaping from those who live in error;

2 Peter 3:1–3, 17–18

Greek (SBLGNT)

1 Ταύτην ἤδη, ἀγαπητοί, δευτέραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπιστολήν, ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν, 2 μνησθῆναι τῶν προειρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων προφητῶν καὶ τῆς τῶν ἀποστόλων ὑμῶν ἐντολῆς τοῦ κυρίου καὶ σωτῆρος, 3 τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐν ἐμπαιγμονῇ ἐμπαῖκται κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι … 17 ὑμεῖς οὖν, ἀγαπητοί, προγινώσκοντες φυλάσσεσθε ἵνα μὴ τῇ τῶν ἀθέσμων πλάνῃ συναπαχθέντες ἐκπέσητε τοῦ ἰδίου στηριγμοῦ, 18 αὐξάνετε δὲ ἐν χάριτι καὶ γνώσει τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος. ἀμήν.

English (BSB)

1 Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking 2 by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles. 3 Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. … 17 Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. 18 But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

English (WEB)

1 This is now, beloved, the second letter that I have written to you; and in both of them I stir up your sincere mind by reminding you 2 that you should remember the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior, 3 knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts … 17 You therefore, beloved, knowing these things beforehand, beware, lest being carried away with the error of the wicked, you fall from your own steadfastness. 18 But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.

Glossary of Greek and Theological Terms

Greek words are listed by transliteration, with the Greek form and the verse in Jude where it appears. Lexical summaries draw on Abbott-Smith’s Manual Greek Lexicon of the New Testament (1922) unless noted.

Greek words

agapē (ἀγάπη), vv. 2, 12, 21. “Love.” In the plural (v. 12), “love feasts,” the community’s shared meals. See Chapter 6.

agapētoi (ἀγαπητοί), vv. 3, 17, 20. “Beloved,” Jude’s address to his readers.

agalliasis (ἀγαλλίασις), v. 24. “Exultation, exuberant joy.”

akarpos (ἄκαρπος), v. 12. “Fruitless.”

alogos (ἄλογος), v. 10. “Without reason”; τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα, “irrational animals.”

amōmos (ἄμωμος), v. 24. “Without blemish,” used of sacrificial animals, and morally “faultless.”

antilogia (ἀντιλογία), v. 11. “Contradiction, dispute, rebellion.” In the LXX it is used for the “water of contention” (Meribah).

anydros (ἄνυδρος), v. 12. “Waterless.”

aphobōs (ἀφόβως), v. 12. “Without fear,” here meaning without reverence.

apodiorizō (ἀποδιορίζω), v. 19. “To mark off; to make divisions.” NT hapax.

aptaistos (ἄπταιστος), v. 24. “Without stumbling, sure-footed.” NT hapax.

archangelos (ἀρχάγγελος), v. 9. “Archangel, chief messenger” (LSV). Used of Michael.

archē (ἀρχή), v. 6. “Beginning; rule, domain.” The angels’ assigned position (LSV “principality”).

asebēs, asebeia, asebeō (ἀσεβής, ἀσέβεια, ἀσεβέω), vv. 4, 15, 18. “Impious/ungodly,” “impiety,” “to act impiously.” Jude’s key description of the intruders.

aselgeia (ἀσέλγεια), v. 4. “Licentiousness, shameless excess.”

atheteō (ἀθετέω), v. 8. “To set aside, reject.”

aidios (ἀΐδιος), v. 6. “Everlasting.”

aiōn, aiōnios (αἰών, αἰώνιος), vv. 7, 13, 21, 25. “Age” and “age-long, eternal.” The LSV renders αἰώνιος “continuous.”

blasphēmeō, blasphēmia (βλασφημέω, βλασφημία), vv. 8–10. “To slander, revile”; “slander.” Used of abusive speech against anyone, not only against God.

deigma (δεῖγμα), v. 7. “A specimen, example (as a warning).” NT hapax.

despotēs (δεσπότης), v. 4. “Master, owner, sovereign.” Used of Jesus.

diabolos (διάβολος), v. 9. “Slanderer, accuser; the Devil.”

diakrinomai (διακρίνομαι), vv. 9, 22. ‘To dispute’ (v. 9) or ‘to doubt, waver’ (v. 22).

dikē (δίκη), v. 7. “Justice; the penalty carried out.”

doulos (δοῦλος), v. 1. “Slave, servant.” Also an honorific (“servant of the LORD”).

doxa, doxai (δόξα, δόξαι), vv. 8, 24, 25. “Glory”; in the plural (v. 8), “glorious ones,” that is, angels.

ekporneuō (ἐκπορνεύω), v. 7. “To give oneself up to sexual immorality.” NT hapax.

ekrizoō (ἐκριζόω), v. 12. “To uproot.”

eleos, eleaō (ἔλεος, ἐλεάω), vv. 2, 21, 22, 23. “Mercy”; “to show mercy.” In the LXX ἔλεος chiefly translates Hebrew ḥesed.

elenchō (ἐλέγχω), v. 15. “To expose, convict.”

empaiktēs (ἐμπαίκτης), v. 18. “Scoffer, mocker.” In the NT only here and 2 Pet 3:3.

enypniazomai (ἐνυπνιάζομαι), v. 8. “To dream.” In the LXX, used of the false prophet as “dreamer” (Deut 13).

epagōnizomai (ἐπαγωνίζομαι), v. 3. “To contend for.” NT hapax.

epaphrizō (ἐπαφρίζω), v. 13. “To foam up.” NT hapax.

epithymia (ἐπιθυμία), vv. 16, 18. “Desire, craving.”

epoikodomeō (ἐποικοδομέω), v. 20. “To build upon.”

gongystēs (γογγυστής), v. 16. “Grumbler, murmurer.” NT hapax.

hagioi (ἅγιοι), vv. 3, 14. “Holy ones”: God’s people (v. 3) or angels (v. 14).

hagiōtatos (ἁγιώτατος), v. 20. “Most holy.” The only superlative of ἅγιος in the NT.

hapax (ἅπαξ), vv. 3, 5. “Once, once for all.”

harpazō (ἁρπάζω), v. 23. “To seize, snatch.”

hyperonkos (ὑπέρογκος), v. 16. “Swollen, excessive; arrogant (of speech).”

hypechō (ὑπέχω), v. 7. “To undergo, suffer (a penalty).” NT hapax.

katenōpion (κατενώπιον), v. 24. “Before, in the presence of.”

klētos (κλητός), v. 1. “Called.”

koinos (κοινός), v. 3. “Common, shared.”

kratos (κράτος), v. 25. “Power, dominion.” Common in doxologies.

kyriotēs (κυριότης), v. 8. “Lordship, dominion.”

megalōsynē (μεγαλωσύνη), v. 25. “Greatness, majesty.”

mempsimoiros (μεμψίμοιρος), v. 16. “Complaining of one’s lot, querulous.” NT hapax.

metatithēmi (μετατίθημι), v. 4. “To change, transfer; to turn one thing into a pretext for another.”

miainō (μιαίνω), v. 8. “To defile.”

oikētērion (οἰκητήριον), v. 6. “Dwelling, habitation.”

ouai (οὐαί), v. 11. “Woe!” The prophetic announcement of judgment.

paradidōmi (παραδίδωμι), v. 3. “To hand over, deliver.” The technical term for passing on tradition.

parapherō (παραφέρω), v. 12. “To carry away.”

pareisdyō (παρεισδύω), v. 4. “To slip in secretly.” NT hapax.

phthinopōrinos (φθινοπωρινός), v. 12. “Of late autumn.” NT hapax.

phylassō (φυλάσσω), v. 24. “To guard, protect.” Near synonym of τηρέω.

physikōs (φυσικῶς), v. 10. “Naturally, by instinct.” NT hapax.

planē (πλάνη), v. 11. “Error, deception, wandering.”

planētēs (πλανήτης), v. 13. “Wanderer”; ἀστέρες πλανῆται, “wandering stars.” The source of English “planet.” NT hapax.

plēthynō (πληθύνω), v. 2. “To multiply.” πληθυνθείη: “may it be multiplied” (optative).

poimainō (ποιμαίνω), v. 12. “To shepherd, tend.”

prographō (προγράφω), v. 4. “To write beforehand.”

psychikos (ψυχικός), v. 19. “Natural, soulish, unspiritual.”

sklēros (σκληρός), v. 15. “Hard, harsh”; “harsh words.”

sōtēr (σωτήρ), v. 25. “Savior.” A title also given to kings and emperors in the Greco-Roman world.

spilas (σπιλάς), v. 12. “Reef, rock in the sea”; in later Greek, “stain.” NT hapax. See Chapter 6.

spiloō (σπιλόω), v. 23. “To stain, defile.”

syneuōcheomai (συνευωχέομαι), v. 12. “To feast together.” In the NT only here and 2 Pet 2:13.

tēreō (τηρέω), vv. 1, 6, 13, 21. “To keep, guard, preserve.” Jude’s key word.

zophos (ζόφος), vv. 6, 13. “Deep gloom,” associated with the underworld.

Grammatical and theological terms

Aorist. A Greek verb form that presents an action as a whole, without reference to its duration.

Canon. The list of books a community recognizes as Scripture.

Critical text. A Greek text reconstructed by editors from the manuscripts in order to approximate the earliest recoverable text (for example, NA28, SBLGNT).

Byzantine text / Majority Text. The form of the Greek text found in the majority of (mostly later) manuscripts, edited by Robinson and Pierpont among others.

Doxology. A formula ascribing glory to God.

Etymological fallacy. The mistake of assuming that a word’s origin or component parts determine its meaning in use.

Hapax legomenon (plural hapax legomena). A word that occurs only once in a given body of literature, here the New Testament.

LXX (Septuagint). The Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, used widely by Greek-speaking Jews and early Christians.

Optative. A Greek verb mood used for wishes and prayers. It is rare in the New Testament.

Participle. A verbal adjective (“having been loved,” “praying”).

Perfect tense. A Greek tense presenting a completed action with continuing results.

Pre-existence (of Christ). The belief that the Son existed before his human birth.

Prophetic aorist. The use of a past tense to describe a future event as certain.

Pseudepigrapha. Ancient Jewish (and Christian) writings attributed to biblical figures, such as 1 Enoch and the Testament of Moses.

Pseudonymity. Writing under another person’s name.

Second Temple Judaism. Judaism from the rebuilding of the temple (late sixth century BC) to its destruction in AD 70.

Targum. An Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew scriptures.

Textus Receptus (TR). The printed Greek text of the Reformation era, which underlies Tyndale, the Geneva Bible, and their successors.

Theophany. An appearance of God.

Type / typology. A person or event in Scripture understood as a pattern of later persons or events.

Watchers. In 1 Enoch, the angels who descended to earth and took human wives (Gen 6:1–4).

Bibliography

Every work listed here is in the public domain or under a free license, and every work listed was retrieved and read directly; the specific passages relied on were checked against it. Works that would have required permission to quote, and works that could not be consulted directly, have been removed from this edition (see “Sources not used” at the end). Full details of the verification process are in the project file research/source-ledger.md.

1. Manuscripts

Institut für Neutestamentliche Textforschung (INTF), Münster. New Testament Virtual Manuscript Room (NTVMR). Transcriptions of Jude in P72, P78, 01 (Sinaiticus), 02 (Alexandrinus), 03 (Vaticanus), 04 (Ephraemi Rescriptus), 018 (K), 020 (L), 044 (Ψ), and 1739, with manuscript metadata (dates). https://ntvmr.uni-muenster.de/. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Retrieved 6–7 November 2026.

Sources not used

Earlier drafts of this book referred to modern commentaries, lexicons, grammars, and studies, among them the commentaries of Richard Bauckham, Peter Davids, Gene Green, J. N. D. Kelly, Jerome Neyrey, Thomas Schreiner, and others; Bruce Metzger’s Textual Commentary; the BDAG lexicon; Daniel Wallace’s grammar; and studies by Tommy Wasserman, Duane Watson, and J. T. Milik. These works are valuable, but they are under copyright and could not be consulted directly for this edition, so every claim that depended on them has been removed or re-established from the free sources above.
